questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with acute onset of pain in his scrotum. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a swollen erythematous scrotum and the right testis has gone up. Cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right testicular torsion

The given clinical vignette along with negative cremasteric reflex and positive Deming's sign (right testes gone up) is suggestive of testicular torsion.

Etiology and risk factors-

* High investment of the tunica vaginalis(like a clapper in a bell). Most common cause.

* Inversion of the testis.

* Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis.

Clinical features of testicular torsion are - scrotal pain and swelling, erythema, negative cremasteric reflex, nausea, and vomiting, testis seems high in the scrotum and twisted cord can sometimes be palpated.

* Prehn’s Sign is used to differentiate the torsion of testis from acute epididymo orchitis. In the case of acute epididymo orchitis, the pain gets relieved on the elevation of the testis but not in torsion of testes.

* Deming’s sign: Spasm of the cremaster muscle and the cord twisting cause the affected testis to be positioned higher in torsion testes.

Doppler ultrasound scanning can confirm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis, but the false-positives are high.

Urgent scrotal exploration in case of doubtful diagnosis.  A transverse scrotal incision is taken. If the testis is viable, twisting is prevented by fixation with three non-absorbable sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe.

Differential diagnosis -

* Epididymo-orchitis - Here dysuria associated with the accompanying urinary infection is commonly present. In epididymo-orchitis elevation of the testis reduces the pain while it makes it worse in torsion.

* Torsion of a testicular appendage - Here the most common structure to twist is the appendix of the testis, which can be visible as a small dark spot. In most cases, it is indistinguishable from torsion testis. Hence in cases of doubt surgical exploration is done.
questions.learning: Right testicular torsion — The given clinical vignette along with negative cremasteric reflex and positive Deming's sign (right testes gone up) is suggestive of testicular torsion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Feature of angular cheilitis, stomatitis, and glossitis is seen in which vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency (ariboflavinosis) classically presents with a clinical triad of oral-mucocutaneous signs: angular cheilitis (painful cracks at the corners of the mouth), stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth lining), and glossitis (a swollen, "magenta-colored" tongue). These findings are often accompanied by seborrheic dermatitis and a sore throat. Niacin deficiency (Option A) causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). Cobalamin (Vitamin B12) deficiency (Option C) primarily causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological issues, although it can also cause glossitis. Vitamin C deficiency (Option D) causes scurvy, which is characterized by bleeding gums and petechiae. Riboflavin is essential for the function of FAD and FMN coenzymes in cellular energy metabolism. Deficiency is most common in populations with low intake of dairy products and meat. Treatment involves simple oral riboflavin supplementation and dietary improvement. While not life-threatening on its own, these oral signs are vital indicators of broader nutritional status in clinical practice

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: From which of the following substrates is cholesterol synthesized?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a vital structural component of cell membranes and a precursor for steroid hormones and bile acids. The entire 27-carbon structure of cholesterol is synthesized solely from Acetyl-CoA molecules. The pathway begins with the condensation of two Acetyl-CoA molecules to form acetoacetyl-CoA, eventually leading to the rate-limiting step catalyzed by HMG-CoA reductase. Malonyl-CoA (Option B) is the critical building block for fatty acid synthesis, not cholesterol. Phenylalanine (Option C) is an essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis and the tyrosine pathway. Oxaloacetate (Option D) is a key intermediate in the TCA cycle and gluconeogenesis. Because every single carbon atom in the cholesterol sterol ring is derived from the acetate units provided by Acetyl-CoA, it remains the definitive primary substrate for the entire biosynthetic pathway. This metabolic source is the target for statin therapy
questions.learning: Cholesterol is a vital structural component of cell membranes and a precursor for steroid hormones and bile acids. The entire 27-carbon structure of cholesterol is synthesized solely from Acetyl-CoA molecules.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following should be the treatment of choice for renal cell carcinoma with tumor less than 4 cm in size?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

Partial nephrectomy (also known as nephron-sparing surgery) is the treatment of choice for tumors <4 cm.

Indications for partial nephrectomy:

• Tumors < 4cm
• Well-selected tumors between 4-7 cm
• Bilateral tumors
• Tumor in solitary kidneys
• Patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction.

Recently, partial nephrectomy is also increasingly being performed for stage T1b tumors.

Treatment of renal cell carcinoma:

RCC is a radio and chemoresistant tumor.

Staging
Description
Management

Stage 1
Tumor <7 cm, confined to the kidney
Partial nephrectomy

Stage 2
Tumor >7 cm, confined to the kidney
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 3
Tumor extends into the major veins or adrenal gland with intact Gerota’s fascia or regional lymph nodes involved.
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 4
Tumor invades beyond Gerota fascia (including contiguous extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland)

• Debulking surgery
• mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus, sirolimus
• Tyrosine kinase inhibitors: sunitinib, sorafenib

Radical nephrectomy consists of the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes. The adrenal gland is no longer removed except in cases of obvious tumor involvement. Lymphadenectomy is indicated only in high-risk patients with large primary tumors and enlarged lymph nodes.

Cryoablation is indicated in the T1a stage of RCC if surgery cannot be performed. It is also indicated in advanced/metastatic tumors.

Note: Sunitinib and sorafenib are also used in GIST and hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A tumor in the anterior pituitary pressing on the optic chiasma will present as a case of ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bitemporal hemianopia

A lesion in the optic chiasma will present as bitemporal hemianopia, due to the decussation of nasal fibres which are affected.

Other notable defects:

* Pie in the sky defects

* Superior quadrantic hemianopia

* Involvement of Meyer’s loop - inferior fibers of optic radiations

* Contralateral temporal lobe

* Pie in the floor defects

* Inferior quadrantic hemianopia

* Involvement of Baum’s loop - superior fibers of optic radiations

* Contralateral parietal lobe

* Homonymous hemianopia

* Involvement of retrochiasmal regions such as optic tract, geniculate body, optic radiations.

* Sparing of the macula and more congruous field defect (both sides have the same extent of field loss) when the occipital cortex is involved.

Pearl PF0246: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient presented with pain on the left side of the chest. On examination, there was dullness on percussion on left infra-axillary area. X-ray Chest showed left opaque hemithorax. Which one of the following is an indication for tube thoracentesis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural fluid glucose < 60 mg/dL

• The patient has a left-sided pleural effusion causing dullness to percussion and an opaque hemithorax. Tube thoracostomy (intercostal chest tube drainage) is indicated when the pleural fluid suggests a complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema, particularly when the pleural fluid glucose is <60 mg/dL.
• A low pleural fluid glucose indicates high metabolic activity of bacteria and inflammatory cells and impaired glucose transport across the inflamed pleura.

Why not the other options?

• A. Straw-coloured fluid: Common in uncomplicated pleural effusions and does not itself indicate chest-tube drainage.
• B. Pleural fluid pH >7.2: A pH >7.20 generally argues against a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage. pH <7.20 is the important threshold.
• D. Pleural fluid LDH <600 IU/L: A low LDH does not indicate complicated infection. Markedly elevated LDH supports an inflammatory/exudative process.
questions.learning: Pleural fluid glucose 7.2: A pH >7.20 generally argues against a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage. pH <7.20 is the important threshold. • D.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a defense mechanism?
questions.explanation: Defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies used by the mind to cope with anxiety and protect the self. Replacement is not a recognized psychological defense mechanism in standard psychoanalytic theory. Sublimation (Option A) is a mature defense mechanism where socially unacceptable impulses are transformed into socially acceptable actions. Displacement (Option B) involves redirecting an emotional impulse from its original target to a less threatening one. Altruism (Option D) is a mature defense where one deals with conflict by meeting the needs of others. Other common mechanisms include denial, projection, and reaction formation. Recognizing these mechanisms is essential in psychiatry and clinical practice to understand how patients cope with trauma and emotional stress. While "replacement" might describe a simple substitution in behavior, it does not fulfill the theoretical definition of an unconscious ego defense. **************
questions.learning: Defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies used by the mind to cope with anxiety and protect the self. Replacement is not a recognized psychological defense mechanism in standard psychoanalytic theory.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with features of lethargy, and poor oral intake. On examination, a cataract was seen. Urine Benedict's test was positive but negative for Glucose. What will be the enzyme deficiency in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The given clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with lethargy, and poor oral intake, with examination revealing a cataract and urine benedict's test was positive but negative for glucose, is suggestive of classical galactosemia and enzyme deficient is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to uridine diphosphate galactose. This leads to the accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain.

Clinical features:

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.

* Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataracts.

* Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

In uridyl transferase deficiency, the epimerase is present in adequate amounts, so that the galactosemic individual can still form UDPGal from glucose. This explains how normal growth and development of affected children can occur despite the galactose-free diets.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and mucic acid test are positive. Direct enzyme assay using erythrocytes establishes the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

Other options:

Option A: Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme, involved in maintaining intracellular glucose concentration by catalysing the first step in glucose metabolism, i.e., phosphorylation of intracellular glucose.  Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature.

Option B: Galactokinase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. Only cataract is seen in the deficiency of this enzyme because galactose-1-phosphate is not formed. Hence no toxic effects of this compound are manifested.

Option D: Phosphofructokinase is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and is necessary for the ATP-dependent conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-diphosphate. Tauri's disease is type VII glycogen storage disorder that results due to the deficiency of phosphofructokinase.
questions.learning: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase — The given clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with lethargy, and poor oral intake, with examination revealing a cataract and urine benedict's test was positive but negative for glucose, is suggestive of…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a case of face presentation during labor, which diameter is seen?
questions.explanation: In face presentation, the fetal head is in a state of complete extension, making the face the presenting part with the chin (mentum) as the denominator. The engaging diameter in a fully extended head is the submentobregmatic diameter, which measures approximately 9.5 cm. This diameter allows for a favorable vaginal delivery if the mentum is in an anterior position. Mentobregmatic (Option A) refers to a 13.5 cm diameter seen in brow presentation, which is the largest diameter and often leads to obstructed labor. Suboccipitobregmatic (Option B) is the 9.5 cm diameter associated with a well-flexed vertex presentation, which is the most common and favorable for normal delivery. Occipitofrontal (Option C) is a 11.5 cm diameter found in a deflexed vertex presentation. Consequently, the submentobregmatic diameter is the specific anatomical landmark for a face presentation
questions.learning: In face presentation, the fetal head is in a state of complete extension, making the face the presenting part with the chin (mentum) as the denominator.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient is found to have elevated blood pressure along with a reduced heart rate. Which physiological mechanism most likely explains this response?
questions.explanation: The physiological response of a decreased heart rate (bradycardia) in response to high blood pressure (hypertension) is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex. High pressure stretches baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, which send increased signals to the medulla. The medulla responds by increasing parasympathetic (vagus) outflow and inhibiting sympathetic outflow, leading to a drop in heart rate and systemic vasodilation. Inhibition of baroreceptors (Option B) occurs during hypotension, resulting in compensatory tachycardia. The Bezold-Jarisch reflex (Option C) causes bradycardia and hypotension but is typically triggered by ventricular ischemia, not high blood pressure. Chemoreceptors (Option D) primarily respond to hypoxia and hypercapnia, generally leading to sympathetic activation and increased heart rate. The baroreceptor reflex is the body's fastest-acting mechanism for short-term blood pressure stability, such as during positional changes. This reflex helps counteract hypertension to maintain internal homeostasis
questions.learning: The physiological response of a decreased heart rate (bradycardia) in response to high blood pressure (hypertension) is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-month-old child presented with umbilical discharge. Abdomen examination was normal except for the below finding. The next step of management is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. USG Abdomen

The given clinical image is that of a congenital umbilical anomaly such as patent urachus, urachal cyst, and vitelline cyst (resulting from the persistence of omphalomesenteric duct). The next best step is the USG abdomen to diagnose if the anomaly is cystic, fibrous or fistula and it's connections.

Omphalomesenteric duct abnormalities: Vitello intestinal duct or omphalomesenteric duct is the connection between the yolk sac and the midgut during embryonic life, which eventually gets obliterated. The persistence of the vitellointestinal duct leads to various abnormalities depending on which part of the duct remains patent.

• Persistence of the proximal intestinal end of the duct leads to Meckel’s diverticula.
• Persistence of the distal end near the umbilicus leads to the umbilical polyp or sinus.
• Persistence of the distal end with mucus retention leads to the cyst, which may be associated with the intestine or the umbilicus by a fibrous band.
• A fully patent vitellointestinal duct can lead to an enterocutaneous fistula.

Patent urachus occurs due to the failure of urachus to obliterate, resulting in a connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

Urachal cyst occurs when the urachus fails to obliterate but there is no connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

The given image below shows a urachal cyst (UC) attached to Meckel’s diverticulum (MD) on one side and urinary bladder (UB) on the other side with a patent tract- urachus (U).
questions.learning: USG Abdomen — The given clinical image is that of a congenital umbilical anomaly such as patent urachus, urachal cyst, and vitelline cyst (resulting from the persistence of omphalomesenteric duct).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The given type of population pyramid indicates all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Developed countries

The given image shows an age pyramid/population pyramid with a broad base and tapering top. The age pyramid is plotted as a younger age at the bottom and older age at the top. Hence this age pyramid represents a higher young population. This pyramid is typical of developing countries, and not developed countries.

This type of pyramid also indicates an increasing population because of high young population reflecting high fertility.

Pearl PF1861: Population Pyramid

* The age or population pyramid is used to represent the age/sex structure of a population.

* Below is the age pyramid of India (2017).

* The age pyramid of India has a broad base and a tapering top, as it is with most developing countries.

* As a nation develops the lower portion of the pyramid will start constricting and the upper portion will start increasing.

* Developed countries usually will have a bulge in the middle with a narrow base, as shown below in the age pyramid of Switzerland.
questions.learning: Developed countries — The given image shows an age pyramid/population pyramid with a broad base and tapering top. The age pyramid is plotted as a younger age at the bottom and older age at the top.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a slowly progressive swelling around the wrist joint that has been increasing over the past three months. An X-ray image of the wrist is provided. Based on the clinical history and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteoclastoma, also known as Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) of the bone, is the most likely diagnosis. It typically occurs in young adults (aged 20–40) and is characteristically located in the epiphysis of long bones, most commonly the distal radius or distal femur. The X-ray shows the classic "soap bubble appearance"—an eccentric, purely lytic lesion that extends to the subchondral bone without a sclerotic rim. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) is a pediatric tumor that appears in the diaphysis with an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction. Osteosarcoma (Option B) usually presents with a "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle in the metaphysis. Osteochondroma (Option D) is a benign, bone-capped growth that protrudes from the bone surface (exostosis). GCT is locally aggressive and can occasionally metastasize to the lungs. Treatment usually involves thorough curettage of the tumor followed by bone grafting or the use of bone cement (polymethylmethacrylate) to reduce the risk of recurrence
questions.learning: Osteoclastoma, also known as Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) of the bone, is the most likely diagnosis. It typically occurs in young adults (aged 20–40) and is characteristically located in the epiphysis of long bones, most commonly the distal radius or distal femur.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In patients who are susceptible to refeeding syndrome, several electrolyte disturbances are commonly observed. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is NOT typically associated with refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is reintroduced too rapidly to severely malnourished patients. The physiological hallmark is a massive release of insulin in response to carbohydrates, which causes a rapid shift of electrolytes from the extracellular space into the cells. This leads to profound Hypophosphatemia (Option D, the most common and dangerous sign), Hypokalemia (Option A), and Hypomagnesemia. Hypocalcemia (Option C) can also occur secondary to magnesium depletion. Hyperkalemia (Option B) is not associated with refeeding syndrome; instead, the problem is a life-threatening deficiency of serum potassium. These electrolyte drops can cause cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and seizures. Clinicians must identify high-risk patients (e.g., those with anorexia nervosa, chronic alcoholism, or marasmus) and "start low and go slow" with caloric intake while vigilantly monitoring and replacing electrolytes. Hyperkalemia is more typical of conditions like acute renal failure or cell lysis syndromes, which are pathophysiologically distinct from the anabolic shift seen in refeeding

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man presents with gradually worsening drooping of the eyelids that becomes more pronounced by evening and improves after rest or in the morning. He also experiences easy fatigability that increases as the day progresses. The ptosis shows marked, temporary improvement following application of an ice pack over the eyes. Based on these features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fatigable ptosis (eyelid drooping that worsens with activity or as the day progresses) is the hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. The positive ice pack test (Option A) is highly suggestive; cold temperatures decrease acetylcholinesterase activity, allowing more acetylcholine to remain in the synaptic cleft, which briefly improves muscle strength. Huntington chorea (Option B) involves movement disorders and dementia. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) causes progressive muscle wasting and permanent weakness rather than diurnal fatigability. External ophthalmoplegia (Option D) refers to paralyzed eye muscles but is a descriptive sign that can be caused by MG, not a standalone diagnosis here. Therefore, the characteristic combination of worsening evening symptoms and improvement with cold/rest confirms Myasthenia Gravis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of fatigable ptosis (eyelid drooping that worsens with activity or as the day progresses) is the hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Integrin connects with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fibronectin

Integrin connects with fibronectin.

Integrins are transmembrane glycoproteins (integral proteins) that allow cells to attach to extracellular matrix constituents such as laminin, fibronectin and collagen. It helps in linking the intracellular cytoskeleton functionally and structurally with the outside world.
questions.learning: Fibronectin Integrin connects with fibronectin. Integrins are transmembrane glycoproteins (integral proteins) that allow cells to attach to extracellular matrix constituents such as laminin, fibronectin and collagen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presented to emergency with fever, agitation and delirium. She was on regular medication of Carbimazole 40 mg daily, but missed her doses for the last 2 days. Which of the following scoring systems would you like to do to assess severity of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Burch-Wartofsky score

The patient has fever, agitation, delirium, and recent discontinuation of carbimazole, suggesting thyroid storm, a life-threatening complication of severe thyrotoxicosis. The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) is the most widely used clinical scoring system to assess the likelihood and severity of thyroid storm.

Why is B correct?

• The Burch-Wartofsky score assigns points based on:

• Temperature
• Central nervous system manifestations (agitation, delirium, seizures, coma)
• Tachycardia
• Heart failure
• Atrial fibrillation
• Gastrointestinal/hepatic dysfunction
• Precipitating event (e.g., stopping antithyroid drugs, infection, surgery)

Interpretation:

• <25 → Thyroid storm unlikely
• 25–44 → Impending thyroid storm
• ≥45 → Highly suggestive of thyroid storm

Why not the other options?

• A. DAS 28 score: Measures disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis.
• C. Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS): Assesses disability in multiple sclerosis.
• D. Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score: Evaluates organ dysfunction in sepsis and critically ill patients, not thyroid storm.
questions.learning: Burch-Wartofsky score — The patient has fever, agitation, delirium, and recent discontinuation of carbimazole, suggesting thyroid storm, a life-threatening complication of severe thyrotoxicosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. What associated complication is shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scleromalacia perforans

Scleromalacia perforans is the associated complication of rheumatoid arthritis that is shown in the image.

Scleromalacia perforans is a specific type of necrotizing scleritis without inflammation, characterized by progressive scleral thinning. The uveal tissue appears to shine through it. Spontaneous perforation is a rare complication of the condition. It is typically seen in elderly women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. A yellowish patch of melting sclera can be seen. This is due to the obliteration of blood supply.

Clinical features include pain, photophobia, and lacrimation. The affected eye appears red. Medical management includes steroids and immunosuppressants. In severe cases, surgical treatment by scleral patch graft may be done.

Other options:

Option B - Ciliary staphyloma is used to describe the bulge of an area of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. Common causes include scleritis, developmental glaucoma, and end-stage primary or secondary glaucoma. Thinning of the sclera, secondary to perforating injury, can also result in the condition.

Option C - Coloboma is a congenital anomaly, that develops due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It is characterized by poorly developed uveal tissue. In some cases, it might be deficient. The lens, choroid, and retina may also be involved.

The image below shows coloboma of the right eyelid.

Option D - Malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva appears as a mass near the limbus. It can be pigmented or non-pigmented. It is usually seen in elderly patients. The choroid, iris, ciliary body, and eyelids can also develop the tumor.

The image below shows malignant melanoma of the choroid.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Components of the MELD (2016) score are all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Albumin

Albumin is not a component of the MELD (2016) score.

The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) is used as an indicator of short-term survival in patients with end-stage liver disease and to determine organ allocation priorities for liver transplantation. The components of the original MELD model were:

• Serum creatinine
• Serum bilirubin
• INR (international normalized ratio)

In 2016, it was modified to incorporate serum sodium (the MELD-Na score).

The latest MELD 3.0 scoring system has added two additional components:

• Serum albumin
• Female gender

Patients with high scores have poor prognoses without intervention and should therefore be prioritized for transplantation if eligible.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of these is not a test for the measurement of ovarian reserve?
options: Serum FSH in the early follicular phase
Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase

Ovarian reserve tests reflect quantity of remaining follicles. Day-2/3 FSH, AMH, and Antral Follicle Count are validated markers. Ovarian reserve refers to the quantity and functional capacity of the remaining ovarian follicles and predicts response to ovarian stimulation in infertility treatment. Estradiol (E2), though measured in the early follicular phase, is not a reliable ovarian-reserve indicator—levels fluctuate and can even appear normal despite diminished reserve by suppressing FSH. Hence option D is not a true ovarian reserve test.

1. Serum FSH (Day 2–3 of Cycle)

Measured in the early follicular phase (Day 2–3).

Principle

If ovarian reserve decreases → ovaries respond poorly → FSH increases due to reduced negative feedback.

| FSH Level | Interpretation

| --------- | --------------

| <10 IU/L | Normal ovarian reserve

| 10–15 IU/L | Reduced reserve

| >15 IU/L | Poor reserve

2. Antral Follicle Count (AFC)

Number of 2–10 mm follicles seen in ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound.

| AFC | Interpretation

| --- | --------------

| >15 | Good reserve

| 8–15 | Normal

| <5 | Poor ovarian reserve

3. Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)

Produced by:

Granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles.

Advantages

• Most reliable ovarian reserve marker
• Cycle independent
• Declines with age

| AMH Level | Interpretation

| --------- | --------------

| >3.5 ng/mL | High reserve / PCOS

| 1–3.5 ng/mL | Normal

| <1 ng/mL | Low ovarian reserve
questions.learning: Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase Ovarian reserve tests reflect quantity of remaining follicles. Day-2/3 FSH, AMH, and Antral Follicle Count are validated markers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A woman being treated with cetirizine for allergic rhinitis complains of excessive drowsiness. Which alternative antihistamine would be most suitable due to its minimal sedative effects?
questions.explanation: Cetirizine is a second-generation antihistamine that is generally non-sedating, but it can cause sleepiness in sensitive individuals. For such patients, Fexofenadine is the best alternative. Fexofenadine is also a second-generation agent but has even lower penetration into the central nervous system, resulting in minimal to no sedative effects. Hydroxyzine (Option A), Diphenhydramine (Option B), and Promethazine (Option D) are all first-generation H1 receptor antagonists. These drugs are highly lipophilic, cross the blood-brain barrier easily, and are well-known for their potent sedative and hypnotic properties, making them entirely inappropriate as non-drowsy alternatives. Therefore, for a patient requiring clear daytime cognitive function while managing allergies, fexofenadine is the standard clinical choice
questions.learning: Cetirizine is a second-generation antihistamine that is generally non-sedating, but it can cause sleepiness in sensitive individuals. For such patients, Fexofenadine is the best alternative.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Match the following

1) Hirschsprung's disease
A) MRCP

2) Posterior urethral valve
B) CT scan

3) Choledochal cyst
C) Rectal biopsy

4) Intussusception
D) Micturating cystourethrogram
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-C,2-D,3-A, 4-B

The correct option is 1-C,2-D,3-A, 4-B

• Hirschsprung's disease - Rectal biopsy
• Posterior urethral valve - Micturating cystourethrogram
• Choledochal cyst - MRCP
• Intussusception - CT scan

Hirschsprung's disease:

• Rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of Hirschsprung’s disease. The affected part shows the absence of ganglion cells, hypertrophy of nerve trunks, and positive immunostaining for acetylcholinesterase.
• Water-soluble contrast enema: It shows the presence of a contracted aganglionic rectum, transition zone, and a dilated normally innervated colon.
• Anorectal manometry: It shows the failure of the relaxation of the internal anal sphincter.

Surgical intervention is the only definitive treatment available, and includes the Swenson, Duhamel, and Soave procedures.

Contrast enema image in Hirschsprung's disease-

Posterior urethral valve (PUV):

• Diagnosis of this condition is commonly made during the antenatal period with an ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder. Pulmonary hypoplasia secondary to oligohydramnios may be detected in some complicated cases. In cases that are not detected during the antenatal period, these children usually present with urinary infection in the neonatal period or with uremia and renal failure.
• The confirmatory investigation for PUV is a micturating/voiding cystourethrogram. It demonstrates poor bladder emptying and dilated posterior urethra.
• It is treated by cystoscopic resection or ablation of the valve.

Preoperative(a) and postoperative(b) micturating cystourethrogram images in a patient with PUV is shown below. The dilated posterior urethra seen in the first image is resolved in the second image after surgery.

Choledochal cyst:

• MRI/MRCP is highly useful to access the biliary anatomy especially the relation between the lower end of the bile duct and the pancreatic duct.
• Ultrasound is helpful to identify the presence of an abnormal cyst.
• CT scan can be used to delineate the extent of intrahepatic or extrahepatic dilatation

MRCP image showing multiple intrahepatic biliary duct cystic dilatations-

Intussusception:

CT scan is the investigation of choice. It may show the characteristic target sign.

USG findings in intussusception include:

• Target sign (also known as the doughnut sign)
• Pseudokidney sign
• Crescent in a doughnut sign

Barium enema shows the characteristic coiled spring appearance.

USG image showing the target sign:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with disorientation following a road traffic accident. CT scan shows no hemorrhage but reveals cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure. Which drug is appropriate for the initial management of increased intracranial pressure?
questions.explanation: In the emergency management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) due to cerebral edema following trauma, Mannitol is the gold-standard, first-line pharmacological intervention (Option B). Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that works by creating an osmotic gradient, drawing fluid from the brain tissue into the vascular space, thereby rapidly reducing brain volume and ICP. Furosemide (Option A) is a loop diuretic that can be used as an adjunct but is not the primary agent for ICP. Acetazolamide (Option C) is used for chronic conditions like idiopathic intracranial hypertension but is ineffective for acute post-traumatic edema. Glycerol (Option D) is an older oral osmotic agent with a slower onset and higher risk of metabolic side effects. Therefore, because of its rapid onset and proven efficacy in trauma settings, Mannitol is the definitive initial choice. It must be administered carefully while monitoring serum osmolality and renal function
questions.learning: In the emergency management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) due to cerebral edema following trauma, Mannitol is the gold-standard, first-line pharmacological intervention (Option B).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An X ray was taken which showed dilated bowel loops as given in the image below. Identify the segment involved.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Jejunum

The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction where the involved segment is the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel) which is characteristic of jejunal involvement. The gas bubbles trapped between the valvulae connivente give a string of beads appearance.

Radiological features of bowel obstruction

• Small bowel - The involved dilated segments are straight and usually centrally located.
• Jejunum - It is characterized by the presence of valvulae connivente with gas bubbles trapped between them. This gives a string of beads/ ladder effect.
• Ileum - The distal ileal obstruction is usually described as featureless.
• Caecum - A rounded gas shadow in the right iliac fossa is suggestive of caecal obstruction.
• Large bowel - The presence of haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction. Haustral folds are irregular and do not cross the entire diameter of the bowel. These are absent in the caecum.

In intestinal obstruction, fluid levels appear as the obstruction progresses. When the fluid levels are prominent, it indicates that the obstruction is advanced. The number of fluid levels also increases if the lesion is more distal.

The most reliable criterion for the diagnosis of small bowel obstruction is the transition zone, seen on CT imaging. It identifies a definite point of obstruction. Dilated small bowel loops are seen proximal to the site of obstruction and collapsed loops are seen distal to the obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements about claudication pain is not true?
options: Rest pain is seen more in the night
Pain in intermittent claudication comes at first step of walking.
The clinical stem does not reflect the site of peripheral arterial obstruction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pain in intermittent claudication comes at first step of walking.

Pain in intermittent claudication is brought on by walking and doesnot start with the first step of walking.

Peripheral artery occlusion or stenosis is predominantly caused by atherosclerosis or atheroma (Option C) and thromboembolic disease. The resulting stenosis or occlusion produces signs and symptoms related to the organ that is supplied by the affected artery. Such occlusion in the lower limbs presents with claudication pain, rest pain, and gangrene. Though the muscle groups affected by claudication are present at one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease, the clinical stem does not reflect the exact site of the peripheral arterial obstruction. (Option D)

Intermittent claudication pain is a feature of arterial stenosis or occlusion that occurs due to the anaerobic metabolism occurring in the muscle. Claudication pain may be of different types and can be differentiated as follows:

• Vascular (intermittent) claudication pain is brought on by walking and is relieved by rest within 5 minutes. (Option B)
• Claudication pain present on taking the first step of walking is classical for osteoarthritis.
• Neurogenic claudication occurs with changes in the position of the back such as bending forward and straightening. It takes more time to be relieved by rest (more than 5 minutes). It may be seen in cases of nerve compression from lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse or spinal stenosis.

Rest pain occurs when the occlusive disease progresses in severity and anaerobic respiration occurs even at rest. Though this pain is present during the day, it is exacerbated on lying down at night (Option A) due to loss of gravity dependant perfusion of the foot. This may be relieved by hanging the foot out of the bed to restore the gravitational effects.
questions.learning: Pain in intermittent claudication comes at first step of walking. Pain in intermittent claudication is brought on by walking and doesnot start with the first step of walking.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought with evisceration of bowel loops from a defect in the abdominal wall to the right of the umbilicus. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastroschisis

The most probable diagnosis for the evisceration of bowel loops, coming out of a defect in the abdominal wall to the right of the umbilicus is gastroschisis. It occurs when there is a failure in the closure of the body wall in the abdominal region.

Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly) allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines. The abdomen is wrapped with transparent plastic wrap, a nasogastric tube is inserted, and fluid resuscitation is initiated.

Depending on the severity, primary closure under general anesthesia or gradual reduction using a preformed silo may be performed. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.

Other options:

Option A: In omphalocele bowel loops fail to return from the physiologic umbilical hernia. Since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, the omphalocele is also covered by the amnion.

Option B: Congenital umbilical hernia occurs due to the incomplete closure or weakness of the muscular umbilical ring. It presents as a soft swelling covered by skin that protrudes during activities like crying, coughing, or straining, and it can be easily pushed back through the fibrous ring at the umbilicus. The hernia contains the omentum or segments of the small intestine.

The image below shows an umbilical hernia:

Option D: Ectopia vesicae/bladder exstrophy is a congenital abnormality that occurs when the lower abdominal wall does not form properly and the bladder protrudes from the abdominal wall, with its mucosa exposed.

The image below shows ectopia vesicae/bladder exstrophy
questions.learning: Gastroschisis — The most probable diagnosis for the evisceration of bowel loops, coming out of a defect in the abdominal wall to the right of the umbilicus is gastroschisis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman is diagnosed with fetal growth restriction on ultrasound during routine evaluation. The diagnosis of early-onset FGR is considered based on gestational age and biometric parameters. Which of the following best defines early-onset fetal growth restriction?
options: Diagnosis before 32 weeks with estimated fetal weight (EFW) or abdominal circumference (AC) <10th percentile
Diagnosis before 32 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile
Diagnosis before 34 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile
Diagnosis after 34 weeks with EFW or AC <10th percentile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diagnosis before 32 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile

Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) refers to a fetus that has failed to achieve its genetically determined growth potential and is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality.

Early-Onset FGR

• Diagnosed before 32 weeks gestation
• Defined by:

• EFW or AC <3rd percentile, or
• Associated severe Doppler abnormalities

Late-Onset FGR

• Diagnosed at or after 32 weeks
• More commonly associated with milder placental insufficiency
• Often defined using EFW/AC <10th percentile with supportive Doppler findings

Clinical Significance of Early-Onset FGR

• Usually due to severe placental insufficiency
• Strongly associated with:

• Preeclampsia
• Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler
• Preterm delivery
• Increased perinatal mortality

Early-onset FGR requires:

• Serial growth scans
• Umbilical artery Doppler studies
• MCA and ductus venosus Doppler assessment
• Timely delivery based on fetal condition
questions.learning: Diagnosis before 32 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) refers to a fetus that has failed to achieve its genetically determined growth potential and is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mlU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose methotrexate

This patient has an unruptured ectopic pregnancy, suggested by:

• Amenorrhea
• Abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding
• Elevated β-hCG
• Adnexal mass containing a gestational sac without cardiac activity

She is an ideal candidate for medical management with single-dose methotrexate because:

• Hemodynamically stable
• Ectopic mass <3.5–4 cm
• No fetal cardiac activity
• β-hCG relatively low (<5000 mIU/mL)

Methotrexate:

• Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
•

Stops rapidly dividing trophoblastic tissue

•

Avoids surgery

• Preserves fallopian tube and fertility

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Expectant management is reserved for falling β-hCG levels and very small ectopic pregnancies
• C. Salpingectomy is used for rupture, instability, or failed medical therapy
• D. Tubal milking has high risk of persistent trophoblastic tissue
