questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient with lymphatic filarisis is being managed as shown in the image below. What is the level of prevention done here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Disability limitation

The image shows an established case of chronic lymphatic filariasis, where hygiene is being maintained to prevent further disability by secondary bacterial infection. Disability limitation is a mode of intervention in tertiary prevention.

Other options:

Option A: Specific protection is a mode of intervention in primary prevention which aims at limiting the number of cases of a particular disease. This includes immunization, use of specific nutrients, chemoprophylaxis, accident protection, and avoidance of allergens.

Option C: Primary prevention is a level of prevention which is defined as action taken prior to the onset of a disease, which removes the possibility that a disease will ever occur. It is accomplished by measures designed to promote general health and well-being.

Option D: Health promotion is a mode of intervention in primary prevention, and is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and improve health. Health promotion may be achieved through health education, environmental modification, nutritional interventions or lifestyle changes.
questions.learning: Disability limitation — The image shows an established case of chronic lymphatic filariasis, where hygiene is being maintained to prevent further disability by secondary bacterial infection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the United Nations definition of a vital events registration system, vital events include which of the following? 1. Foetal deaths 2. School admissions 3. Legal separations 4. College graduations Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

A Vital Registration System (Civil Registration System) is defined by the United Nations as the continuous, permanent, compulsory, and universal recording of vital events occurring in a population. It provides the legal basis for vital statistics and demographic planning.

• 1. Foetal deaths ✓

• Fetal deaths (stillbirths) are recognized vital events and are included in the civil registration system.

• 2. School admissions ✗

• School admissions are administrative events, not vital events.

• 3. Legal separations ✓

• Legal separation is a vital event recognized by the UN because it affects civil status.

• 4. College graduations ✗

• Educational achievements are not vital events.
questions.learning: 1 and 3 A Vital Registration System (Civil Registration System) is defined by the United Nations as the continuous, permanent, compulsory, and universal recording of vital events occurring in a population.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A tourist with a travel history to India presents with complaints of abdominal pain and multiple episodes of watery diarrhea. He reports having food at a local restaurant the previous night. Which of the following antidiarrheal agents is used in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loperamide

The given clinical scenario of a tourist with abdominal pain, and multiple episodes of diarrhea following food intake at an unhygienic place is suggestive of the traveller’s diarrhea, most commonly caused by Enterotoxigenic E.Coli. The antidiarrheal agent used in the given scenario is loperamide.

Loperamide is generally indicated in non-infective diarrhea, but it is also given as an anti-diarrheal agent in traveller's diarrhea in addition to antibiotics.

It is an opioid receptor agonist and slows intestinal motility by direct effects on the circular and longitudinal muscles. It reduces fecal volume and increases viscosity. It is used in traveller's diarrhea for symptomatic treatment in conjunction with antibiotics. It is avoided in patients with dysentery.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a somatostatin analog effective in treating severe secretory diarrhea that occurs due to hormone-secreting tumors in the GIT and pancreas. Its use is limited in traveller's diarrhea.

Option C: Rifaximin is an antibiotic used in the treatment of traveller's diarrhea. It is an alternative to Azithromycin due to poor absorption.

Option D: Bismuth subsalicylate is an over-the-counter (OTC) preparation used as an antidiarrheal agent. It is used in the treatment of traveller's diarrhea but is not preferred over loperamide due to a requirement for large doses, and salicylate toxicity, especially in high-risk groups (pregnancy, children, and individuals who take aspirin).
questions.learning: Loperamide — The given clinical scenario of a tourist with abdominal pain, and multiple episodes of diarrhea following food intake at an unhygienic place is suggestive of the traveller’s diarrhea, most commonly caused by Enterotoxigenic E.Coli.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient comes with a history of clean-cut injury which is not lacerated. He says that he received his last dose of tetanus vaccination about 10 years ago. What should be given next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose tetanus toxoid

A single dose of tetanus toxoid is given as the wound is clean and the last dose was received more than 10 years ago.
questions.learning: Single dose tetanus toxoid — A single dose of tetanus toxoid is given as the wound is clean and the last dose was received more than 10 years ago.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: New A pregnant lady presented to the casualty after she was scratched by a street dog while she was walking on the streets an hour ago. She has only some minor abrasions with no bleeding. What treatment should be offered to her?
options: No treatment as she is pregnant now
Local wound cleaning and rabies vaccine
Local wound cleaning, Rabies vaccine and Immunoglobulins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Local wound cleaning and rabies vaccine

This case is classified under WHO category II since there was no bleeding present at the site of the dog bite and she has to be given Rabies vaccine along with local wound cleaning.

Since Rabies is a lethal disease, there is no contraindication for post-exposure prophylaxis following high-risk exposures, even in pregnancy, infancy, immunocompromised patients, and even in children with AIDS/HIV.

Note:

Patients taking chloroquine have to be given the vaccine intramuscularly as there is a reduced response to the intradermal route.

For pre-exposure prophylaxis, previous allergic reaction to any components of the vaccine is a contraindication.

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment
questions.learning: Local wound cleaning and rabies vaccine — This case is classified under WHO category II since there was no bleeding present at the site of the dog bite and she has to be given Rabies vaccine along with local wound cleaning.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney? 1. It is the most common sporadic renal tumor 2. Associated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3 3. Arises from distal convoluted tubule 4. Cells show intracellular accumulation of PAS + Diastase sensitive substance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common sporadic renal tumor. It typically arises from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal tubule. Tumor cells appear “clear” due to intracellular accumulation of glycogen and lipids, which are PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive (glycogen).

Although ccRCC is classically associated with chromosome 3p deletion (VHL gene mutation), the key diagnostic features are:

• Most common RCC subtype
• Clear cytoplasm due to glycogen/lipid accumulation

Thus, statements 1 and 4 are correct.
questions.learning: 1, 4 Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common sporadic renal tumor. It typically arises from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal tubule.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) due to contraceptive failure can be done up to:
questions.explanation: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act (India), termination of pregnancy due to failure of contraception is permitted up to 20 weeks of gestation. This applies to both married and unmarried women as per recent amendments. Between 20–24 weeks, MTP is allowed only under specific conditions (such as rape survivors, minors, or other special categories) and requires approval by two registered medical practitioners. Contraceptive failure alone is not sufficient for termination beyond 20 weeks. Why other options are incorrect: (B) 24 weeks: Allowed only for special categories, not routine contraceptive failure (C) 32 weeks: Not permitted under MTP Act (D) 12 weeks: Earlier limit for single doctor opinion, but not the maximum limit Therefore, for contraceptive failure, the legal limit is 20 weeks
questions.learning: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act (India), termination of pregnancy due to failure of contraception is permitted up to 20 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with lower abdominal pain. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) performed over two days reveals a left adnexal cystic mass with a cogwheel appearance, incomplete septa, and no vascular flow on Doppler imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydrosalphinx

Transvaginal ultrasound findings of a left adnexal cystic mass, with incomplete septa and no vascular flow along with the complaints of lower abdominal pain suggest the diagnosis of hydrosalpinx.

A hydrosalpinx is a chronic cystic swelling of the fallopian tube that forms after a distal tubal obstruction. The cogwheel appearance and incomplete septa described in the ultrasound can correspond to the appearance of a hydrosalpinx. The lack of vascular flow on Doppler imaging supports this diagnosis. The tubes are enormously distended due to filling with clear serous fluid and become retort-shaped. On histology, the tubal plicae appear flattened. The interstitial end of the tube is open whereas the fimbrial end is indrawn and closed. This permits the dye to enter but not exit the tube during HSG.

It is caused due to:

• Pelvic inflammatory disease
• Endometriosis
• Tuberculosis - tubercular salpingitis may also cause tobacco-pouch appearance, lead pipe appearance and pyosalpinx
• Fallopian tube neoplasms (rare)

It can be an incidental finding during a pelvic exam or ultrasound. The patient may be asymptomatic, or present with infertility or chronic pelvic pain.

On HSG, it appears as terminal sacculation and occlusion of both fallopian tubes with a normal uterine cavity. Usually, a thin-walled, hypoechoic, cystic structure is seen. However, it may appear as multiple hyperechoic mural nodules around the inner circumference of the tube creating a 'beads on a string' appearance.

Treatment:

• Treat the underlying cause
• Laparoscopic salpingostomy - in mild disease
• IVF recommended for women with infertility and severe hydrosalpinx

Other options:

Option B: Malignant ovarian cyst: Malignant ovarian cysts can appear as complex masses with irregular shapes and internal vascularity.

Option C: Follicular cyst: A follicular cyst is a common type of ovarian cyst that occurs when a follicle fails to release an egg. It typically appears as a simple cyst on ultrasound.

Option D: Hemorrhagic cyst: A hemorrhagic cyst results from bleeding into a pre-existing cyst and often shows complex internal echoes and potentially some vascular flow on Doppler imaging.
questions.learning: Hydrosalphinx Transvaginal ultrasound findings of a left adnexal cystic mass, with incomplete septa and no vascular flow along with the complaints of lower abdominal pain suggest the diagnosis of hydrosalpinx.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the points labelled A, B, and C on the strength–duration curve shown in the image below.
options: A. Rheobase, B. Chronaxie, C. Utilization time
A. Chronaxie, B. Utilization time, C. Rheobase
A. Utilization time, B. Rheobase, C. Chronaxie
A. Rheobase, B. Utilization time, C. Chronaxie
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A. Rheobase, B. Chronaxie, C. Utilization time

The strength–duration curve describes the relationship between the minimum stimulus strength and the duration of stimulation required to excite a nerve or muscle. The three key parameters are rheobase, chronaxie, and utilization time, which are used to assess tissue excitability and detect nerve injury or denervation.

Why the labels are correct:

• A. Rheobase: Minimum stimulus strength of very long duration required to produce an action potential.
• B. Chronaxie: Minimum time required to excite a tissue using a stimulus of 2 × rheobase.
• C. Utilization time: Minimum duration required for a rheobase-strength stimulus to produce excitation.
questions.learning: Utilization time — The strength–duration curve describes the relationship between the minimum stimulus strength and the duration of stimulation required to excite a nerve or muscle.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Water hammer pulse is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic regurgitation

Water hammer pulse, also known as Corrigan’s pulse, is characterized by a sharp rise and a rapid fall-off and is seen in aortic regurgitation (AR) due to the fact that arterial pressure falls rapidly in late systole and early diastole.

In AR, the pulse pressure is widened due to systolic hypertension and decreased diastolic pressure. The diastolic pressure is measured at Korotkoff phase IV. In certain patients with AR or a combination of aortic stenosis (AS) and AR, the carotid arterial pulse may exhibit a bisferiens pattern, characterized by two systolic waves separated by a trough.

The apical impulse is heaving and displaced inferiorly. A diastolic thrill may be palpable along the left sternal border.

A2 is usually absent in AR. An early diastolic murmur can be auscultated in chronic AR. It is best heard in the third intercostal space along the left sternal edge.

Severe AS (Option A) would show pulsus parvus et tardus, characterized by the carotid pulse rising slowly to a delayed peak.

Chronic mitral regurgitation (Option D) shows a sharp, low volume upstroke due to reduced cardiac output and acute mitral regurgitation demonstrates narrow pulse pressure.
questions.learning: Aortic regurgitation Water hammer pulse, also known as Corrigan’s pulse, is characterized by a sharp rise and a rapid fall-off and is seen in aortic regurgitation (AR) due to the fact that arterial pressure falls rapidly in late systole and early diastole.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common deficiency observed after gastric bypass/bariatric surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron

Iron deficiency is the most common deficiency observed following gastric bypass or bariatric surgery. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, bypass procedures lead to or exacerbate an existing deficiency by impairing absorption. It is more common in the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD/DS) procedures than in sleeve gastrectomy (SG).
questions.learning: Iron Iron deficiency is the most common deficiency observed following gastric bypass or bariatric surgery. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, bypass procedures lead to or exacerbate an existing deficiency by impairing absorption.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids is likely to aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in the plasma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysine

Lysine would likely aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in plasma because it is a hydrophilic amino acid with a positively charged side chain. In proteins that exist in aqueous environments like blood plasma, hydrophilic amino acids tend to orient toward the outside surface where they can interact favorably with water. This arrangement forms part of the tertiary structure of globular proteins, where hydrophilic residues face outward while hydrophobic residues cluster in the interior.
questions.learning: Lysine Lysine would likely aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in plasma because it is a hydrophilic amino acid with a positively charged side chain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient sustains an injury on the lateral aspect of the knee. After a few days, he develops difficulty in walking due to dragging of foot, along with numbness over the upper lateral side of the leg and dorsum of the foot. Which of the following nerves is most commonly injured in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Common peroneal nerve

The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula on the lateral side of the knee, making it highly vulnerable to injury.

Damage causes foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion (deep peroneal nerve) and sensory loss over the upper lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (superficial peroneal nerve).
questions.learning: Common peroneal nerve — The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula on the lateral side of the knee, making it highly vulnerable to injury.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following can be seen intracellularly in hepatocytes except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Babesia

Babesia is an intracellular parasite of RBCs, not of the hepatocytes.

Its trophozoites invade the RBCs.

The liver is usually not affected as babesia lack an exoerythrocytic phase.
questions.learning: Babesia Babesia is an intracellular parasite of RBCs, not of the hepatocytes. The liver is usually not affected as babesia lack an exoerythrocytic phase.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released from SA node in response to increase in blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acetylcholine

When BP rises, the body tries to slow the heart down

An increase in blood pressure activates the baroreceptor reflex, increasing vagal output to the heart. Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine at the SA node, slowing heart rate.

↑ Blood pressure

↓

Baroreceptors activated (carotid sinus, aortic arch)

↓

Signals to medulla

↓

↑ Parasympathetic (vagal) output

↓

Acetylcholine released at SA node

↓

↓ Heart rate (bradycardia)

This parasympathetic response reduces cardiac output and helps normalize blood pressure. The SA node is primarily controlled by cholinergic vagal input in this reflex.

| System | Neurotransmitter | Effect on Heart

| ------ | ---------------- | ---------------

| Parasympathetic | Acetylcholine | ↓ HR

| Sympathetic | Norepinephrine | ↑ HR
questions.learning: Acetylcholine When BP rises, the body tries to slow the heart down An increase in blood pressure activates the baroreceptor reflex, increasing vagal output to the heart.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding a case-control study is incorrect?
options: It is typically a prospective study
It proceeds from effect to cause
Recall bias is an important limitation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is typically a prospective study

• A case-control study begins by identifying individuals who have a particular disease or outcome (cases) and comparing them with individuals without the disease (controls). Investigators then assess and compare their previous exposure to suspected risk factors.
• Thus, the classical direction of inquiry is:

• Disease/Effect → Previous exposure/Cause

• Case-control studies are conventionally described as retrospective studies because they usually look backward from an established outcome to determine prior exposure. Therefore, describing a case-control study as prospective is incorrect in the conventional exam context.

Why are the other statements correct?

• B. Proceeds from effect to cause: Correct. Subjects are selected according to outcome/disease status, and previous exposures are investigated.
• C. Recall bias is a major problem: Correct. Cases may remember previous exposures differently from controls, resulting in recall bias.
• D. Cost-effective: Correct. Case-control studies are generally quicker and less expensive than cohort studies and require fewer participants.

High-Yield Comparison:

| Feature | Case-Control Study | Cohort Study

| ------- | ------------------ | ------------

| Starts with | Disease/outcome | Exposure

| Direction | Effect → Cause | Cause → Effect

| Classical description | Retrospective | Prospective or retrospective

| Best suited for | Rare diseases | Rare exposures

| Main measure | Odds ratio | Relative risk

| Important bias | Recall bias | Loss to follow-up
questions.learning: It is typically a prospective study • — A case-control study begins by identifying individuals who have a particular disease or outcome (cases) and comparing them with individuals without the disease (controls).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient with elevated calcium and normal alkaline phosphatase undergoes a skull X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hypercalcemia (elevated calcium) and a normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level is highly characteristic of Multiple Myeloma. In this plasma cell malignancy, "punched-out" osteolytic lesions are created by increased osteoclast activity without an accompanying osteoblastic (bone-forming) response; therefore, ALP, which is a marker of osteoblast activity, remains normal. This contrasts with Paget's disease (Option B) or bone metastases from prostate cancer, where ALP is typically significantly elevated. Graves' disease (Option A) is a thyroid disorder and does not typically present with lytic skull lesions. Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML, Option D) primarily involves the bone marrow and blood counts, not focal osteolytic bone destruction. Skull X-rays in Multiple Myeloma classically show multiple, well-circumscribed lytic lesions. Diagnosis is further supported by the presence of an M-spike on protein electrophoresis and Bence-Jones proteinuria
questions.learning: The combination of hypercalcemia (elevated calcium) and a normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level is highly characteristic of Multiple Myeloma. In this plasma cell malignancy, "punched-out" osteolytic lesions are created by increased osteoclast activity…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a clinical manifestation of Parvovirus B19 infection?
options: Persistent anemia or pure red cell aplasia in immunodeficient individuals
Transient aplastic crisis in children with hemolytic anemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Febrile illness with petechial rash

The characteristic clinical manifestation of Parvovirus is febrile illness with an erythematous rash. Petechial rash is seen only in some patients.

Parvovirus B19 is the smallest single-stranded DNA virus belonging to the family Parvoviridae. It is a non-enveloped virus with an icosahedral capsid. The virus is primarily transmitted through respiratory secretions, such as saliva and respiratory droplets. It can also be transmitted vertically from mother to fetus during pregnancy, leading to congenital infection.

Clinical manifestations:

Erythema infectiosum (Fifth Disease): Characterized by a "slapped cheek" rash on the face, the most common manifestation of Parvovirus B19 infection. This is due to erythematous flushing of the cheeks. This is followed by a lacy, macular erythematous rash on the trunk and limbs. The rash typically resolves within 1-3 weeks but may recur with exposure to sunlight or heat.

Arthropathy: Transient arthritis, predominantly affecting the joints of the hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. Arthropathy typically occurs in adults, especially women, and may persist for several weeks to months.

Aplastic Crisis: In individuals with underlying hemolytic disorders, such as sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis, Parvovirus B19 infection can precipitate a transient aplastic crisis. This results in a severe reduction in red blood cell production, leading to anaemia.

Hydrops fetalis: Vertical transmission of Parvovirus B19 during pregnancy can lead to severe complications in the fetus, including hydrops fetalis.
Hydrops fetalis is characterised by fetal oedema, ascites, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion, often resulting in intrauterine death or neonatal complications.

Parvovirus B19 mainly attacks the erythroid progenitor cells and leads to transient arrest of erythropoiesis. However, immunocompromised individuals are at risk of persistent Parvovirus B19 infection which leads to chronic suppression of bone marrow, resulting in persistent anemia or pure red cell aplasia.

Diagnosing Parvovirus B19 infection is primarily based on clinical presentation and confirmed through serological testing, including detecting specific IgM antibodies. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays can also detect viral DNA in blood or other tissues.

The following image shows a slapped cheek appearance seen in Erythema infectiosum (Fifth Disease):

Note: This is a best-out-of-four type of question where all 4 options are factually correct. Petechial rash is seen in several viral infections including Parvovirus B19 infection. However, the characteristic rash of this infection is erythematous. This makes option D the best possible answer.
questions.learning: Febrile illness with petechial rash — The characteristic clinical manifestation of Parvovirus is febrile illness with an erythematous rash. Petechial rash is seen only in some patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old male, chronic heavy smoker, presented with breathlessness. On examination, pulse 96/min, BP 112/70 mm Hg and a pansystolic murmur showing Carvallo’s sign with murmur getting louder on deep inspiration. Which one of the following statements is true regarding examination of JVP in him?
options: C wave is attenuated and V wave is accentuated
V wave and C wave merge
V wave and C wave merge and Y descent is blunted
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. V wave and C wave merge

The patient has tricuspid regurgitation (TR), suggested by a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign). In TR, regurgitation of blood into the right atrium during systole produces giant C-V (CV) waves due to fusion of the C and V waves in the JVP.

Why not the other options?

• A. V wave is attenuated: Incorrect. V wave is markedly prominent in TR.
• B. C wave is attenuated and V wave is accentuated: Incorrect. The C and V waves fuse, forming a giant CV wave.
• D. V wave and C wave merge and Y descent is blunted: Incorrect. Y descent is brisk (prominent) in TR due to rapid right atrial emptying; a blunted Y descent is seen in cardiac tamponade.
questions.learning: V wave and C wave merge — The patient has tricuspid regurgitation (TR), suggested by a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A myopic patient presents with complaints of flashes of light and floaters. Ocular examination reveals a deep anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of myopia, sudden flashes (photopsia), and floaters is highly suggestive of a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). In highly myopic eyes, the elongated globe leads to retinal thinning and lattice degeneration, predisposing the patient to retinal tears. These breaks allow liquefied vitreous to pass into the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the pigment epithelium. A deep anterior chamber is common in high myopia due to the increased axial length. Exudative detachment (Option A) is characterized by "shifting fluid" without tears. Tractional detachment (Option C) occurs due to vitreoretinal bands pulling the retina, often without flashes or floaters. Central serous retinopathy (Option D) typically presents with metamorphopsia and central blurring in young males, rather than flashes. Therefore, RRD is the most probable diagnosis given the risk factors and acute symptoms
questions.learning: The combination of myopia, sudden flashes (photopsia), and floaters is highly suggestive of a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). In highly myopic eyes, the elongated globe leads to retinal thinning and lattice degeneration, predisposing the patient…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A chronic smoker was on nicotine replacement therapy and clonidine tablets for smoking de-addiction. He stopped taking clonidine tablets and now presents with a headache. What is the reason behind this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rebound hypertension

The mechanism that causes headache in this patient, who stopped taking clonidine is rebound hypertension.

Clonidine is an alpha-2 receptor agonist and a centrally acting antihypertensive agent. It treats high blood pressure by stimulating presynaptic α2 receptors in the vasomotor center in the brainstem. This binding has a sympatholytic effect, by suppressing the release of norepinephrine and other sympathomimetics.

Abrupt withdrawal after long-term therapy can result in rebound hypertension, restlessness, and sympathetic overactivity. Dry mouth and sedation are the major side effects of clonidine. It can also cause impotency and constipation.

Phentolamine is used for the control of hypertension due to clonidine withdrawal.
questions.learning: Rebound hypertension — The mechanism that causes headache in this patient, who stopped taking clonidine is rebound hypertension. Clonidine is an alpha-2 receptor agonist and a centrally acting antihypertensive agent.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient underwent lipoma excision 5 weeks ago and now presents with a scar confined to the original incision site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thickened, raised scar that remains confined within the boundaries of the original incision is definitively a Hypertrophic scar (Option C) . These typically develop within weeks of a surgical procedure or injury and may regress over time. In contrast, a Keloid (Option A) is a more aggressive fibrotic lesion that characteristically extends beyond the original boundaries of the wound, invading the surrounding normal skin, and rarely regresses spontaneously. Exuberant granulation (Option B), or "proud flesh," refers to red, friable tissue that grows above the skin level in a non-healing wound, rather than a mature scar. Granulation tissue (Option D) is the normal vascular tissue formed during the healing process. Because the description specifies the scar is exactly within the incision limits, Hypertrophic scar is the correct forensic and dermatological classification. This distinction is vital for planning treatment, as hypertrophic scars often respond well to pressure or silicone sheets
questions.learning: A thickened, raised scar that remains confined within the boundaries of the original incision is definitively a Hypertrophic scar (Option C) . These typically develop within weeks of a surgical procedure or injury and may regress over time.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B with pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN)? 1. PEG-IFN is poorly tolerated compared to nucleoside analogues. 2. Resistance to treatment with PEG-IFN is more common than with nucleoside analogues. 3. PEG-IFN is not useful in patients with cirrhosis. 4. PEG-IFN is administered once weekly for 48 weeks. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

Pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN) in chronic hepatitis B:

• Statement 1. PEG-IFN is poorly tolerated compared to nucleoside analogues: True. PEG-IFN is associated with significant adverse effects (flu-like symptoms, fatigue, depression, cytopenias, thyroid dysfunction), making it less well tolerated than oral nucleos(t)ide analogues such as entecavir or tenofovir.
• Statement 2. Resistance to treatment with PEG-IFN is more common than with nucleoside analogues: False. Viral resistance does not develop to interferon. In contrast, resistance can occur with some nucleos(t)ide analogues (especially older agents like lamivudine), although tenofovir and entecavir have a high barrier to resistance.
• Statement 3. PEG-IFN is not useful in patients with cirrhosis: True. PEG-IFN is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis and is generally not recommended in cirrhotic patients because of the risk of hepatic decompensation. It is mainly used in selected non-cirrhotic or compensated patients.
• Statement 4. PEG-IFN is administered once weekly for 48 weeks: True. The standard regimen is pegylated interferon alfa administered once weekly for 48 weeks.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN) in chronic hepatitis B: • Statement 1. PEG-IFN is poorly tolerated compared to nucleoside analogues: True.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female with breast cancer undergoes investigation which reveals the presence of ER positivity. Presence of ER is important as it is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prognostic marker

• ER positivity tells you how well the tumour will respond to endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors), making it a prognostic > predictive marker (remains controversial)
• Although ER status correlates with a better prognosis, its clinical value also lies in predicting the benefit of hormonal treatment; it is not diagnostic, nor a surrogate molecular subtype marker on its own.
questions.learning: Prognostic marker • ER positivity tells you how well the tumour will respond to endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors), making it a prognostic > predictive marker (remains controversial) • Although ER status correlates with a better prognosis,…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of gabapentin?
options: Binding to and blockade of the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Binding to and blockade of the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels

Gabapentin exerts its anticonvulsant and analgesic effects by binding to the α2δ subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing calcium influx into nerve terminals. This decreases the release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate, substance P, and norepinephrine, making it effective in neuropathic pain and focal seizures. Despite its structural similarity to GABA, gabapentin does not act on GABA receptors.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sodium channel blockade: Mechanism of phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and lacosamide.
• C. Opioid receptor blockade: Mechanism of naloxone and naltrexone.
• D. NMDA receptor antagonism: Mechanism of ketamine, memantine, and dextromethorphan, not gabapentin.
questions.learning: Binding to and blockade of the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels Gabapentin exerts its anticonvulsant and analgesic effects by binding to the α2δ subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing calcium influx into nerve…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young man undergoes a lumbar sympathectomy with excision of both L1 sympathetic ganglia. What is the most common complication associated with this procedure?
questions.explanation: Lumbar sympathectomy is sometimes performed for vascular diseases of the lower limbs or hyperhidrosis. The sympathetic nerves originating from the L1 and L2 ganglions are responsible for the coordinated closure of the internal urethral sphincter during ejaculation. When these ganglions are removed bilaterally, the internal sphincter fails to close, causing semen to enter the bladder instead of being expelled through the urethra, a condition known as retrograde ejaculation. Impotence (Option A), or erectile dysfunction, is primarily a parasympathetic function (S2-S4) and is usually not affected by lumbar sympathectomy. Bladder dysfunction (Option C) and incontinence (Option D) are complex processes involving somatic, sympathetic, and parasympathetic control; while minor changes may occur, retrograde ejaculation is the specific and most characteristic complication of L1/L2 sympathetic chain disruption. Patients must be counseled regarding this risk, especially if they are of reproductive age, as it can lead to infertility despite normal erectile function and desire
questions.learning: Lumbar sympathectomy is sometimes performed for vascular diseases of the lower limbs or hyperhidrosis. The sympathetic nerves originating from the L1 and L2 ganglions are responsible for the coordinated closure of the internal urethral sphincter during…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Match the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1

Mitochondrial inheritance is classically seen in Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy due to mtDNA mutations. Inherited only from mother.

X-linked recessive disorders include Duchenne muscular dystrophy caused by dystrophin gene deletion. Features:

Spinobulbar muscular atrophy is caused by trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion. Also called: Kennedy disease

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with a spiral fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The X-ray findings are shown in the image. Which of the following nerves is most commonly injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radial nerve

In a spiral fracture of the shaft of the humerus, the radial nerve is most commonly injured because it runs in the radial (spiral) groove on the posterior surface of the humeral shaft.

Injury leads to wrist drop due to paralysis of wrist and finger extensors, along with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.
questions.learning: Radial nerve — In a spiral fracture of the shaft of the humerus, the radial nerve is most commonly injured because it runs in the radial (spiral) groove on the posterior surface of the humeral shaft.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy had received a full course rabies vaccine taken in December 2018. His pet dog which has been fully vaccinated now (November 2019) bit him on the toe. Bleeding was present at the site of the bite. What would be the line of treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 doses of vaccine on Day 0 & 3

This boy should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

Management of a new dog bite in a previously immunized individual with either pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is as follows:

• Category I: Wound treatment only
• Category II/ III:

• Wound treatment with soap and running water for 15 min and apply antiseptic
• Receive Anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) 2 doses ID (0.1 ml, 1 site)/ 2 doses IM (1 VIAL, 1 site) on days 0 and 3.

*Note: In developing countries like India, the vaccination status of animals alone, doesn't play a significant role in determining the initiation of prophylaxis in humans.
questions.learning: 2 doses of vaccine on Day 0 & 3 This boy should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gradually progressive, nonspecific symptoms over several months. He reports painless swelling in the neck due to enlarged lymph nodes and a recent onset of hearing loss, which is found to be conductive on evaluation. Otoscopic examination shows a dull tympanic membrane, and further assessment reveals reduced mobility of the soft palate. Considering this constellation of findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of painless neck nodes (lymphadenopathy), unilateral conductive hearing loss (due to Eustachian tube obstruction and serous otitis media), and decreased palate mobility is the classic clinical triad for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC). The "dull tympanic membrane" reflects the middle ear effusion common in these patients. NPC often presents silently in the Rosenmüller's fossa. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (Option B) typically involves major salivary glands. Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (Option C) is a benign, highly vascular tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, not 60-year-olds. Quinsy (Option D) is an acute peritonsillar abscess causing severe pain, fever, and trismus, not chronic lymphadenopathy and hearing loss. In an older patient presenting with unilateral ear effusion and neck nodes, the nasopharynx must always be examined to rule out carcinoma. Therefore, NPC is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of painless neck nodes (lymphadenopathy), unilateral conductive hearing loss (due to Eustachian tube obstruction and serous otitis media), and decreased palate mobility is the classic clinical triad for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of muscles used in ejaculation?
options: Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction
Ischiocavernosus relaxation-External urethral sphincter contraction-Bulbospongiosus contraction
Ischiocavernosus relaxation-External urethral sphincter contraction-Bulbospongiosus relaxation
Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus relaxation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction

The correct sequence of muscles used are Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction.

There are 2 stages involved in this process - emission of the sperms into the prostatic urethra and ejaculation.

1.Emission:

* The sperm produced in the testes is brought into the urethra with contraction of the vas deferens and the ampulla and reach the seminal vesicles.

* Then contractions of the muscular coat of the prostate gland followed by contraction of the seminal vesicles expel prostatic and seminal fluid also into the urethra, forcing the sperm forward.

* All these fluids mix in the internal urethra with mucus already secreted by thebulbourethral glands to form the semen.

2.Ejaculation:

* The filling of the internal urethra with semen elicits sensory signals that are transmitted through the pudendal nerves to the sacral regions of the cord, giving
the feeling of sudden fullness in the internal genital organs.

* These sensory signals further exciter rhythmic contraction of the internal genital organs and cause contraction of the ischiocavernosus to further move the semen into the prostatic urethra.

* Retrograde ejaculation is prevented by the contraction of the internal urethral sphincter and relaxation of external urethral sphincter to help push the semen into the spongy urethra.

* The bulbocavernosus muscles contracts and compress the bases of the penile erectile tissue and cause rhythmic wave like increases in pressure in the erectile tissue of the penis and the genital ducts and urethra, which move the semen from the urethra to the exterior which is called ejaculation.

An image showing the muscles involved is shown below:
questions.learning: Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction The correct sequence of muscles used are Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Dense irregular collagen is found in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermis

Dense irregular collagen is found in dermis.

Irregular connective tissue is of three types: Loose, dense and adipose. Dense connective tissue is located in regions which are under consistent mechanical stress and where protection is required for the ensheathed organs. The abundant collagen fibres in the dermis run in a haphazard manner. This protects the skin.

It is usually present in :

• Reticular layer of the dermis
• Superficial connective tissue sheaths of the muscle and nerves
• Adventitia of large vessels
• Capsules of various organs and glands (e.g, testis, sclera, periosteum, perichondrium)

On the other hand, dense regular collagen fibres are found in tendons.
questions.learning: Dermis Dense irregular collagen is found in dermis. Irregular connective tissue is of three types: Loose, dense and adipose.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Cough on scratching the external acoustic canal is due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Auricular branch of vagus

Cough on scratching the external acoustic canal is due to the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve).

Arnold's nerve supplies the concha and corresponding eminence on the medial surface. It also supplies the posterior wall and floor of the external auditory canal. Scratching or mechanical stimulation of the ear leads to activation of Arnold's nerve, which evokes reflex cough (ear-cough reflex/otorespiratory reflex).

Causes of referred otalgia
Nerve responsible
Site

Temporomandibular joint and dental conditions, parotid infections/tumor, and anterior 2/3rd of tongue
Auriculotemporal nerve
Tragal area, crus of the helix, and anterior wall and roof of the external auditory canal.

Acute tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, carcinoma base of the tongue or tonsils (oropharynx)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's)
Medial surface of the tympanic membrane, and middle ear

Carcinoma of the larynx (cough), hypopharynx, epiglottis, vallecula, esophagus, and thyroid
Auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's/Alderman's nerve)
Concha, posterior wall, and floor of the external auditory canal

Cervical spondylitis
Great auricular nerve (C2,3)
Lateral and medial surfaces of the pinna

Acoustic neuroma
Facial nerve (nervus intermedius/nerve of Wrisberg)

Concha, retro auricular groove, and posterosuperior part of the external auditory meatus. Numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall known as Hitzelberger's sign, is seen in acoustic neuroma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which term is used to describe the practice of disseminating a particular belief system with the aim of influencing public opinion and behavior?
questions.explanation: Health propaganda is defined as the communication of information or a particular belief system with the specific intent to influence public opinion and behavior, often using emotional appeals rather than objective facts. It is typically one-way and aims for immediate persuasion or "indoctrination". In contrast, health education (Option C) is a two-way process designed to empower individuals with knowledge, allowing them to make their own informed health decisions based on scientific evidence. Health information (Option D) refers to the dissemination of raw, objective health facts without a specific behavioral agenda. A health doctrine (Option A) is a formal set of principles or beliefs held by an organization. The key differentiator for propaganda is its manipulative nature and focus on behavioral control rather than autonomous learning. Understanding this distinction is vital for public health practitioners to ensure their community outreach remains ethical, empowering, and grounded in the principles of authentic education rather than mere influence
questions.learning: Health propaganda is defined as the communication of information or a particular belief system with the specific intent to influence public opinion and behavior, often using emotional appeals rather than objective facts.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following best represents the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status III?
options: Severe systemic disease with threat to life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe systemic disease

Severe systemic disease best fits into grade 3 of the ASA classification.

American Society of Anesthesiologists classification is used to define relative risk prior to conscious sedation and surgical anesthesia.

It is simple, reproducible and strongly correlates to perioperative risk.

American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status classification of patients-

Class 1: Normal healthy patient
Class 2: Patient with mild systemic disease (no functional limitations)
Class 3: Patient with severe systemic disease (some functional limitations)
Class 4: Patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (functionality incapacitated)
Class 5: A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation
Class 6: A brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes

questions.text: Based on the graphs provided showing different occupational groups and their risk of developing fever, which occupation demonstrates the highest likelihood of experiencing fever?
questions.explanation: The bar graph (A) shows the proportion of individuals with fever (blue) and no fever (orange) across different occupational groups. To determine which occupation has the highest likelihood of fever, we compare the relative height of the blue (fever) portion in each category. 1. White-collar workers have the highest blue segment, close to about 90%, indicating the largest proportion of fever cases. 2. Industrial workers show a moderate level (around 60–65%). 3. Farmers have slightly lower levels (around 55–60%). 4. Housewives have the lowest proportion of fever (around 35–40%). The pie chart (B) shows the distribution of total workers, not the risk of fever, so it does not affect the answer to this question. Thus, based on the highest proportion of fever cases, white-collar workers demonstrate the greatest likelihood of experiencing fever

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman is evaluated for worsening urinary urgency and incontinence. The patient has had no abdominal pain, dysuria, or changes in urinary frequency. The patient feels unsteady while ambulating and walks slowly with small steps. Her family also reports that she has become forgetful and has difficulty planning and executing various activities that she used to perform regularly. MRI of the brain reveals chronic white matter changes with no infarction, hemorrhage, or mass lesions. There is diffuse ventriculomegaly with no sulcal enlargement. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stretching of descending cortical fibers

This patient has the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH):

• Gait disturbance (magnetic/shuffling gait)
• Urinary incontinence/urgency
• Cognitive decline (executive dysfunction)

Pathophysiology of urinary incontinence in NPH:

• Ventriculomegaly with normal sulfi causes stretching of periventricular white matter
• Specifically affects descending frontal cortical fibers that normally inhibit the micturition reflex
• Loss of cortical inhibition → detrusor overactivity → urgency and incontinence

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the term for the process of converting unconjugated substances into their conjugated forms?
questions.explanation: The process of converting unconjugated (often lipid-soluble) substances into conjugated (water-soluble) forms is a key part of Phase II metabolism in the liver. The most common form of this is glucuronidation, where glucuronic acid is attached to the substance. This makes the molecule more polar, allowing it to be easily excreted in the bile or urine. Glycation (Option A) is the non-enzymatic binding of sugar to proteins (e.g., HbA1c). Glycosylation (Option B) is the enzymatic addition of sugars to proteins or lipids during cell signaling. Oxidation (Option D) is a Phase I metabolic reaction that often introduces a functional group but does not involve conjugation. A classic example of glucuronidation is the metabolism of bilirubin. Heme breakdown produces unconjugated bilirubin, which is toxic and insoluble. The liver enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) conjugates it with glucuronic acid to form water-soluble conjugated bilirubin, which can then be safely excreted. Deficiencies in this process lead to jaundice, as seen in Gilbert or Crigler-Najjar syndromes
questions.learning: The process of converting unconjugated (often lipid-soluble) substances into conjugated (water-soluble) forms is a key part of Phase II metabolism in the liver.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about Crohn's disease?
options: For effective treatment of a Crohn's mass, only antibiotics are prescribed.
Symptomatic relapse after surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection.
The proximal ileum is most commonly involved in Crohn's disease.
On endoscopic examination, continuous lesions are visualised, which are diagnostic of Crohn's disease.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Symptomatic relapse after surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection.

Symptomatic relapse of Crohn's disease after surgery is not related to the presence of the disease during resection.

The course of the disease after surgery is unpredictable since surgery does not cure Crohn's disease. Instead, the probability of relapse increases with the time since resection.

Other options:

Option A: Antibiotics alone cannot treat a Crohn's mass effectively. Abscesses can be treated with metronidazole and ciprofloxacin and should also undergo drainage (and resection if needed).

Option C: The terminal ileum is most commonly involved in Crohn's disease.

Option D: On endoscopic examination, discontinuous "skip" lesions are visualized. These are irregular areas of inflamed mucosa that are ulcerated with mucopurulent exudate separated by intervening, normal-appearing intestinal mucosa.
questions.learning: Symptomatic relapse after surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection. Symptomatic relapse of Crohn's disease after surgery is not related to the presence of the disease during resection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a vaccination campaign, a man fears that the vaccine may cause impotence. Which type of barrier to immunization is the healthcare provider addressing in this situation?
questions.explanation: In health communication, a Cultural barrier arises when a patient's beliefs, values, or traditional myths interfere with the acceptance of medical advice or interventions. The patient's concern that a vaccine causes impotency is a classic example of a "health myth" or deep-seated cultural anxiety often used to resist public health programs. A physical barrier (Option A) would be an actual obstacle to receiving the vaccine, such as distance or lack of supply. An environmental barrier (Option B) refers to external conditions like noise or weather. A physiological barrier (Option C) would be an actual physical impairment in the patient, like hearing loss, that prevents them from understanding the doctor. Addressing cultural barriers requires sensitivity, community engagement, and the involvement of trusted leaders to dispel myths with scientific facts. Overcoming these misconceptions is essential for achieving high immunization coverage and successfully eradicating infectious diseases in populations where such rumors may be prevalent
questions.learning: In health communication, a Cultural barrier arises when a patient's beliefs, values, or traditional myths interfere with the acceptance of medical advice or interventions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with chest pain and breathlessness that worsen in the supine position and improve on sitting up. On examination, heart sounds are muffled. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits the classic clinical features of Pericardial Effusion: pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that are relieved by sitting forward (positional relief). The hallmark physical finding is muffled (distant) heart sounds due to the fluid surrounding the heart. In severe cases, this can lead to Beck’s triad (muffled sounds, JVP distension, and hypotension) indicating cardiac tamponade. The provided X-ray shows the characteristic "Water-bottle heart" appearance, where the heart shadow is globular and massively enlarged. Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B) would show a "boot-shaped" heart. Transposition of great arteries (Option C) classically shows an "egg-on-a-string" heart . Pulmonary hypertension (Option D) shows enlarged pulmonary arteries but not a globular heart shadow. Diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography, which can visualize the fluid in the pericardial sac. Treatment involves treating the underlying cause or performing pericardiocentesis
questions.learning: The patient exhibits the classic clinical features of Pericardial Effusion: pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that are relieved by sitting forward (positional relief).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In evaluating occupational health hazards related to long-term asbestos exposure, which type of cancer is most strongly associated with asbestos, particularly among workers in industries such as construction, shipbuilding, and automotive repair?
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma is an aggressive and rare form of cancer that develops in the mesothelium, the thin protective lining covering most internal organs. The strongest and most well-documented risk factor for mesothelioma is exposure to asbestos fibers. When asbestos is disturbed, it releases microscopic fibers that can be inhaled or swallowed, eventually lodging in the pleura (the lining of the lungs) or peritoneum (the lining of the abdomen). These fibers cause chronic inflammation and genetic damage, leading to malignant transformation, often with a long latency period of 20 to 50 years. While asbestos also increases the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer), mesothelioma is the most specific and notable occupational cancer associated with it. Acute myeloid leukemia (Option B) is linked to benzene or radiation. Hepatic angiosarcoma (Option C) is classically associated with vinyl chloride exposure. Skin carcinoma (Option D) is primarily caused by UV radiation or arsenic. Thus, for workers in construction or shipbuilding, mesothelioma remains the hallmark malignancy of asbestos exposure
questions.learning: Mesothelioma is an aggressive and rare form of cancer that develops in the mesothelium, the thin protective lining covering most internal organs. The strongest and most well-documented risk factor for mesothelioma is exposure to asbestos fibers.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gradual progressive hearing loss. On examination, he has difficulty perceiving high frequency sounds, but other findings are normal. Which structure is primarily affected in this condition?
options: Inner hair cell of basal turn
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inner hair cell of basal turn

High-frequency hearing loss in elderly patients (presbycusis) primarily involves damage to the inner hair cells at the basal turn of the cochlea.

• Base (basal turn) → detects high-frequency sounds
• Apex → detects low-frequency sounds

Pathophysiology:

• Age-related degeneration of hair cells (especially inner hair cells)
• Most pronounced at the basal turn → early loss of high-frequency hearing

Why other options are incorrect:

• Stria vascularis: Affects endolymph production (metabolic hearing loss)
• Tectorial membrane: Structural role, not primary site here
• Outer hair cells: Amplify sound, but inner hair cells are primary sensory receptors

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In an experiment, a value of 39 was mistakenly recorded as 93. Which of the following statistical measures is most likely to be affected by this error?
options: Mean will remain same, median will increase
Mean and median both will increase
Mean will increase, median will remain same
Both mean and median will decrease
questions.explanation: In biostatistics, the mean is highly sensitive to extreme values (outliers) because it is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the total number. Recording 93 instead of 39 significantly increases the total sum, which directly causes the mean to increase. Conversely, the median is a "robust" measure of central tendency representing the middle value in a sorted data set. As long as both 39 and 93 are positioned on the same side of the middle value (e.g., both are larger than the median), replacing one with the other does not change the central rank; thus, the median remains the same. Option B is incorrect because the median is rarely affected by single errors at the extreme ends. Options A and D are mathematically incorrect based on these properties. This concept is critical for researchers, emphasizing why the median is often a better measure of central tendency for skewed data sets containing outliers or recording errors
questions.learning: In biostatistics, the mean is highly sensitive to extreme values (outliers) because it is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the total number.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 38-year-old man who presents with intermittent discharge of pus and blood from an external opening in the perianal region?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of recurrent discharge of pus and blood from a persistent external opening near the anus is diagnostic of a fistula-in-ano (Option D). This condition is a chronic abnormal tract connecting the anal canal (internal opening) to the skin surface (external opening), usually following the drainage of a previous perianal abscess. A pilonidal sinus (Option A) would be located at the base of the spine in the natal cleft. A perianal abscess (Option B) involves an acute, painful collection of pus, whereas a fistula is the chronic, discharging remnant. Hemorrhoids (Option C) cause bleeding or prolapse but do not present with a cutaneous discharging opening. The location of the opening relative to the anus can help predict the path of the tract using Goodsall's rule (posterior openings usually have a curved tract to the midline). Surgical management involves fistulotomy or fistulectomy
questions.learning: The patient’s history of recurrent discharge of pus and blood from a persistent external opening near the anus is diagnostic of a fistula-in-ano (Option D).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the best imaging study for earliest diagnosis of cerebral infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diffusion weighted MRI

The best imaging modality for the early diagnosis of cerebral infarction is diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI), which can detect infarcts as early as 30 minutes of onset and identify cytotoxic oedema within a few hours of ischemic stroke.

However, the initial investigation in suspected stroke cases is non-contrast CT due to its rapid acquisition time, widespread availability, and cost-effectiveness. It helps quickly rule out hemorrhagic stroke and facilitates the timely administration of intravenous tPA in eligible patients.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Absolute refractory period is due to:
options: Closure of active gates of sodium channel
Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel

Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel.

Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in. They can either be closed, open, or inactive.

When the stimulus causes activation of the open gates, sodium rushes into the cell causing the membrane potential to become more positive. After 0.5 to 1 millisecond, the inactive gate automatically closes and no stimulus, no matter how strong, can excite the nerve. This is called the absolute refractory period.
questions.learning: Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel. Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in.

questions.text: Identify the sign shown on x-ray.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Double ring sign

The double ring (double halo) sign on X-ray indicates a button battery lodged in the esophagus, not a simple coin.

• Double rim/halo appearance → characteristic of button battery
• Caused by bilaminar structure of battery
• Medical emergency due to rapid mucosal injury (alkali burn, necrosis, perforation)

Clinical importance:

• Must be removed urgently (within hours)
• Can cause tracheoesophageal fistula, perforation, mediastinitis

Differentiation:

• Coin: Single uniform circular opacity (no double rim)
• Button battery: Double ring sign + step-off on lateral view

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What do chaperones assist in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein folding

Chaperones assist in protein folding. They are a type of heat-shock protein weighing 70 kDa (hsp70).

Mechanism of action:

* They bind to the short sequences of hydrophobic amino acids of an extended polypeptide.

* They effectively shield the new polypeptide being synthesized from aggregating, so as to provide them an opportunity to form an appropriate secondary structure.

* In instances where a protein is thermodynamically trapped in a misfolded dead-end form, the chaperones can rescue the protein by unfolding these hydrophobic ends, providing the protein a second chance to fold productively.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The type of hypoxia based on the graph is_____ (Consider the plot in red as normal)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anemic hypoxia

The graph represents the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve that would be seen in anemic hypoxia and normal. The X-axis represents the partial pressure of oxygen(PO2). The Y-axis represents the percentage saturation between the hemoglobin and the oxygen.

The graph indicates two lines: a red line representing normal hemoglobin and a purple line representing reduced hemoglobin levels. The red line corresponds to an arterial blood oxygen content of approximately 19 mL/dL, and venous blood oxygen content of 14 mL/dL. On the other hand, the purple line represents an arterial blood oxygen content of 9 mL/dL and venous blood oxygen content of 4 mL/dL.

This scenario demonstrates a 50% decrease in oxygen saturation of hemoglobin, while the partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) remains within the normal range. This condition is characterized as anemic hypoxia.

In anemic hypoxia, the blood oxygen content is decreased. The patients might not experience any difficulty during rest because 2,3-DPG increases in the red blood cells. However, they may have difficulty during exercise because of a limited ability to increase O2 delivery to the active tissues.

Conditions that cause a right shift in the oxygen hemoglobin curve are: (Conditions with the increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

• Hypoxia
• Hypercarbia
• Decreased pH
• Increased temperature
• Increased 2,3-biphosphoglycerate

Conditions that cause a left shift in the oxygen hemoglobin curve

• Increased oxygen
• Decreased carbon dioxide
• Increased pH
• Decreased temperature
• Decreased 2,3-biphosphoglycerate
• Fetal hemoglobin.
questions.learning: Anemic hypoxia — The graph represents the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve that would be seen in anemic hypoxia and normal. The X-axis represents the partial pressure of oxygen(PO2).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with thinning of hair and scaling of the scalp. On taking further history, it is found that she consumes raw eggs in her diet regularly. The given manifestations are due to the deficiency of which of the following vitamins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Biotin

The given clinical scenario of scaling and alopecia and the history of raw egg consumption are suggestive of biotin deficiency.

Raw egg white contains a glycoprotein known as avidin, which tightly binds to biotin and renders it unabsorbable from the intestine. Hence, there can be a biotin deficiency state.

Biotin deficiency may cause:

• Dermatitis, scaling, seborrheic, and erythematous rash
• Mental status changes (depression, hallucinations)
• Hyperesthesia
• Alopecia
• Atrophic glossitis

In infants, biotin deficiency presents as hypotonia, lethargy, and apathy. In addition, infants may develop alopecia and a characteristic rash that includes the ears.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old student presents with ocular redness, foreign body sensation, and excessive tearing following the use of a contact lens. An interface contrast microscopy from his corneal scraping is shown below. What would be the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

The given clinical history and the demonstration of polygonal cysts in interface contrast microscopy are suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by acanthamoeba.

Acanthamoeba culbertsoni is an opportunistic protozoan pathogen. It exists as trophozoite form and resistant cystic form. Both these forms are infective. The trophozoite is large and characterized by spine-like pseudopodia (acanthopodia).

Human beings acquire the infection by inhalation of cysts or trophozoites, directly through traumatized skin or eyes, or ingestion of cysts.

It chiefly presents as two chronic conditions:

* Acanthamoeba keratitis

* Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis

Acanthamoeba keratitis is an infection of the eyes that typically develops from the entry of the amebic cyst through abrasions on the cornea. Most of the cases are associated with the use of contact lenses.

Patients usually present with photophobia, excessive tearing, redness, and foreign body sensation and it can be bilateral in contact lens users.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture. The cysts are smaller (12-25 μm) and polygonal or star-shaped.

Topical administration of biguanides or chlorhexidine with or without diamidine agents can be used for the management of acanthamoeba keratitis. In severe cases penetrating keratoplasty can be done.

The below image shows the ring lesion seen in acanthamoeba keratitis.

The below image shows cysts of acanthamoeba in lactophenol cotton blue staining.

Other options:

Option B- Naegleria fowleri causes a brain infection, primary amebic meningoencephalitis that leads to brain tissue destruction. Their cysts are spherical and have a smooth double wall.

Option C- Entamoeba histolytica causes intestinal and extraintestinal amebiasis. Their cysts are spherical in shape. A mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form.  An amebic ulcer is a typical lesion seen in intestinal amebiasis which is a flask-shaped ulcer in cross-section. Amebic liver abscess is extraintestinal amebiasis which has a center of abscess that contains thick colored brown pus termed anchovy sauce pus.

Option D- Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living ameba that causes granulomatous amebic encephalitis. Their cyst is usually spherical and surrounded by a three-layered cyst wall.
questions.learning: Acanthamoeba — The given clinical history and the demonstration of polygonal cysts in interface contrast microscopy are suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by acanthamoeba.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst?
options: Resection of the cyst along with the adjacent bowel
questions.explanation: Chylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are benign, well-encapsulated lymphatic malformations. Because they typically do not infiltrate the intestinal wall and have a blood supply independent of the bowel, complete enucleation is the preferred treatment. This allows for total removal of the cyst while preserving the adjacent intestine. Aspiration (Option A) is inadequate due to extremely high rates of recurrence and risk of infection. Resection of the adjacent bowel (Option C) is only necessary if the cyst is firmly adherent to mesenteric vessels or has an enterogenous origin. Conservative management (Option D) is avoided because these cysts can cause complications like torsion, hemorrhage, or rupture. Therefore, surgical enucleation is the definitive standard of care
questions.learning: Chylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are benign, well-encapsulated lymphatic malformations. Because they typically do not infiltrate the intestinal wall and have a blood supply independent of the bowel, complete enucleation is the preferred treatment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of the global hunger index?
questions.explanation: The Global Hunger Index (GHI) is a multidimensional tool used to measure and track hunger at national and regional levels. It is calculated using four key indicators: 1. Undernourishment: Representing the share of the population with inadequate food supply (Option C). 2. Child Wasting: Reflecting acute malnutrition (Option B). 3. Child Stunting: Reflecting chronic malnutrition. 4. Child Mortality: Specifically the Under-Five Mortality Rate (U5MR) (Option A). The Infant Mortality Rate (death before 1 year of age) (Option D) is not a specific component of the GHI, as the index focuses on the broader under-five category to capture the long-term effects of hunger and poor nutrition. GHI scores are used to raise awareness about hunger levels and to advocate for policies that improve food security. While infant mortality is an important health indicator, it is not one of the direct variables used to calculate this specific index
