questions.text: The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for which of the following structures:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right atrium

The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium.

The costal margin, xiphoid process, and the mid-clavicular line are seen in this image. The examiner draws a laterally convex line that extends from a level below the 2nd costal cartilage (as clued in by the sternal angle) i.e., 3rd costal cartilage to about 3 spaces below i.e., the 6th costal cartilage. This line is about 1.2 cms lateral to the sternal edge. These suggest that the region marked corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium.

The projection of the cardiac borders, of an average adult, onto the anterior thoracic wall forms a trapezoid.  This can be mapped out using the percussion method by looking for cardiac dullness.

The varying heart borders and the corresponding surface markings are as follows:

• Upper border: Slopes gently from the second left costal cartilage to the third right costal cartilage. It corresponds to the left atrium.
• Right border: Convex to the right and runs from the third to the sixth right costal cartilages, 1–2 cm lateral to the sternal edge. It corresponds to the right atrium.
• Inferior border or acute border: Runs leftwards from the 6th right costal cartilage to the cardiac apex which is located approximately 9 cm lateral to the midline, often in the left 5th intercostal space or level with the 5th or 6th rib. It corresponds to the right ventricle.
• Left border or obtuse border: Convex laterally on the left. It extends superomedially from the cardiac apex to meet the second left costal cartilage about 1 cm from the left sternal edge. It corresponds to the left ventricle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with HIV who is currently on antiretroviral therapy consisting of zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine is diagnosed with tuberculosis. Considering potential drug interactions, which of the following TB drugs should be changed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rifampicin

In HIV–TB coinfection, rifampicin must be modified/substituted in patients receiving NNRTI-based ART (e.g., nevirapine) due to significant drug interactions.

• Mechanism of interaction:

o    Rifampicin is a potent CYP450 inducer

o    ↓ plasma levels of nevirapine (NNRTI) → risk of ART failure

• Clinical implication:

o    Avoid co-administration with nevirapine when possible

o    Substitute rifampicin with rifabutin or adjust ART regimen

• Why not others: Isoniazid, ethambutol, streptomycin: no major CYP450 induction → safe with ART

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man with IHD presents with sudden, severe, generalized abdominal pain and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, the pulse rate is 118bpm, rhythm is irregularly irregular, BP is 90/60 mmHg. The abdomen appears soft, non-distended, and bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following could be a likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute mesenteric ischemia

The given clinical scenario of a patient with sudden onset severe abdominal pain which is out-of-proportion to the physical examination findings along with atrial fibrillation is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia.

Mesenteric ischemia may be acute or chronic. The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is most likely affected. An embolus is the most common cause of SMA occlusion. Possible sources for SMA emboisation include:

• Left atrium in atrial fibrillation
• Previous history of ischemic heart disease/myocardial infarction
• Vegetations on mitral and aortic valves associated with endocarditis
• An atheromatous plaque from an aortic aneurysm.

Other causes of mesenteric ischemia include:

• Atherosclerosis of mesenteric vessels
• Vasculitides
• Venous thrombosis in factor V Leiden mutation
• Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia due to alterations in splanchnic blood flow.

The most important clue to an early diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain in a patient with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerosis. The pain is typically in the central abdomen and out of proportion to the physical findings.

Associated clinical features include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distension, peritonitis, and the passage of bloody stools.

The gold standard for the diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is angiography, and management is laparotomy. The goal of operative exploration is to resect the compromised bowel and restore blood supply via embolectomy.

Other options:

Option B: A pulsatile abdominal mass is seen in the case of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acute pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation.

Options A and D: Acute severe pancreatitis and peptic ulcer perforation have no association with atrial fibrillation. They usually present with pain over the upper abdomen associated with guarding and rigidity on examination.
questions.learning: Acute mesenteric ischemia — The given clinical scenario of a patient with sudden onset severe abdominal pain which is out-of-proportion to the physical examination findings along with atrial fibrillation is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic female who was treated with steroids and remdevisir for COVID now presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is a non-contagious fungal disease most commonly caused by Rhizopus oryzae that is acquired through the inhalation of fungal spores from air. It may occur during COVID infection or after a few weeks (usually around the 3rd week) of recovery from it. Reasons for increase in mucormycosis cases in COVID patients are:

* Uncontrolled hyperglycemia due to any reason. COVID per se has a tendency to worsen diabetes and also precipitate diabetes in previously normal individuals.

* Misuse and irrational use of steroids. Steroid overuse can cause new-onset diabetes.

* Leucopenia associated with COVID

* Prolonged ICU stay, unhygienic humidifiers, and irrational use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

* Pre-existing comorbidities such as hematological malignancies, use of immunosuppressants, and solid organ transplantation.

A high index of suspicion is required for the early diagnosis of mucormycosis. Checklist of sentinel signs/ symptoms of mucormycosis to be monitored in patients admitted with COVID-19 are:

* Relatively early disease (Nose and sinuses):

* Headache and nasal obstruction (especially if severe or persistent and not responding to medications)

* Nasal crusting, brownish or blood-tinged nasal discharge

* Facial pain, pain over sinuses

* Paraesthesia/ loss of sensation over half of the face

* Discoloration of the skin or localized facial puffiness

* Loosening of teeth, discoloration, ulceration, or eschar over the palate

* Moderately advanced disease (Eye/orbital involvement):

* Eye swelling or redness, eye pain

* Double vision, drooping of the eyelid, blurring, and loss of vision.

* Very advanced disease (Intracranial involvement):

* Involvement of cranial nerves II-VI suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis

* Signs of MCA thrombosis

Diagnosis:

* KOH mount and microscopy

* Histopathology of debrided tissue shows presence of ribbon-like aseptate hyphae (5-15 µ thick) branching at right angles.

* Culture can be done but treatment should be started on clinical suspicion.

* CT of sinuses, CT chest for suspected pulmonary involvement ( presence of more than 10 nodules, reverse halo sign are highly suggestive of mucor), and MRI brain to look for the extent of intracranial involvement.

Management:

* Treatment of co-morbid illness and strict glycemic control.

* Anti-fungal therapy started early on high clinical suspicion even prior to microbiological confirmation can reduce mortality. Treatment involves a combination of surgical debridement and antifungal therapy.

* Liposomal Amphotericin B (5-10mg/kg) is the drug of choice and has to be continued for 3-6 weeks. It should be diluted in 5% dextrose and is incompatible with normal saline and Ringer lactate. Step-down therapy to be done with oral posaconazole or isavuconazole. Renal function must be monitored during the entire treatment period.

* Early surgical debridement after stabilization of systemic illness and ensuring facilities for post-surgical care and ventilation.

Other options:

Option A: Invasive aspergillosis leads to the formation of black or greyish membrane in the nasal mucosa. The maxillary sinus may contain a fungus ball containing semisolid cheesy-white or blackish material.

Option C: Foreign body nose presents with foul-smelling unilateral discharge.

Option D: Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction by a polypoidal mass.
questions.learning: Mucormycosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a non-contagious fungal disease most commonly caused by Rhizopus oryzae that is acquired through the inhalation of fungal spores from air.

questions.text: Which options are correctly matched? 1. Gefitinib: EGFR (HER-1) 2. Sunitinib: EGFR (HER-1) 3. Trastuzumab: HER-2 4. Nilotinib: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

1. Gefitinib: EGFR (HER-1) — Correct

• Targets: EGFR-mutated (L858R mutation) NSCLC

2. Sunitinib: EGFR (HER-1) — Incorrect

• Sunitinib mainly inhibits: Tyrosine kinases: VEGFR/PDGFR/c-KIT

• Monoclonal antibody against HER-2/neu breast cancer

4. Nilotinib: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor — Correct

Second-generation:

• BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor
• Used in: CML

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male arrived at the ER with altered mental status and hematemesis that began a day ago. He has a 20-year history of alcoholism, with his most recent binge occurring a week prior. An ultrasound revealed altered echo texture of liver and mild portal vein dilation. CT scan brain was normal. He was started on intravenous pantoprazole and antiemetics. What should be the next step in his management?
options: Start a course of broad spectrum antibiotics
Order a liver biopsy to asses for fibrosis
Perform an endoscopy to look for varices
Administer intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Administer intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacement

The next immediate step in managament of upper gastrointestinal bleeding is administration of intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacement.

USG findings and history of alcoholism are suggestive of cirrhosis leading to portal hypertension. The upper GI endoscopy provides a definitive diagnosis and aids in predicting the risk of bleeding with an option to treat via band ligation or sclerotherapy. (Option C)

The management of esophageal variceal bleeding involves:

• Resuscitation with IV fluids, airway protection(intubation to protect airway and prevent aspiration), and oxygen
• Blood transfusion to maintain Hb between 7-9g/dL
• Antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone before endoscopy (Option A)
• An attempt at hemostasis with octreotide or terlipressin or vasopressin
• Upper GI endoscopy within 12 hours after fluid resuscitation to confirm the source of the bleed
• Endoscopic variceal band ligation or sclerotherapy
• In case, of failure or rebleeding - Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)
questions.learning: Administer intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacement The next immediate step in managament of upper gastrointestinal bleeding is administration of intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacement.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The stain done on a section of liver shown below is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sweet's reticulin stain

The above stain demonstrates reticular fibers of the liver and hence has to be reticulin stain.

Reticulin stain

• Stained by 2 procedures, Gordon and Sweet’s reticulin stain (most common) and Gomori reticulin stain.
• They demonstrate reticulin fibers and basement membrane.
• Reticulin fibers: thin, type 3 collagen, widespread in connective tissue
• Basement membrane: type 4 collagen fibers and laminin.

Reticulin stain is used to shows the normal architecture of the liver and thereby help detect disrupted architecture in hepatocellular carcinoma and hepatocellular proliferation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best represents the definition of culture?
options: It is static and not related to health and disease
A set of beliefs which are static
Rules set according to religion which are dynamic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Socially acquired learned behaviour

Culture is the socially acquired learned behaviour. It is passed onto generations through formal and informal learning. It is the representation of customs, beliefs, laws, arts, and moral values of a society. Cultural factors have a large part to play in health.

Other closely related terms include:

Customs are the traditionally accepted ways of behaving that are specific to a society. They can be folkways, which are referred to as the right ways of doing things in less vital areas of human conduct. Mores are stringent customs followed by a society.

Socialization is the process by which a person in a society imbibes its beliefs, customs, etc. through daily interaction with its members.

A community is a social group determined by geographical boundaries and/or common values and interests.

Acculturation is the process by which there is the diffusion of cultures between two culturally different groups of people. Acculturation does not take place by folklore.

Folklore is the passage of customs and beliefs of a community through generations, merely by word of mouth.
questions.learning: Socially acquired learned behaviour Culture is the socially acquired learned behaviour. It is passed onto generations through formal and informal learning.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of a category III dog bite and reports having received post-exposure prophylaxis for a dog bite six months ago. What should be the next step in management?
options: Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0 &3
Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0,3 & 7
Wound cleaning + intramuscular (IM) vaccine + rabies immune globulin (RIG)
questions.explanation: Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) management depends on the patient's prior vaccination status. For a person who has previously completed a full course of pre-exposure or post-exposure prophylaxis (as this patient did six months ago), the protocol is streamlined. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and national guidelines, such individuals do NOT require Rabies Immune Globulin (RIG), even for Category 3 bites. Instead, they require immediate wound cleaning with soap and water for 15 minutes and a booster series of two doses of the modern rabies vaccine, administered intramuscularly or intradermally on day 0 and day 3. Options C and D are incorrect because the additional dose on day 7 and the administration of RIG are only necessary for previously unvaccinated (naive) individuals. Option A is incorrect because wound cleaning alone is insufficient to prevent rabies, which is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear. This simplified two-dose "re-exposure" regimen is effective due to the immunological memory established by the previous vaccination.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Muscle inserted on lesser trochanter?
questions.explanation: The lesser trochanter is a posteromedial projection at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur. It serves as the primary insertion point for the Iliopsoas complex, which includes the Psoas major and the Iliacus muscles. This muscle group is the most powerful flexor of the hip joint. Psoas minor (Option B) is absent in about 40% of the population and, when present, inserts onto the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence of the pelvis, not the femur. Obturator internus (Option C) and Piriformis (Option D) are lateral rotators of the hip that insert onto the greater trochanter (specifically the medial surface and apex, respectively). Knowledge of these insertions is clinically important in orthopedics, particularly regarding avulsion fractures of the lesser trochanter in adolescents or pathological fractures in adults, which often indicate significant mechanical stress or metastatic disease affecting the primary hip flexor's attachment point
questions.learning: The lesser trochanter is a posteromedial projection at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur. It serves as the primary insertion point for the Iliopsoas complex, which includes the Psoas major and the Iliacus muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Killian's dehiscence is seen between___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cricopharyngeus and Thyropharyngeus

Killian's dehiscence is seen between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles.

The inferior constrictor muscle is made up of 2 parts: The upper thyropharyngeus made of oblique fibres and the lower cricopharyngeus made of transverse fibres. Between the two muscles, there is a potential gap which is called as the pharyngeal dimple or Killian's dehiscence.

This is the site of weakness in the pharyngeal wall and therefore is the potential site for the development of the diverticula- Zenker's diverticula.

Another site of weakness in the pharyngeal wall is the Laimer's triangle, which is present between the cricopharyngeus and the circular muscle of the oesophagus.

Pearl PF0326: Zenker’s Diverticulum

* Hypopharyngeal diverticulum

* False diverticulum

* Pulsion diverticulum

* Acquired diverticulum, seen in the elderly (>60 years)

* Herniation is through the Killian’s triangle (a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor) in the posterior pharyngeal wall

* Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

* Investigation of choice: Barium swallow (Lateral X rays)

* Treatment

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

Zenker’s diverticulum

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The area marked with green color in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ejection phase

The green-colored segment of the left ventricular pressure–volume (PV) loop represents the ventricular ejection phase. This phase begins when the left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, causing the aortic valve to open, and ends when the aortic valve closes. During this period, left ventricular volume decreases from end-diastolic volume (EDV) to end-systolic volume (ESV) as blood is ejected into the aorta.

• The green curve extends from point D to point F:

• D: Aortic valve opens.
• F: Aortic valve closes.

• During this phase:

• Left ventricular pressure initially rises, then falls.
• Left ventricular volume decreases due to ejection of blood.
• Stroke volume = EDV − ESV is generated.

Why not the other options?

• A. Isovolumetric contraction phase: Vertical line from C → D. Both mitral and aortic valves are closed; pressure rises rapidly with no change in ventricular volume.
• C. Isovolumetric relaxation phase: Vertical line from F → A. Both valves are closed; pressure falls rapidly with no change in volume.
• D. Rapid ventricular filling phase: Part of the A → C segment after mitral valve opening, where ventricular volume increases.

questions.text: A postmenopausal woman with ovarian mass and CA-125 = 1000 U/mL. What is the most probable diagnosis?

CA-125 is commonly elevated in epithelial ovarian tumors, particularly serous carcinoma.

| Mild elevation | Benign conditions

| Very high (>500) | Suggests malignancy

Spread of Serous Ovarian Cancer

Common spread:

• Transcoelomic spread in peritoneal cavity
• Omental metastasis (omental cake)
• Ascites formation

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 24-year-old pregnant woman is receiving lithium therapy for bipolar disorder. Discontinuation of lithium during pregnancy is advised to prevent the risk of which fetal congenital abnormality?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a highly effective mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, but it is a known teratogen when taken during pregnancy, especially during the first trimester. The specific congenital heart defect associated with maternal lithium use is "Ebstein anomaly" (Option A). This condition involves the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle, leading to "atrialization" of the ventricle and severe tricuspid regurgitation. VACTERL defects (Option B) are a cluster of anomalies (Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, etc.) with multifactorial origins. Coarctation of the aorta (Option C) and supravalvular aortic stenosis (Option D, classic for Williams syndrome) are not specifically linked to lithium exposure. While the absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly from lithium is lower than previously thought, it is significantly higher than the baseline population risk. Pregnant women on lithium require a detailed fetal echocardiogram between 18–22 weeks to screen for cardiac malformations and a careful risk-benefit discussion regarding medication management during gestation. **************
questions.learning: Lithium is a highly effective mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, but it is a known teratogen when taken during pregnancy, especially during the first trimester.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is indicated by variable decelerations on a CTG? CTG - Cardiotocography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cord compression

Variable decelerations on CTG are typically associated with umbilical cord compression in cases of cord prolapse and may disappear with the change in position of the patient.

Variable decelerations are abrupt in onset, often appear as V-shaped or U-shaped on CTG, and frequently show shouldering (brief accelerations before and after the deceleration). They vary in timing, depth, and duration.

Other options:

Option A: Head compression leads to early decelerations on CTG. They are gradual and mirror uterine contractions.

Option C: Fetal Hypoxia leads to Late deceleration on CTG. They are gradual decelerations that begin after the peak of contraction.

Option D: Uteroplacental insufficiency leads to Late deceleration on CTG.

Pearl PF2188: Deceleration patterns on cardiotocography (CTG)

Early deceleration: seen in head compression

Late deceleration: Seen in uteroplacental insufficiency, foetal hypoxia

Variable deceleration: Seen in umbilical cord compression
questions.learning: Cord compression Variable decelerations on CTG are typically associated with umbilical cord compression in cases of cord prolapse and may disappear with the change in position of the patient.

• Early-onset FGR → <32 weeks

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with HIV presents with recurrent cough and fever. Which culture medium is most appropriate for diagnosing the causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: A patient with HIV presenting with cough and fever strongly suggests tuberculosis (TB), as immunocompromised individuals are highly susceptible to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is a specialized, egg-based solid culture medium used as the gold standard for isolating this pathogen. It contains malachite green to inhibit the growth of contaminating flora and supports the slow growth of mycobacteria. Regarding the distractors, Tinsdale medium (Option A) and Loeffler serum slope (Option D) are specifically used for the cultivation and identification of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, the causative agent of diphtheria. MacConkey agar (Option C) is a selective and differential medium designed for Gram-negative bacteria, particularly enteric pathogens like E. coli, and does not support the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Therefore, LJ medium remains the appropriate diagnostic choice for confirming TB in this clinical scenario, allowing for further drug susceptibility testing once the slow-growing colonies emerge

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of ulcer?
questions.explanation: The ulcer shown is located in the gaiter area (the medial aspect of the lower leg), which is the classic site for a venous ulcer. These ulcers result from chronic venous insufficiency and are typically shallow with irregular, sloping edges. Arterial ulcers (Option A) are usually found on the toes or heels, are very painful, and have "punched-out" edges. Diabetic and Neuropathic ulcers (Options C and D) typically occur on the weight-bearing pressure points of the foot, such as the metatarsal heads or the heel, and are often painless due to associated neuropathy. The location and appearance of the lesion in the image are pathognomonic for venous disease

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was working in a field and he suddenly collapsed on a hot summer afternoon. On examination, there were no physical signs of dehydration. His serum electrolytes level was normal. The doctor found that the body temperature was 106 degrees Fahrenheit. Which of the following symptoms is least likely to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sweating

The given clinical vignette in a patient with no signs of dehydration and body temperature of 106oF is highly suggestive of heatstroke. Sweating is absent in heatstroke.

Heatstroke/ thermic fever/ heat hyperpyrexia is due to the failure of the heat regulation center of the hypothalamus. It is caused by failure of cutaneous circulation and sweating. The predisposing factors include high temperature, increased humidity, minor infections, old age, lack of acclimatization, alcoholism.

Heatstroke can be:

• Exertion-induced heat stroke is seen in people with prolonged exposure to or physical exertion in high temperatures, usually without adequate training.
• Sedentary heatstroke is a disease of elderly or infirm people whose cardiovascular systems are unable to adapt to the stress of a hot environment and release sufficient heat such that body temperature rises.

All the signs of shock are present. Patients usually present with a sudden collapse accompanied by loss of consciousness. Typical vital sign abnormalities include tachypnea, tachycardias, hypotension, and a widened pulse pressure. Other specific signs include rapid Kussmaul type of breathing, the absence of sweating with dry, hot skin, delirium, coma, convulsions, rhabdomyolysis, multiorgan failure.

Although there is no single specific diagnostic test, clinical features of exposure to heat stress, CNS dysfunction, and core temperature >104.9-degree Fahrenheit (> 40.5 degrees Celsius) help establish the preliminary diagnosis. The body temperature must be measured rectally.

Treatment includes rapidly cooling the body with ice water till the rectal temperature falls below 1020F.

Autopsy findings include the presence of edema and reduction of Purkinje's cells in the cerebellum.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of severe vaginal irritation and pruritus. On examination, you note a greenish- yellow, frothy discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of severe irritation/itching and a characteristic greenish-yellow, frothy vaginal discharge is diagnostic for Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. On examination, the cervix may also show punctate hemorrhages, known as a "strawberry cervix." Bacterial vaginosis (Option A) has a fishy odor and a greyish-white, non-frothy discharge. Candidiasis (Option C) involves a thick, white discharge and intense itching but no frothiness. Gonorrhea (Option D) primarily affects the cervix and causes a purulent, yellow discharge rather than a frothy vaginal one. Diagnosis is confirmed by seeing motile, pear-shaped trichomonads on a saline wet mount. Unlike BV, Trichomoniasis is a true STI; therefore, treatment of the male partner is mandatory to prevent reinfection, even if he is asymptomatic. The drug of choice for both the patient and her partner is oral metronidazole or tinidazole
questions.learning: The clinical combination of severe irritation/itching and a characteristic greenish-yellow, frothy vaginal discharge is diagnostic for Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the content present in the contraceptive shown below?
questions.explanation: The image displays a vaginal contraceptive sponge (such as Today Sponge). These devices are impregnated with a spermicide, and the most common and standard active ingredient used is Nonoxynol-9. Nonoxynol-9 works by disrupting the cell membrane of the spermatozoa, rendering them immobile and unable to fertilize the egg. Menfegol (Option B) and Octoxynol-8 (Option C) are also spermicides, but they are significantly less common in commercial sponge formulations compared to Nonoxynol-9. The sponge provides triple protection by acting as a mechanical barrier over the cervix, absorbing semen, and releasing spermicide over a 24-hour period. While convenient and available over-the-counter, it is less effective than hormonal or intrauterine methods. Clinicians must counsel users that Nonoxynol-9 does not protect against STIs and may even increase the risk of HIV transmission due to localized mucosal irritation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Defective fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase enzyme is associated with _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 1 Tyrosinemia

Defective fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase enzyme is associated with type I tyrosinemia (tyrosinosis). It is the most common type of tyrosinemia.

There are three types of tyrosinemias:

• Type 1 (Hepatorenal tyrosinemia): Fumaryl acetoacetate hydrolase deficiency
• Type 2 (Oculocutaneous tyrosinemia/Richner-Hanhart syndrome): Tyrosine transaminase deficiency
• Type 3 (Neonatal tyrosinemia)
questions.learning: Type 1 Tyrosinemia Defective fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase enzyme is associated with type I tyrosinemia (tyrosinosis). It is the most common type of tyrosinemia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Posthumous child is a
options: Child delivered after the death of parents
Child delivered after the death of biological father
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Child delivered after the death of biological father

The child delivered after the death of the biological father, or a child delivered after the death of the biological mother, usually when delivered by a cesarean section is a posthumous child.

Illegitimate child is a child born out of wedlock i.e. when the parents are not married.

Supposititious child or fictitious child is when a woman pretends to go through pregnancy and delivery. Later, she produces a living child as her own for obtaining money or for the purpose of claiming the property.
questions.learning: Child delivered after the death of biological father The child delivered after the death of the biological father, or a child delivered after the death of the biological mother, usually when delivered by a cesarean section is a posthumous child.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient sustains a head injury after being struck on the skull by a falling hammer. Subsequent CT imaging demonstrates characteristic findings related to this mechanism of trauma. Based on the nature of the injury and the typical appearance on imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A high-force impact to a small, localized area of the skull—such as being hit by a hammer—characteristically results in a Depressed skull fracture. In this type of injury, a fragment of the skull is driven inward toward the brain. On a head CT (bone window), this appears as an area where the bone is displaced below the level of the surrounding skull vault. Epidural Hematoma (Option A) would show a biconvex lens-shaped bleed. Concussion (Option B) is a functional brain injury that typically shows no visible abnormalities on CT. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option D) would show blood within the sulci and cisterns. Depressed skull fractures are significant because they may be "open" (if the skin is torn) and can cause direct underlying brain contusions or dural tears, leading to an increased risk of infection and post-traumatic epilepsy. If the bone is depressed by more than the thickness of the skull, surgical elevation is often required to minimize complications
questions.learning: A high-force impact to a small, localized area of the skull—such as being hit by a hammer—characteristically results in a Depressed skull fracture. In this type of injury, a fragment of the skull is driven inward toward the brain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic discomfort, and increased urinary frequency. On examination, the uterus is irregularly enlarged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), pelvic pressure, and urinary frequency combined with an irregularly enlarged uterus are diagnostic of uterine leiomyomas, or fibroids. These are common benign smooth muscle tumors originating from the myometrium. Endometriosis (Option A) causes severe pelvic pain and abnormal bleeding but typically does not enlarge the uterus unless adenomyosis is also present. An ovarian cyst (Option B) usually presents as a smooth adnexal mass rather than an irregularly enlarged uterine body. PCOS (Option D) involves hormonal disturbances like acne and hirsutism along with irregular cycles, but it does not cause uterine enlargement. Fibroids cause urinary symptoms by exerting direct pressure on the bladder. Diagnosis is confirmed by pelvic ultrasound, which characterizes the size and location of the fibroids. Therefore, leiomyoma is the most consistent clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The symptoms of heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), pelvic pressure, and urinary frequency combined with an irregularly enlarged uterus are diagnostic of uterine leiomyomas, or fibroids.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What objective tests are utilized to assess an individual's hearing ability?
questions.explanation: Objective hearing tests are those that do not require the active cooperation or subjective response of the patient, making them essential for infants and non-cooperative individuals. BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry), OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions), and Tympanometry are all categorized as objective tests. BERA measures the electrical activity of the auditory nerve. OAE measures the sound generated by the outer hair cells of the cochlea. Tympanometry (Option D) evaluates middle ear function and pressure. In contrast, PTA (Pure Tone Audiometry, Option C) is a subjective test because it requires the patient to signal when they hear a specific sound. Therefore, any option including PTA is technically incorrect when specifically asked for "objective" tests. Thus, the combination of BERA, OAE, and Tympanometry (Option A) is the definitive set of objective auditory diagnostic tools. Understanding this classification is fundamental for planning neonatal hearing screenings and evaluating adult patients with suspected malingering
questions.learning: Objective hearing tests are those that do not require the active cooperation or subjective response of the patient, making them essential for infants and non-cooperative individuals.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During the procedure of epidural anesthesia, which spinal structure is not traversed or penetrated by the needle?
questions.explanation: Epidural anesthesia involves the injection of local anesthetic into the epidural space, which lies just outside the dural sac. Therefore, the "Dura" (Option D) should "not be penetrated" by the needle. If the dura is punctured, it results in a "dural tap" or "wet tap," which can lead to a post-dural puncture headache. To reach the epidural space using a midline approach, the needle must pass through several structures in order: skin, subcutaneous tissue, the "supraspinous ligament" (Option A), the "interspinous ligament" (Option B), and the "ligamentum flavum" (Option C). The clinician identifies the epidural space using the "loss of resistance" technique once the needle passes through the dense ligamentum flavum. In contrast, spinal (subarachnoid) anesthesia requires the penetration of the dura and arachnoid mater to reach the cerebrospinal fluid. Precise knowledge of spinal anatomy is vital for the safe and successful performance of regional anesthesia techniques in obstetric and surgical patients
questions.learning: Epidural anesthesia involves the injection of local anesthetic into the epidural space, which lies just outside the dural sac. Therefore, the "Dura" (Option D) should "not be penetrated" by the needle.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with a progressively enlarging fleshy growth on the sclera that is extending onto the cornea toward the pupillary area, causing discomfort and visual disturbance. What is the most appropriate management for this progressive pterygium?
questions.explanation: A pterygium is a benign, wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of the bulbar conjunctiva that can invade the cornea. When the pterygium is progressive and begins encroaching on the visual axis (pupil) or causing significant astigmatism, surgical intervention is mandatory. The current gold standard management is surgical excision followed by a conjunctival autograft (CAG). This technique involves covering the bare sclera with a piece of the patient's own healthy conjunctiva, which significantly reduces the high rate of recurrence compared to simple excision alone. Keratoplasty (Option A) is only indicated for severe scarring after removal. Observation (Option C) is inappropriate for a growth that is actively threatening vision. Beta-radiation (Option D) is an older technique used to prevent recurrence but has been largely replaced by autografting due to potential long-term scleral melting. Thus, excision with autograft is the definitive treatment

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For a woman at 8 weeks of gestation requesting medical termination of pregnancy (MTP), the correct dose of misoprostol via the mucosal route (buccal or sublingual) is 800 micrograms.
questions.explanation: For medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) up to 9 weeks (63 days) of gestation, the standard pharmacological regimen recommended by the WHO and Indian national guidelines involves a combination of Mifepristone and Misoprostol. After administering 200 mg of Mifepristone orally, the subsequent dose of Misoprostol should be 800 mcg (Option D). This dose is typically administered 24–48 hours later via the vaginal, buccal, or sublingual (mucosal) routes to ensure high efficacy in inducing uterine contractions and expulsion of the products of conception. Doses of 200 mcg (Option A) or 400 mcg (Option C) are insufficient for early MTP and are more commonly used for cervical ripening or labor induction at term. A 600 mcg dose (Option B) is used for the prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage. Therefore, 800 mcg is the definitive standard dose for first-trimester medical abortion
questions.learning: For medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) up to 9 weeks (63 days) of gestation, the standard pharmacological regimen recommended by the WHO and Indian national guidelines involves a combination of Mifepristone and Misoprostol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with carcinoma endometrium is treated with pelvic external beam irradiation to the whole pelvis. Which of the following organs is most radiosensitive in the pelvic region?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovary

Among the options most radiosensitive organ is ovary> rectum> bladder> vagina.

The radiation tolerance dose for the ovary is 2-3 Gy whereas the vagina 90 Gy.

The radiation dose necessary to induce ovarian failure is age-dependent. A single dose of 3-4 Gray can induce amenorrhea in almost all women >40 yrs of age. In young women, oogenesis is much less sensitive to radiation as compared to the elderly.

* Most radioresistant organ: Vagina

* Radiation most commonly affects the stratum basalis layer of the skin.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to you with complaints of 18 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomiting twice in the last 4 hours. The child is irritable but drinking fluids. The optimal therapy for this child is______

Correct answer: B. Oral rehydration therapy with ORS

Oral rehydration therapy is the first line of treatment used in treating acute diarrheas due to all aetiologies, in all age groups, and in all countries and the recommended fluid is ORS.

Recommended formulation: Reduced osmolarity ORS solution, which has a reduced concentration of sodium (75 mmol/liter) and glucose (75 mmol/liter) helps in reducing the adverse effect of hypertonicity on net fluid absorption.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a police investigation, skeletal remains are recovered from a crime scene. Which forensic test would be most useful in distinguishing human bones from those of a dog?
questions.explanation: When skeletal remains are found, the first task of the forensic anthropologist is to determine if the bones are human or animal. The Precipitin test is a standard serological test used to identify the species of origin for biological materials, including bone extracts. It works by reacting the unknown sample with species-specific anti-sera; a positive reaction (precipitation) confirms the presence of proteins from that specific species (e.g., human). Acid-phosphatase (Option B) is used to screen for semen. LDH (Option C) is an enzyme marker of tissue damage. The Teichmann test (Option D) is used to confirm the presence of blood by forming hemin crystals. Differentiating human from canine (dog) bones is a routine requirement in forensic investigations to determine if a full criminal inquiry is warranted. While gross anatomical features often distinguish the two, the Precipitin test provides definitive biochemical proof of the species

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the standard treatment for empyema thoracis?
questions.explanation: Empyema thoracis is defined as the presence of pus in the pleural cavity, usually as a complication of pneumonia. The standard of care for managing empyema requires a two-pronged approach: "chest tube drainage" (intercostal drain) to evacuate the infected fluid and "systemic antibiotics" to treat the underlying infection. Antibiotics alone (Option A) are insufficient because they cannot penetrate the thick, acidic, and often loculated pus in the pleural space effectively. An ICD alone (Option C) removes the fluid but does not address the bacterial source. "Wait and watch" (Option D) is dangerous, as untreated empyema can lead to fibrothorax and lung entrapment, necessitating more invasive surgery like decortication. Management may also include intrapleural fibrinolytics or Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) if the empyema is complex or loculated. Early and aggressive drainage combined with appropriate antimicrobial therapy is essential to ensure resolution and prevent long-term respiratory impairment in these patients

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, along with chest indrawing and nasal flaring. There are no other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumonia

According to IMNCI guidelines, a 2–12 month old infant with fast breathing (respiratory rate ≥50/min) is classified as pneumonia. In this case, a respiratory rate of 66/min indicates fast breathing for age.

• Age-specific fast breathing:
• <2 months: ≥60/min
• 2–12 months: ≥50/min
• 1–5 years: ≥40/min
• Chest indrawing in infants may be present due to compliant chest wall and does not always indicate severe disease
• Severe pneumonia is diagnosed when there are danger signs such as inability to feed, lethargy, convulsions, or central cyanosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following factors is least likely to be involved in the development of beriberi?
questions.explanation: Beriberi is caused by a severe deficiency of Thiamine (Vitamin B1). A Vegan diet (Option B) is least likely to cause this deficiency because thiamine is widely available in many plant-based foods, including whole grains, legumes, seeds, and nuts. In contrast, the other options are significant risk factors. Chronic alcohol intake (Option D) is a leading cause of deficiency due to impaired absorption and poor diet. Bariatric surgery (Option C) leads to severe malabsorption and is a well-recognized trigger for acute thiamine deficiency. Chronic use of diuretics (Option A), particularly loop diuretics, increases the renal excretion of thiamine, potentially leading to depletion in patients with heart failure. Beriberi can manifest in "dry" (neurological) or "wet" (cardiovascular) forms. While vegans must be careful about Vitamin B12, they typically have adequate thiamine intake, making it an improbable cause for beriberi compared to clinical malabsorption or metabolic depletion scenarios
questions.learning: Beriberi is caused by a severe deficiency of Thiamine (Vitamin B1). A Vegan diet (Option B) is least likely to cause this deficiency because thiamine is widely available in many plant-based foods, including whole grains, legumes, seeds, and nuts.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Flipping of which molecule occurs during apoptosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phosphatidylserine

Phosphatidylserine (PS) is the molecule that flips out during apoptosis.

Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a phospholipid and a key component of the inner leaflet of cell membranes, playing a critical role in cell structure and signalling. It is particularly abundant in the brain, where it contributes to neuronal function, synaptic activity, and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier.

Phosphatidylserine (PS) switching is the process where PS translocates from the inner to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, serving as an "eat-me" signal for apoptosis. This externalization is crucial for the recognition and clearance of apoptotic cells by phagocytes.

Other options:

Options B and D: Phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine remain predominantly in the inner leaflet during normal cell conditions.

Option C: Sphingomyelin is typically found in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane and does not play a significant role in apoptotic signalling.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male patient presented with headache, nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis since early morning. He was diagnosed with depression 4 months back and has been taking medication. He gives the history of attending an office party the previous night where he consumed some red wine. On examination, his BP was 190/120. Which of the following medications must have caused this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phenelzine

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cheese reaction.

Here, the patient was most probably on phenelzine (non-selective and irreversible MAO inhibitor) and developed the clinical features of cheese reaction on having tyramine-rich food (red wine, cheese, milk).

Phenelzine is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor that is used to treat MDD resistant to first and second-line antidepressants. It acts to prevent the degradation of serotonin and norepinephrine. The common adverse effect associated with this is a hypertensive crisis as seen with ingestion of tyramine-rich foods (cheeses). Inhibition of gastrointestinal MAO reduces the degradation of tyramine which then enters the systemic circulation and promotes catecholamine release. Other side effects are weight gain, sexual dysfunction, and suicidal thoughts.

The drug of choice to treat hypertensive crisis in cheese reactions is phentolamine.

MAO-inhibitor with SSRI causes serotonin syndrome. Symptoms are fever, altered mental status, rigidity, hyperreflexia, and autonomic dysfunction.

Selegiline and rasagiline do not functionally inhibit MAO-A. They do not cause cheese reaction with doses used in clinical practice.

Other options:

*

Prazosin: Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It is commonly used to treat conditions like hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).  It is not known to cause hypertensive crises like the patient's presentation.

*

Phentolamine: Phentolamine is a non-selective alpha-adrenergic receptor antagonist. It is used in medical settings to treat hypertensive emergencies, such as those caused by excessive catecholamine release or drug interactions. In this case, phentolamine might be used to manage the hypertensive crisis caused by phenelzine and red wine.

*

Propranolol: Propranolol is a beta-blocker, and it works by blocking the effects of norepinephrine and other stress hormones. It is commonly prescribed to manage conditions like hypertension, angina, and certain types of arrhythmias.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The patient complains of repeated episodes of crusting in the nose with occasional bleeding. She had undergone surgery for nasal obstruction four months back. On examination, the following finding is seen. Which surgery has the highest likelihood to result in this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Submucosal resection

The given clinical vignette of a patient with complaints of repeated episodes of crusting in the nose with occasional bleeding and a history of nasal surgery for nasal obstruction is likely to have undergone correction of her DNS(Deviated Nasal Septum). The image is that of septal perforation; SMR (Submucosal resection ) has a higher likelihood of causing the same.

Septal perforation can occur after nasal surgery. Features depend on the size of the perforation. Smaller perforations can present with whistling while the larger perforations will present with epistaxis and crust formation. Therefore, septoplasty has become a more favored treatment of DNS than SMR due to its conservative approach.

Septoplasty is a conservative technique in the surgical correction of septal deformity. The key advantage is that it can be carried out as a daycare procedure, most of the bone and cartilage are retained, and complications are less. The deformed septum may corrected by various techniques like scoring the concave side, shaving, and wedge excision. Sometimes realignment by joining straight pieces of the septum outside the nose and replacing them can be done which is called extra-corporeal septoplasty.

The indications for an SMR are:

• DNS causing symptoms of nasal obstruction and recurrent headaches.
• DNS causing obstruction of paranasal sinuses and middle ear, resulting in recurrent sinusitis and otitis media.
• Recurrent epistaxis from a septal spur.
• As a part of septorhinoplasty, for cosmetic correction of external nasal deformities.
• As a preliminary step in hypophysectomy or vidian neurectomy.

It is contraindicated in children below 17 years of age, during acute respiratory infection, bleeding diathesis, untreated diabetes, or hypertension.

In this procedure, mucoperichondrial and mucoperiosteal flaps are raised on both sides of the septum. Bony and cartilaginous parts of the septum are excised. This is followed by extensive dissection of the septum removing all deformed bony and cartilaginous parts of the septum and preserving only a caudal and a dorsal strut of cartilage.

There is a greater chance of complications associated with SMR that include bleeding, septal hematoma, septal abscess, perforation, depression of the nasal bridge, retraction of the columella, and persistence of the deviation. The flapping of the nasal septum and toxic shock syndrome following SMR can also occur.

Conservative procedure

Not done in < 18 yrs

Killian’s incision is used

Other options:

Option A: FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery) is a minimally invasive procedure to enlarge nasal drainage pathways and improve sinus ventilation; rarely causes septal perforation.

Option C: Denker Approach is a surgical technique to access the maxillary sinus, pterygopalatine, and infratemporal fossae, used for large sinonasal tumors and extensive sinus pathology.

Option D: Endoscopic Surgical Treatment of Odontogenic Maxillary Sinusitis involves middle or inferior meatotomy; inferior meatotomy is preferred for foreign bodies or sinus floor cysts.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A teenager develops rapid swelling of the face, lips, and tongue along with difficulty breathing within minutes of eating prawns. What type of hypersensitivity reaction does this represent?
questions.explanation: The teenager is experiencing an acute systemic allergic reaction, likely anaphylaxis, following the ingestion of shellfish. This is the classic example of Type 1 (immediate) hypersensitivity. Type 1 reactions are mediated by IgE antibodies. Upon exposure to the allergen (prawns), IgE-primed mast cells and basophils rapidly degranulate, releasing inflammatory mediators like histamine. This results in vasodilation (swelling of lips and tongue) and bronchoconstriction (difficulty breathing) within minutes. Type 2 hypersensitivity (Option B) involves IgG or IgM antibodies attacking specific cell-surface antigens, like in hemolytic anemia. Type 3 (Option C) involves immune complex deposition, as in serum sickness. Type 4 (Option D) is a delayed-type, T-cell mediated response, such as the tuberculin test or contact dermatitis, which takes 48-72 hours to develop. The rapid onset of symptoms after an allergen identifies a Type 1 response
questions.learning: The teenager is experiencing an acute systemic allergic reaction, likely anaphylaxis, following the ingestion of shellfish. This is the classic example of Type 1 (immediate) hypersensitivity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which cranial nerve provides sensory innervation to the orbit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trigeminal nerve

The sensory innervation of the orbit is provided by the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

• Trigeminal nerve (CN V) → main sensory nerve of the face

• Ophthalmic division (V1) supplies:

• Cornea (highly sensitive)
• Conjunctiva
• Eyelids
• Lacrimal gland
• Orbit and surrounding structures

Important branches of V1:

• Nasociliary nerve → corneal sensation (afferent limb of corneal reflex)
• Frontal nerve
• Lacrimal nerve

Why not others:

• Vagus nerve (CN X): Visceral functions, no orbital sensory role
• Oculomotor nerve (CN III): Motor to extraocular muscles + parasympathetic to pupil
• Facial nerve (CN VII): Motor to facial muscles; lacrimation (parasympathetic), but no sensory supply to orbit

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme is found to be deficient in Von Gierke's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose-6- phosphatase

The enzyme deficient in Von Gierke's disease is glucose-6- phosphatase.

Von Gierke's disease is an autosomal recessive glycogen storage disorder, caused due to deficiency of the glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme.

Clinical presentation is often in infancy (usually at 3-4 months), and usually presents with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemic seizures, or both. Affected children have fat cheeks (doll-like faces), relatively thin extremities, short stature, and protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly, and enlarged kidneys. Easy bruising and epistaxis are common due to increased bleeding time. Other findings include delayed puberty, polycystic ovaries, osteopenia, pancreatitis, neutropenia, hepatic adenoma, and renal diseases.

Clinical presentation and laboratory findings of hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, ketosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia point to a suspected diagnosis of von Gierke's disease. A definitive diagnosis can be made by liver biopsy or gene-based variant analysis by single-gene sequencing or gene panels. Histopathology of the liver shows the intracytoplasmic accumulation of glycogen.

Treatment focuses on maintaining euglycemia. Nasogastric infusion of glucose or uncooked cornstarch is administered in infancy. For older children, uncooked cornstarch may be given orally. Dietary avoidance of fructose and galactose is necessary for these patients. Orthotropic liver transplantation is a potential cure for von Gierke's disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man who has recently returned from India presents with abdominal cramps and multiple episodes of watery diarrhea after consuming street food. Based on this clinical scenario, which antidiarrheal drug would be most appropriate for treatment?
questions.explanation: The patient has acute watery diarrhea after consuming street food, which is typical of traveler’s diarrhea. In uncomplicated cases (no blood in stool, no high fever), the primary goal is symptomatic relief, and loperamide is commonly used. Loperamide is an opioid receptor agonist that acts on the intestinal wall to reduce gut motility, allowing increased absorption of water and electrolytes. This leads to reduced stool frequency and improved consistency, providing rapid relief. It is widely used in mild to moderate traveler’s diarrhea and is often the first-line symptomatic treatment in exam scenarios. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Octreotide → Used for severe secretory diarrhea (e.g., VIPoma), not routine cases (C) Rifaximin → Antibiotic; used in moderate cases, but not primary symptomatic drug (D) Bismuth subsalicylate → Mild effect; less effective than loperamide

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida presents with painful vaginal bleeding during the first trimester. Ultrasonography shows a well-defined gestational sac with central embryonic echoes and detectable fetal cardiac activity, indicating a viable fetus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Threatened abortion is defined by vaginal bleeding occurring before 20 weeks of gestation while the cervical os remains closed. The crucial diagnostic finding on ultrasound (USG) in this case is the presence of fetal cardiac motion and a healthy-appearing embryo, which confirms that the pregnancy is still viable despite the bleeding. In an Inevitable abortion (Option A), the cervical os would be dilated, and fetal cardiac activity might be absent or the gestational sac would be low-lying. An Incomplete abortion (Option C) would show retained products of conception on USG with an open cervix. A Complete abortion (Option D) would show an empty uterine cavity on USG. Because the fetus is currently alive and the pregnancy continues, the clinical state is one of "threat" only. Management involves bed rest and observation, as many threatened abortions proceed to a normal full-term delivery. Therefore, Threatened abortion is the most accurate clinical diagnosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In the diagnosis of typhus, an antigen derived from Proteus species is used. What is this type of antigen known as?
questions.explanation: The Weil-Felix test for diagnosing typhus uses certain strains of Proteus bacteria because they share common antigens with Rickettsia. These are called heterophile antigens, defined as antigens that occur in unrelated species but are similar enough to cause cross-reactivity with the same antibodies. For example, antibodies produced during epidemic typhus agglutinate with Proteus OX19. Regarding the distractors, sequestered antigens (Option A) are hidden from the immune system (e.g., lens protein) and do not involve cross-reactivity. Superantigens (Option B) are potent immune activators like TSST-1 that bypass normal antigen presentation. Isoantigens (Option C) vary among individuals of the same species, such as blood group antigens. Because the test relies specifically on the "unrelated" cross-reaction between Proteus and Rickettsia, heterophile antigen is the correct term

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is allosteric activator of Pyruvate carboxylase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acetyl CoA

Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of gluconeogenesis:

Reaction:

Pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → Oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi

The enzyme is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA.

Why Acetyl-CoA?

• High levels of acetyl-CoA indicate that fatty acid β-oxidation is active.
• This signals that energy is abundant and that pyruvate should be diverted toward gluconeogenesis rather than entering the TCA cycle.
• Acetyl-CoA therefore activates pyruvate carboxylase, increasing the formation of oxaloacetate (OAA).

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Insulin ❌

• Insulin promotes glycolysis and glycogen synthesis while inhibiting gluconeogenesis.
• It does not allosterically activate pyruvate carboxylase.

• C. AMP ❌

• AMP is a marker of low cellular energy.
• It inhibits gluconeogenesis (notably fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase) and stimulates glycolysis.

• D. ADP ❌

• ADP also reflects a low-energy state.
• It inhibits several ATP-dependent steps of gluconeogenesis, including pyruvate carboxylase activity indirectly by signaling energy deficiency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented after a road traffic accident (RTA) with a head injury. CT head is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depressed skull fracture

The clinical history and the CT image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the left frontal bone.

A depressed skull fracture occurs when a portion of the skull is pushed inward due to trauma, creating a depression in the bone. This type of fracture can occur as a result of a direct impact to the head, such as in a road traffic accident.

The management of depressed skull fractures:

* The first step is to order a CT scan to know the degree of depression and to exclude the presence of an intracranial hematoma or contusion.

* The depressed fracture is elevated and managed as an open fracture (surgery) if:

* The degree of depression is greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull

* The wound is are open and grossly contaminated

* There are focal neurological deficits

* Less severe depressed fractures are managed by the closure of the overlying scalp laceration, if present.

Other options:

Option A: Concussion refers to a temporary disturbance in brain function following head trauma and typically does not show up on CT scans.

Option B: Epidural hematoma often appears as a lens-shaped collection of blood on CT scans.

Option D: Subarachnoid hemorrhage may appear as diffuse or localized blood on imaging.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Theophylline causes diuresis by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenosine antagonism

The diuretic effect of theophylline is due to blockade of adenosine (A1) receptors.

Theophylline is a methylxanthine drug that acts by:

• Inhibition of phosphodiesterase enzyme (PDE). PDE3 inhibition causes relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle and PDE4 inhibition causes inhibition of the release of cytokines and chemokines which further leads to a decrease in immune cell migration and activation.
• Blockade of adenosine receptors, which inhibits bronchoconstriction. However, blockade of A1 receptors in the glomerular afferent arteriole and PCT causes diuresis.
• Activating enzyme histone deacetylase-2, which is responsible for its anti-inflammatory action
questions.learning: Adenosine antagonism — The diuretic effect of theophylline is due to blockade of adenosine (A1) receptors. Theophylline is a methylxanthine drug that acts by: • Inhibition of phosphodiesterase enzyme (PDE).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45 year male presented to OPD with complaints of swelling on the upper back. It has been present for nearly a year and has not increased in size. On examination, the swelling is non pulsatile, and slip sign is positive approximately measuring 5*5 cm. Which of the following statements is likely true?
options: Excision can be done if the patient makes a request
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Excision can be done if the patient makes a request

The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old male presenting with a non-pulsatile swelling on the upper back, which has not increased in size for nearly a year and measures approximately 5*5 cm with a positive slip sign, suggests a benign lesion like a lipoma. If the patient requests it, excision can be performed.

Lipomas are benign tumors of adipose tissue. It can occur anywhere and at any depth. It can be encapsulated or diffuse, superficial or deep.
On examination, they are nontender and non-pulsatile. Because of the soft consistency, they may appear to be fluctuant but they are not. The slip sign is positive.
Diagnosis is mostly clinical. Biopsy is rarely indicated in case of clinical doubt of malignant transformation. All lipomas need not be excised. Lipomas can be excised on suspicion of malignant transformation and sometimes at the patient's request.
Imaging is required in cases of deep-seated tumors only.

Other options:

Option A: Lipomas have a very low risk of malignant transformation into liposarcoma.
Option B: While FNAC (Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology) can be used to confirm the diagnosis, it is not always necessary for a typical lipoma.
Option C: PET scans are generally not needed for benign conditions like lipomas. They are used in cases where malignancy is suspected.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: During spermatogenesis, which hormone is responsible for inhibiting the secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)?
questions.explanation: Inhibin, specifically Inhibin B, is the primary hormone secreted by Sertoli cells in the testes that negatively regulates the secretion of Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary. This feedback mechanism is crucial for controlling the rate of spermatogenesis. While testosterone (Option A) and other androgens (Option D) also provide negative feedback, they primarily act on the hypothalamus and pituitary to inhibit the secretion of Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), rather than FSH directly. Luteinizing Hormone (Option C) serves to stimulate the Leydig cells to produce testosterone and does not have an inhibitory role in this pathway. Therefore, Inhibin is the specific factor responsible for the targeted inhibition of FSH during the male reproductive cycle
questions.learning: Inhibin, specifically Inhibin B, is the primary hormone secreted by Sertoli cells in the testes that negatively regulates the secretion of Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the correct order of End plate potential at the neuromuscular junction:
options: Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release → Na+ channel opens → Action potential
Na+ channel opens → Action potential → Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release
Ach Release → Na+ channel opens → Action potential → Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal
Action potential → Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release → Na+ channel opens
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release → Na+ channel opens → Action potential

Ca²⁺ entry in Axon Terminal → ACh Release → Na⁺ channel opens → Action potential

The Full Sequence

| Step | Event | Location

| ---- | ----- | --------

| 1 | Motor nerve AP arrives | Axon terminal

| 2 | Ca²⁺ enters via VGCC | Axon terminal

| 3 | ACh released into synaptic cleft | Presynaptic

| 4 | ACh binds nicotinic receptors | Motor end plate

| 5 | Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx | Postsynaptic membrane

| 6 | End plate potential generated | Motor end plate

| 7 | If EPP reaches threshold → muscle AP | Muscle fiber

Key Conceptual Point

The question asks specifically about end plate potential — this is a postsynaptic event that begins with ACh binding, NOT with the muscle action potential.

The EPP is the graded potential at the motor end plate caused by Na⁺ influx. It is what leads to the muscle action potential, so the action potential comes last in this sequence.

Why Other Options Fail

B — Starts with Na⁺ channel opening before ACh release. Na⁺ channels open because ACh binds — can't happen first.

C — Starts with ACh release, skipping Ca²⁺ entry. ACh cannot be released without the Ca²⁺ trigger — this is the step that couples electrical signal to vesicle fusion.

D — Starts with action potential. This confuses the muscle AP with the nerve AP. The sequence being asked is what happens after the nerve AP arrives — the nerve AP is the trigger, not part of the EPP sequence itself.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old female with a previous history of rheumatic fever presented with shortness of breath, palpitations, and orthopnea. On auscultation loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur were heard. Which of the following valvular heart diseases best explains the additional heart sound?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mitral Stenosis (MS)

The above clinical scenario of a 19-year-old female with a history of rheumatic fever, presenting with a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur, is consistent with Mitral stenosis.

MS is a valvular heart disease, most commonly caused by rheumatic fever. Other causes include:

* Mitral annular calcification with leaflet involvement

* Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis

* Left atrial myxoma

* Infective endocarditis with large vegetation

The murmur of MS corresponds to the P wave of the ECG.

MS leads to increased pressure in the left atrium. Left atrial abnormality may cause broad, notched P waves in the limb leads and a biphasic P wave in lead V1 with a prominent negative component representing delayed depolarisation of the left atria. P wave may become tall and peaked in the lead II and upright in lead V1 due to severe pulmonary hypertension or when tricuspid stenosis complicates mitral stenosis, leading to right atrial enlargement. The QRS complex is usually normal. In severe pulmonary hypertension, right axis deviation and RV hypertrophy can be seen.

Auscultatory findings in mitral stenosis are:

* A mid-diastolic murmur

* The first heart sound (S1) is accentuated

* The opening snap (OS) is after the A2 sound. It is best heard during the expiration and at the apex of the heart

* The OS is followed by a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur, which is heard best at the apex with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position. This murmur correlates with the severity of the stenosis.

Chronic inflammation causes the thickening of the valve leaflets and the shortening and fusion of chordae tendineae, leading to the formation of a funnel-shaped or fish-mouth valve. Calcification immobilizes the leaflets and narrows the valve further.

Other options:

Option A: Tricuspid stenosis presents as a mid-diastolic murmur, but is not commonly associated with Rheumatic fever.

Option B: Mitral regurgitation presents as a holosystolic murmur.

Option D: Aortic regurgitation presents as an early diastolic murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
The blood investigation of a patient is given below. What is the probabale diagnosis?

HBsAg - Nonreactive

HBeAg - Nonreactive

IgG anti-HbcAg - Reactive

IgM anti-HbcAg - Nonreactive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Remote infection with hepatitis B

The most probable diagnosis is remote infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV).

A non-reactive HbsAg rules out active HBV infection (Options A and B).

Non-reactive IgM anti-HbcAg suggests that the patient is not in the window period (Option C).

Reactive IgG HBcAg is seen in the late convalescence stage and remains lifelong.

Option A: In acute hepatitis B, HBsAg is reactive, HBeAg can be reactive in highly infectious individuals, and IgM Anti HBcAg is reactive. Anti-Hbs is reactive in recovery.

Option B: In chronic hepatitis B, HBsAg is reactive, and IgG Anti HBcAg is reactive. Anti-HBs is non-reactive.

Option D: Core window period is a phase where even though hepatitis infection is present, HBsAg is non-reactive. Diagnosis is based on the presence of IgM Anti HBcAg.
questions.learning: Remote infection with hepatitis B — The most probable diagnosis is remote infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV). A non-reactive HbsAg rules out active HBV infection (Options A and B).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The most common cause of seizures in a 2-year- old child is febrile seizures, which typically occur between 6 months and 5 years of age and are associated with a rapid rise in body temperature due to infection.
questions.explanation: In the pediatric population between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, febrile seizures are the most common cause of convulsive episodes (Option C). These are seizures triggered by a rapid rise in body temperature, usually associated with common childhood viral infections, in the absence of an intracranial infection or metabolic imbalance. While head trauma (Option A), severe malnutrition (Option B), and underlying neurological deficits (Option D) are important causes of symptomatic seizures, they are statistically much less frequent than simple febrile convulsions in this specific age group. Most febrile seizures are generalized, brief, and carry an excellent prognosis without the need for long-term antiepileptic therapy. Clinicians must focus on ruling out meningitis and managing the underlying fever. Therefore, given the 2-year-old age mark, febrile seizures remain the most prevalent etiology
