questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with multiple, recurrent episodes of syncope. His ECG shows P waves at a rate of 75 bpm and QRS complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This question is a duplicate of Question 155. The patient presents with syncope (fainting) and an ECG showing atrioventricular dissociation (P-rate 75, QRS-rate 35). This is diagnostic for complete (3rd-degree) heart block. Syncope resulting from this sudden cardiac output drop is termed Stokes-Adams syndrome. Mobitz Type II (Option A) is a 2nd-degree block where the PR interval is constant but some P-waves are not followed by QRS complexes; it often progresses to complete block. First-degree block (Option C) involves simple PR prolongation and is usually asymptomatic. WPW syndrome (Option D) involves an accessory pathway causing pre-excitation and a delta wave on ECG, not heart block. Complete heart block in an elderly patient is a high-risk condition and is the most common indication for permanent pacemaker implantation. The term "Stokes-Adams" remains a classic clinical eponym for this life-threatening interaction between arrhythmia and cerebral perfusion
questions.learning: This question is a duplicate of Question 155. The patient presents with syncope (fainting) and an ECG showing atrioventricular dissociation (P-rate 75, QRS-rate 35).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a known history of lung cancer presents with shortness of breath and dizziness. On physical examination, breath sounds are markedly diminished over the left lower scapular region. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a known history of lung cancer, the development of dyspnea (shortness of breath) and reduced breath sounds over a specific lung area (the left lower scapular region) is highly suggestive of a malignant pleural effusion. This occurs when cancer cells spread to the pleura, causing fluid to accumulate in the pleural space, which compresses the underlying lung and blocks sound transmission. Pneumothorax (Option D) also causes reduced breath sounds but typically presents more acutely with a sudden "pop" or sharp pain. Constrictive pericarditis (Option A) and Cardiac tamponade (Option C) would present with distant heart sounds and elevated neck veins rather than localized absent breath sounds. Diagnosis of pleural effusion is confirmed by chest X-ray showing a "meniscus sign" and blunting of the costophrenic angle. Management involves therapeutic thoracocentesis (draining the fluid) for symptom relief and cytological analysis to confirm the malignant nature of the effusion
questions.learning: In a patient with a known history of lung cancer, the development of dyspnea (shortness of breath) and reduced breath sounds over a specific lung area (the left lower scapular region) is highly suggestive of a malignant pleural effusion.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Based on the given clinical details, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of inspiratory stridor in infants. It is a congenital condition in which the supraglottic laryngeal structures are soft and floppy, causing them to collapse inward during inspiration and partially obstruct the airway. The characteristic clinical features include loud, high-pitched inspiratory stridor that typically worsens when the infant is crying, feeding, or lying supine and improves when the infant is prone. On laryngoscopic examination, classical findings include an omega-shaped epiglottis, shortened aryepiglottic folds, and redundant arytenoid mucosa. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Vocal cord paralysis usually presents with a weak or hoarse cry and may be associated with aspiration. 2. Subglottic stenosis causes biphasic stridor and is often linked to a history of prolonged intubation. 3. Laryngeal papilloma presents with progressive hoarseness due to wart-like lesions on the vocal cords. 4. Most cases of laryngomalacia are benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously by 18–24 months as the laryngeal cartilages mature
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of inspiratory stridor in infants. It is a congenital condition in which the supraglottic laryngeal structures are soft and floppy, causing them to collapse inward during inspiration and partially obstruct the airway.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man from Nellore, Andhra Pradesh, presents with characteristic dental lesions. Based on his geographic background and the typical appearance of these lesions, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image displays "mottling of enamel," characterized by brownish stains and pitting, which is the pathognomonic clinical sign of dental fluorosis. This condition occurs due to chronic ingestion of excessive fluoride during the period of tooth development. The geographic clue—Nellore, Andhra Pradesh—is highly significant as several districts in Andhra Pradesh are known endemic belts where groundwater contains high fluoride levels. Selenosis (Option A) typically leads to hair loss and nail changes. Plumbism (Option B), or lead poisoning, often presents with a bluish-black "Burtonian line" on the gums rather than enamel mottling. Lathyrism (Option D) is a neurological disorder caused by consuming grass pea and does not affect the teeth. Dental fluorosis is a permanent cosmetic and structural defect. In severe cases, it can be accompanied by skeletal fluorosis, which causes crippling bone and joint deformities. Prevention relies on providing defluoridated water or alternate water sources in endemic regions
questions.learning: The image displays "mottling of enamel," characterized by brownish stains and pitting, which is the pathognomonic clinical sign of dental fluorosis. This condition occurs due to chronic ingestion of excessive fluoride during the period of tooth development.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Ring sequestrum is seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pin tract infection

Ring sequestrum is seen in a pin tract infection.

Sequestrum is a fragment of dead bone lying within a cavity formed by necrosis. Infection at a pin site in an external fixation construct leads to a ring sequestrum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a recent history of pneumonia develops a pleural effusion. On pleural fluid analysis, which finding is most characteristic of a parapneumonic effusion?
options: Pleural protein/plasma protein ratio less than 0.5
Pleural LDH less than 2/3rd of plasma LDH
Pleural LDH less than 0.6 of plasma LDH
questions.explanation: A pleural fluid pH of less than 7.2 is a critical indicator of a complicated parapneumonic effusion. This acidic state occurs because of increased metabolic activity by bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space, leading to lactic acid accumulation. According to Light’s Criteria, parapneumonic effusions are exudative, meaning they must have a pleural/serum protein ratio and a pleural/serum LDH ratio . Thus, Options A, B, and D are incorrect as they describe transudative characteristics. Complicated effusions often feature low glucose ( mg/dL) and high LDH levels ( U/L). Recognizing a low pH is essential because it serves as an absolute indication for chest tube drainage (thoracostomy) to prevent the development of a trapped lung or loculated empyema
questions.learning: A pleural fluid pH of less than 7.2 is a critical indicator of a complicated parapneumonic effusion. This acidic state occurs because of increased metabolic activity by bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space, leading to lactic acid accumulation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A mother brought her 3-month-old male child to the hospital, who is currently unable to pass urine. A similar issue was reported 15 days ago. The catheter could be passed without difficulty. The image of the micturating cystourethrogram is given below. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Destruction of valves

The given image of a micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) shows dilated prostatic urethra and transverse filling defects corresponding with the posterior urethral valves and the most appropriate management for this condition is destruction of valves.

Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children. The pathological valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit within them, which typically lie just distal to the verumontanum. They act as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow.

Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder in fetus along with oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary infections in the neonatal period or with uremia and renal failure. Clinically a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present. The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography.

The initial step in treatment is to insert a urinary catheter to drain the urine and decompress the bladder and upper urinary tracts. A small polyethene feeding tube (No. 5 or No. 8 French) is inserted into the bladder, which can be difficult because the tube's tip can coil in the prostatic urethra. A Foley catheter should not be used because the balloon can cause severe bladder spasms, which can result in severe ureteral obstruction.

Endoscopic valve ablation and symptomatic management of urinary tract infections are the definitive treatments.

The below image shows the micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) with dilated prostatic urethra and transverse filling defects (constriction) corresponding with the posterior urethral valves.

The ultrasound shows the typical 'key-hole' sign in which the bladder and the proximal urethra are dilated.
questions.learning: Destruction of valves — The given image of a micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) shows dilated prostatic urethra and transverse filling defects corresponding with the posterior urethral valves and the most appropriate management for this condition is…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl has a low hemoglobin level. What is the recommended therapeutic dose of iron-folic acid?
options: 45 mg elemental iron + 400µg folic acid once daily
60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid twice daily
100 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid once daily
100 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid twice daily
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid twice daily

All children between 10-19 years of age diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia should receive therapeutic iron-folic acid (IFA) supplementation, which is higher than the prophylactic dose. In many Indian public health/PSM examination questions, the recommended therapeutic regimen for school-aged children with anemia is:

• 60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid twice daily for 3 months, followed by reassessment of hemoglobin.
questions.learning: 60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid twice daily All children between 10-19 years of age diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia should receive therapeutic iron-folic acid (IFA) supplementation, which is higher than the prophylactic dose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A biopsy from a lung mass is shown below. Which immunohistochemical marker is most likely to be positive in this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chromogranin A

Recognize the immunohistochemical profile of neuroendocrine tumors of the lung (especially small cell carcinoma). These tumors express neuroendocrine markers, including Chromogranin A, Synaptophysin, CD56 (NCAM), and INSM1. Chromogranin A positivity confirms neuroendocrine differentiation and helps distinguish these tumors from other primary lung malignancies.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cytokeratin: Marker of epithelial origin; positive in most carcinomas, including small cell carcinoma, but not specific for neuroendocrine differentiation.
• B. S-100: Marker for melanoma, Schwann cells, sustentacular cells, and some dendritic cells.
• C. CD1a: Marker for Langerhans cells, positive in Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
questions.learning: Chromogranin — A Recognize the immunohistochemical profile of neuroendocrine tumors of the lung (especially small cell carcinoma). These tumors express neuroendocrine markers, including Chromogranin A, Synaptophysin, CD56 (NCAM), and INSM1.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In a child with severe acute malnutrition who presents with shock, which intravenous fluid should be preferred for initial management?
questions.explanation: Treating shock in a child with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) is delicate because these children are highly susceptible to fluid overload and heart failure. According to WHO guidelines, the prioritized fluid is a half-strength isotonic solution that also contains sugar to prevent hypoglycemia, specifically Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose. If this is unavailable, half-strength Darrow's solution with 5% dextrose is also an option. Standard Normal Saline (Option A) or Ringer's lactate (Option B) are too high in sodium content and can exacerbate electrolyte imbalances and cardiac strain in the malnourished child. 10% dextrose (Option C) addresses hypoglycemia but does not provide the volume expansion necessary for shock. Fluid boluses in SAM are given at a slower rate (typically 15 mL/kg over 1 hour) compared to well-nourished children, with frequent monitoring of respiratory and heart rates. Therefore, the dextrose-saline/lactate combination is the safest and correct choice
questions.learning: Treating shock in a child with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) is delicate because these children are highly susceptible to fluid overload and heart failure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases are included in the scheme, which has the logo as given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CVD, Cancer, Diabetes, Stroke

The logo shows the NPCDCS scheme that has separate components for cancer and other non-communicable diseases like diabetes, cardiovascular disease and stroke.

The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) has specialized facilities in district hospitals.

It has been implemented in over 100 districts in 21 states.

At the subcentre level under NPCDCS, screening and referral is done.

NOTE: Non-alcoholic fattly liver disease (NAFLD) has been integrated with NPCDCS in 2021.
questions.learning: CVD, Cancer, Diabetes, Stroke — The logo shows the NPCDCS scheme that has separate components for cancer and other non-communicable diseases like diabetes, cardiovascular disease and stroke.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the most suitable dietary modification for a middle-aged man with a rare form of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency presenting with high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
options: High protein and low carbohydrate intake
High carbohydrate and low fat intake
High fat and low carbohydrate intake
questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) is the enzyme complex that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle. A deficiency in PDH leads to the shunting of pyruvate into lactic acid, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis. The most effective dietary management for these patients is a ketogenic diet, which is characterized by high fat and low carbohydrate intake. This diet provides an alternative fuel source by generating ketone bodies that can be converted into acetyl-CoA bypassing the defective PDH step. High carbohydrate intake (Options B and D) would exacerbate the condition by increasing pyruvate and lactic acid levels. While high protein (Option A) is part of many diets, it is not the primary mechanism for bypassing the PDH defect. Therefore, a high-fat, low-carbohydrate regimen is the specific dietary therapy used to manage metabolic acidosis in PDH deficiency
questions.learning: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) is the enzyme complex that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle. A deficiency in PDH leads to the shunting of pyruvate into lactic acid, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with progressive anaemia and cervical lymphadenopathy. The peripheral smear is shown below. Which CD markers will be present in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23

The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing smudge cells is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, which is positive for CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, and CD5+.

Loss of tumour-suppressor genes in chromosome 13 results in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non-specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients.

The chromosomal defects in CLL include

* Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)

* Deletion of 11q

* Trisomy 12q

* Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic features of CLL are CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, and CD5+.

On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates, which are referred to as proliferation centres. These proliferation centres are pathognomonic to CLL when present.

Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.

Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

Other options:

Option A: CD10, CD22, and CD79 are positive in Burkitt lymphoma.

Option B: CD10, CD19, and CD22 are positive in follicular lymphoma.

Option D: CD10, CD19, and CD79 are positive in pre-B cell acute lymphoid leukaemia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A firearm entry wound is shown below. What is the most likely range of firing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Distant

A distant-range firearm entry wound is characterized by the presence of an abrasion collar (contusion collar) and a grease/wipe collar, with absence of burning, blackening (soot), and tattooing (powder stippling) because the flame, smoke, and unburnt powder particles do not reach the target at long distances.

Why is C correct?

• Abrasion collar ✓ – Produced as the bullet stretches and abrades the skin while entering.
• Grease (wipe) collar ✓ – Formed by deposition of grease, dirt, lead, and lubricant from the bullet onto the wound margins.
• No tattooing or blackening ✓ – Indicates the muzzle was beyond the range of powder particle deposition, consistent with distant firing.

Why not the other options?

• A. Close range: Tattooing, blackening, and sometimes burning are usually present.
• B. Contact range: Muzzle is in contact with the skin; features include muzzle imprint, searing, blackening within the wound, and possible stellate tears (especially over bony areas).
• D. Exit wound: Typically lacks an abrasion and grease collar and is often irregular with everted margins.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-month-old infant presents with an empty scrotal sac and bilateral inguinal masses on examination. What is the appropriate next step in the management of this child?
options: Surgical exploration within the next 2 weeks
Wait and watch for spontaneous descent within the next 6 months
questions.explanation: Undescended testes (cryptorchidism) are common in neonates. In a 1-month-old infant, the most appropriate management is a "wait and watch" approach (Option D) . Spontaneous descent of the testes into the scrotum occurs in the majority of cases within the first 6 months of life. If the testes remain undescended beyond 6 to 12 months, surgical intervention is then warranted. Performing orchiopexy now (Option C) or surgical exploration in 2 weeks (Option B) is premature, as physiological descent is still likely. Karyotyping (Option A) is indicated if there are other signs of ambiguous genitalia or bilateral impalpable testes, but not for simple inguinal masses in an otherwise normal infant. Therefore, because descent is a continuing developmental process in early infancy, observation for at least 6 months is the standard clinical guideline to avoid unnecessary surgery. Consequently, Option D is the definitive next step
questions.learning: Undescended testes (cryptorchidism) are common in neonates. In a 1-month-old infant, the most appropriate management is a "wait and watch" approach (Option D) .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with difficulty seeing from the left side in both eyes, while central vision remains intact, and there is no history of recent trauma. Which condition best explains his visual field disturbances?
questions.explanation: A patient with difficulty seeing from the left side in both eyes has a left-sided homonymous hemianopia, indicating a lesion in the right visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma. The fact that central vision remains clear is the defining feature of macular sparing. This specific pattern strongly suggests a lesion in the occipital cortex, most commonly due to a stroke involving the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). The macula is spared because the macular representation in the visual cortex has a dual blood supply from both the PCA and the middle cerebral artery. A standard homonymous hemianopia (Option B) would include the loss of central vision if the lesion was in the optic tract. Quadrantanopia (Option A) involves only one-fourth of the visual field. Heteronymous hemianopia (Option C) affects opposite sides in both eyes (e.g., bitemporal), characteristically seen in chiasmal lesions. Accurate field testing is vital for localizing neurological lesions
questions.learning: A patient with difficulty seeing from the left side in both eyes has a left-sided homonymous hemianopia, indicating a lesion in the right visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has a history of ocular injury caused by a flying foreign body and is later diagnosed with hemochromatosis. Which substance is most likely responsible for the abnormal deposition seen in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of a "flying foreign body injury" and subsequent diagnosis of hemochromatosis points to iron as the involved substance. Intraocular iron foreign bodies can cause a condition called siderosis, where iron undergoes electrolytic dissociation and deposits in ocular tissues. This leads to toxic degenerative changes, including a pathognomonic rusty ring in the lens capsule (the earliest sign) and pigmentary retinal dystrophy. While systemic hemochromatosis is a metabolic disorder, a metallic intraocular foreign body provides a local source of iron deposition. Aluminum (Option B) typically causes fibrosis but not the widespread toxic changes seen in siderosis. Wood (Option C) and glass (Option D) are non-metallic and often inert, though wood carries a high risk of bacterial infection (endophthalmitis). CT scanning is the investigation of choice to localize metallic foreign bodies. Removal via magnets or forceps is the standard treatment
questions.learning: The patient’s history of a "flying foreign body injury" and subsequent diagnosis of hemochromatosis points to iron as the involved substance. Intraocular iron foreign bodies can cause a condition called siderosis, where iron undergoes electrolytic…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs does not belong to the class of alkylating agents?
questions.explanation: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is an antimetabolite, specifically a pyrimidine analog, not an alkylating agent. It works by inhibiting the enzyme thymidylate synthase, thereby blocking the synthesis of thymidine and disrupting DNA production. Melphalan (Option A), Cyclophosphamide (Option B), and Busulfan (Option C) are all classic alkylating agents. Alkylating agents work by attaching an alkyl group to DNA, typically at the guanine base, which leads to DNA cross-linking, strand breaks, and eventually cell apoptosis. Cyclophosphamide is a nitrogen mustard, Melphalan is used for multiple myeloma, and Busulfan is often used for chronic myeloid leukemia. While both antimetabolites and alkylating agents are used in cancer chemotherapy, they have distinct biochemical mechanisms and belong to different pharmacological classes. Because 5-FU interferes with metabolic pathways rather than directly alkylating DNA, it is the correct answer to this "not" question
questions.learning: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is an antimetabolite, specifically a pyrimidine analog, not an alkylating agent. It works by inhibiting the enzyme thymidylate synthase, thereby blocking the synthesis of thymidine and disrupting DNA production.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following hormones is the major product of the fetal adrenal glands?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. DHEA

The major steroid products of the fetal adrenal gland are DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) and DHEA-S.

They serve as important substrates for estrogen synthesis in the placenta.

The fetal-adrenal-placental axis is vital for normal childbirth. Placental corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulates the fetal adrenal gland to produce DHEA-S and cortisol. Cortisol further stimulates the production of placental CRH, creating a positive feedback loop that enhances adrenal steroid hormone production.

The steroid products released by the fetal adrenal gland have effects on the placenta and membranes. These effects contribute to transforming the myometrium from a quiescent to a contractile state.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is an autosomal recessive condition in which cortisol synthesis in the adrenal gland is affected. Cortisol deficiency increases the secretion of ACTH, which leads to adrenocortical hyperplasia and overproduction of intermediate metabolites.
questions.learning: DHEA — The major steroid products of the fetal adrenal gland are DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) and DHEA-S. They serve as important substrates for estrogen synthesis in the placenta.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the most commonly used test in screening for neonatal hearing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Otoacoustic emissions (OAE)

Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) are used in the universal neonatal hearing screening protocol.

In India, a two-stage screening protocol is followed according to which infants are screened first with otoacoustic emissions (OAE). Infants who fail the OAE are screened with auditory brainstem response (ABR) or Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA), which is also the definitive test. All babies kept in NICU must be screened by BERA test as per the protocol.

The first screening is usually conducted at birth or before discharge. Conducting the first screening before discharge is preferred to ensure better coverage and reduce loss to follow-up. A second screening is scheduled anytime between 1–3 weeks or during the next scheduled visit at 6 weeks.

All babies with abnormal BERA should undergo detailed ENT evaluation and hearing-aid fitting (cochlear implants) and auditory rehabilitation must be done before 6 months of age.

Other options

Option A: Conduction audiometry is used in older children and adults to measure hearing thresholds, requiring active cooperation, which is not feasible in neonates.

Option C: Brainstem evoked response audiometry (BERA): While BERA is more precise and can detect auditory pathway issues up to the brainstem, it is more time-consuming and costly. It is typically used for confirmation if OAE results are abnormal.

Option D: Clap and smile is an outdated, subjective test and is not reliable for neonatal hearing screening.
questions.learning: Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) are used in the universal neonatal hearing screening protocol. In India, a two-stage screening protocol is followed according to which infants are screened first with otoacoustic emissions (OAE).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is amplified in an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DNA

In an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus DNA is amplified.

COVID-19 virus (Coronavirus) is a single-stranded linear RNA virus. RT-PCR is used to identify the RNA of this virus by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

The steps of RT-PCR can be explained as follows:

* Isolation of RNA

* Reverse transcription- Synthesis of DNA from RNA by using an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase

* Polymerase chain reaction- Using heat-stable DNA polymerase, such as Taq polymerase, DNA is amplified

* Separation of the PCR products-  by agarose gel electrophoresis

* Visualisation of the amplified DNA (with ethidium bromide)

(Note again that it is the DNA that is amplified and not RNA even though we are trying to detect an RNA virus)
questions.learning: DNA — In an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus DNA is amplified. COVID-19 virus (Coronavirus) is a single-stranded linear RNA virus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following molecular analysis methods is used to detect RNA ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

RT PCR(Reverse Transcriptase PCR) is a molecular analysis method used for the detection of RNA. It can be used to quantitate mRNA levels by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

The northern blot technique can also be used to detect RNAs. Here, the mixture of mRNA molecules is separated by electrophoresis and then transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and hybridized with radiolabeled probes.

Sanger’s technique:

• This was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins.
• Sanger’s reagent is 1- Flouro 2,4 Dinitro benzene.
• The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin.
• Only dipeptides and tripeptides can be sequenced by this method.

G banding (Giemsa banding):

It is the most common technique used in cytogenetics to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes. It is useful for identifying genetic diseases through the photographic representation of the entire chromosome complement. The metaphase chromosomes are treated with trypsin (to partially digest the chromosome) and stained with Giemsa stain.

Heterochromatic regions, which tend to be rich with adenine and thymine (AT-rich) DNA and relatively gene-poor, stain darker and appear as dark bands in G-banding. In contrast, less condensed chromatin, which tends to be rich with guanine and cytosine (GC-rich) and more transcriptionally active incorporates less Giemsa stain, and these regions appear as light bands in G-banding. The image below shows a G-banding karyogram of a normal human male.

Western blot, also called immunoblots, is a technique used to study protein molecules. The proteins undergo electrophoresis and then are transferred to a membrane. These proteins are then tagged with the specific antibodies and visualized.
questions.learning: RT-PCR RT PCR(Reverse Transcriptase PCR) is a molecular analysis method used for the detection of RNA. It can be used to quantitate mRNA levels by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following are true about oculomotor nerve palsy except _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lateral and upward gaze

Lateral and upward gaze is a sign of trochlear (4th) nerve palsy and not of oculomotor palsy. Oculomotor (3rd) nerve palsy leads to lateral and downward gaze.

3rd Cranial nerve palsy presents with

• Ptosis(option A) due to weakness of levator palpebrae superioris muscle (LPS)
• Abduction and depression in the primary position ("down and out") due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus (6th nerve supply)  and superior oblique muscles (4th nerve supply)
• Dilated pupil(option B), loss of light reflex(option C) and defective accommodation due to parasympathetic palsy (involvement of Edinger Westphal parasympathetic supply)
• Limited adduction, elevation and depression due to ipsilateral paralysis of medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus .

4th cranial nerve palsy presents with superior oblique muscle paralysis.

Clinical findings of trochlear nerve palsy include:

• Hypertropia (elevation) in the primary position
• Extorsion that is greatest in abduction
• Compensatory head posture with contralateral face turn and head tilt with chin slightly depressed. This position is assumed to avoid Diplopia.
• Limitation of depression
• Normal abduction and elevation

The below given image depicts 4th cranial nerve palsy.
questions.learning: Lateral and upward gaze Lateral and upward gaze is a sign of trochlear (4th) nerve palsy and not of oculomotor palsy. Oculomotor (3rd) nerve palsy leads to lateral and downward gaze.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When does secondary post-partum haemorrhage develop?
options: Shortly after the delivery of placenta
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 24 hours - 12 weeks after delivery

Secondary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after delivery.

Types of PPH:

* Primary: haemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth

* Most common cause: atonic PPH

* Secondary: haemorrhage occurring after 24 hours and up to 12 weeks postpartum

* Most common cause: retained placenta

Causes of PPH (mnemonic: 4’T’):

* T - Tone: Atonic PPH

* T - Trauma: Traumatic PPH

* T - Thrombin: Coagulopathy (DIC and hypofibrinogenemia)

* T - Tissue: retained products of conception.
questions.learning: 24 hours - 12 weeks after delivery Secondary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after delivery. Types of PPH: * Primary: haemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth * Most common cause: atonic PPH * Secondary:…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man becomes unable to walk after an accident and subsequently loses his job because of this disability. How should his unemployment be classified?
questions.explanation: According to the WHO International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities, and Handicaps (ICIDH), these terms have specific hierarchical meanings. An Impairment (Option C) is a structural or functional abnormality (e.g., a broken leg). A Disability (Option A) is the resulting restriction in the ability to perform an activity (e.g., "unable to walk"). A Handicap is the social or occupational disadvantage resulting from that impairment or disability that limits the fulfillment of a normal role. In this scenario, the man's "unemployment" is a direct social disadvantage caused by his inability to walk; therefore, the loss of his job is classified as a handicap. Disease (Option D) is the underlying pathological condition. Therefore, because unemployment is an external, societal consequence, "handicap" is the correct forensic and public health classification
questions.learning: According to the WHO International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities, and Handicaps (ICIDH), these terms have specific hierarchical meanings.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of Hirschsprung disease?
options: Failure of migration of neural crest cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure of migration of neural crest cells

Hirschsprung disease occurs due to the failure of migration of the neural crest cells to the bowel wall.

During normal embryogenesis, the neural crest cells migrate from the caecum to the rectum. The enteric neuronal plexuses develop from these migrated neural crest cells.

In Hirschsprung disease, there is an arrest in the migration of these cells, which leads to the development of a distal intestinal segment that is devoid of Meissner (submucosal) and the Auerbach (myenteric) plexus. Hence this segment is referred to as the aganglionic segment.

As a result, there is a lack of coordination in the peristaltic contractions and functional obstruction, which further leads to the dilation of the intestine proximal to the affected segment, leading to congenital megacolon. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating the absence of ganglion cells in biopsy sections.

Some conditions may cause acquired megacolon. These include:

• Chagas disease, due to the loss of ganglion cells
• Visceral myopathy
• Obstruction by neoplasm or inflammatory stricture
• Toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis
• Functional psychosomatic disorders
questions.learning: Failure of migration of neural crest cells Hirschsprung disease occurs due to the failure of migration of the neural crest cells to the bowel wall. During normal embryogenesis, the neural crest cells migrate from the caecum to the rectum.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with COPD is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. Which of the following preoperative measures is most effective in reducing the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Smoking cessation

Recognize that preoperative smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for reducing postoperative pulmonary complications in patients with COPD undergoing elective surgery. Smoking cessation improves mucociliary clearance, reduces airway reactivity and sputum production, and enhances pulmonary function, particularly when stopped ≥4–8 weeks before surgery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Give antibiotics: Not indicated unless there is evidence of an active respiratory infection.
• B. Wait for 3 months: Routine postponement is not recommended; optimization, including smoking cessation, is more beneficial.
• D. Oxygen therapy: Corrects hypoxemia but does not reduce the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications in stable COPD patients.
questions.learning: Smoking cessation Recognize that preoperative smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for reducing postoperative pulmonary complications in patients with COPD undergoing elective surgery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What surgery is being performed in the image shown?
questions.explanation: The image displays the results of a total maxillectomy, characterized by the surgical removal of the entire maxilla, including its anterior, medial, posterior, and inferior walls. This procedure is typically performed for malignant tumors of the maxilla or advanced sinonasal malignancies. The wide exposure seen is achieved through a classical Weber-Ferguson incision. A total ethmoidectomy (Option A) involves removing only the ethmoid air cells for extensive sinus disease, not the maxillary bone. Partial ethmoidectomy (Option B) is even more selective, preserving healthy mucosa. A partial maxillectomy (Option D) would involve removing only a portion of the maxilla, such as the medial wall, while leaving other bony structures intact. Since multiple walls of the maxillary cavity are clearly removed in the surgical field shown, the procedure is definitively identified as a total maxillectomy
questions.learning: The image displays the results of a total maxillectomy, characterized by the surgical removal of the entire maxilla, including its anterior, medial, posterior, and inferior walls.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes an emergency tracheostomy for acute airway obstruction. In the postoperative period, subcutaneous crepitus is noted over the neck and upper chest, consistent with surgical emphysema. Based on this finding, what is the most likely cause of this complication?
questions.explanation: After an emergency tracheostomy, the presence of subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus over neck and chest) indicates leakage of air into surrounding tissues. One of the most common causes in this setting is a high tracheostomy, where the incision is made too close to the larynx (above the 2nd–3rd tracheal rings). A high tracheostomy can lead to improper placement of the tube and inadequate sealing of the airway, allowing air to escape into the subcutaneous tissue planes during respiration. This results in surgical emphysema, especially in emergency procedures where anatomical landmarks may be difficult to identify. Why other options are less appropriate: (B) Tear in posterior tracheal wall → Can cause emphysema but is less common (C) Block in tracheostomy → Leads to respiratory distress, not air leakage (D) Tight suture → Causes local issues, not widespread emphysema
questions.learning: After an emergency tracheostomy, the presence of subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus over neck and chest) indicates leakage of air into surrounding tissues.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents to OPD with low backache. His PSA level are 100ng/ml. Which of the following drug is indicated for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Goserelin

The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA levels are suggestive of prostate cancer. Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer.

Androgen deprivation therapy is the primary medical therapy for prostate cancer. The drugs approved for this indication include leuprolide, goserelin, histrelin, buserelin, and triptorelin.

The agonist action of the GnRH analogues causes increased testosterone production, causing a tumour flare. It can be prevented by concomitant administration of an androgen receptor antagonist such as flutamide, bicalutamide, or nilutamide until downregulation of testosterone is complete.

The combined androgen deprivation therapy with continuous GnRH agonist and an androgen receptor antagonist is as effective as surgical castration in reducing the levels of serum testosterone and its effects.

Other options:

Option A: Somatostatin analogs acts as growth hormone antagonist and are used in the treatment of acromegaly, gigantism, acute control of bleeding from esophageal varices.

Option B: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analog used in the treatment of hepatorenal syndrome.

Option D: Anabolic steroids like testosterone are used to treat osteoporotic bone pain and counteract the effects of long-term corticosteroid use.
questions.learning: Goserelin — The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA levels are suggestive of prostate cancer. Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is punishable under the MTP Act?
options: Non-entry in MTP-register, not sending report to DDHS
questions.explanation: The MTP Act is a strictly regulated piece of legislation designed to provide safe and legal abortion services. Performing an MTP up to 24 weeks (Option A) for specified categories of women is legal. Performing it at an authorized center (Option B) by a qualified Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) (Option C) are the basic requirements for a legal termination. However, the Act also mandates strict administrative compliance. Failure to maintain the MTP register or failure to send the required monthly report to the Director of Health Services (DDHS) is a punishable offense. These administrative requirements are designed to prevent illegal or "back-alley" abortions and to ensure that all terminations are tracked for public health and safety purposes. Violations can lead to fines, imprisonment, and the closure of the facility. Maintaining confidentiality and proper documentation is a legal and ethical duty of the performing RMP
questions.learning: The MTP Act is a strictly regulated piece of legislation designed to provide safe and legal abortion services. Performing an MTP up to 24 weeks (Option A) for specified categories of women is legal.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The UGA codon signals:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Termination of protein synthesis

UGA is one of the three stop codons (along with UAA and UAG) in the standard genetic code. These stop codons signal the termination of protein synthesis by binding to release factors rather than tRNAs, causing the completed polypeptide chain to be released from the ribosome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustained burns and presented to the emergency department. His nasal hair was singed, and burns were noted on his face and neck. His carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) levels were raised to 18%, and his oxygen saturation was 80% on room air. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intubate and mechanical ventilation

This patient has evidence of inhalational injury following burns:

• Facial and neck burns
• Singed nasal hairs
• Elevated carboxyhemoglobin (COHb 18%)
• Hypoxemia (SpO₂ 80%)

The priority is early airway protection because progressive airway edema can rapidly lead to complete airway obstruction. Therefore, early endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation is indicated.

Why not the other options?

• A. 100% O₂ with NRBM: Although 100% oxygen is essential for carbon monoxide poisoning, this patient has signs of inhalational injury with impending airway compromise, so airway protection takes priority.
• C. Resuscitate using Parkland formula: Fluid resuscitation is important for major burns but is not the first priority in a patient with threatened airway.
• D. Hyperbaric O₂ therapy: Considered in selected cases of severe carbon monoxide poisoning (e.g., COHb >25%, neurological symptoms, pregnancy), but does not replace airway management.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with a clinical scenario of obstructive jaundice. Which of the following results can be seen on Van den bergh's reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Direct positive

In a patient with obstructive jaundice , van der bergh reaction gives direct positive result due to conjugated  hyperbilirubinemia .

Van den Bergh reaction is used to determine the serum bilirubin level.

Van den Bergh reaction is a colorimetric method to measure serum bilirubin. It is based on the formation of red azodipyrroles when diazotised sulfanilic acid reacts with bilirubin.

Interpretation:

• In the absence of methanol, the water-soluble conjugated bilirubin reacts rapidly with the reagent and is called direct bilirubin.
• In the presence of methanol, both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin react, providing the total bilirubin.
• Unconjugated (Indirect) bilirubin = Total-direct bilirubin
questions.learning: Direct positive — In a patient with obstructive jaundice , van der bergh reaction gives direct positive result due to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia . Van den Bergh reaction is used to determine the serum bilirubin level.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a crush injury to the right arm. On examination, the limb is pulseless, markedly swollen, and dark red in color. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—a crush injury followed by a pulseless, swollen, and dark red limb—is highly indicative of Compartment Syndrome. In crush injuries, excessive pressure builds up within the inelastic fascial compartments of the limb, compromising blood flow and leading to muscle necrosis. This is a surgical emergency. The "best" and definitive way to manage this case is an immediate Fasciotomy (Option C). A fasciotomy involves making long incisions to open the fascia, thereby relieving the pressure and restoring tissue perfusion. Intraosseous fluids (Option A) are for vascular access. Acidification of urine (Option B) is contraindicated; in crush injuries, the goal is alkalinization of urine to prevent myoglobin-induced renal failure. Hemodialysis (Option D) may be needed later if acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis occurs, but it does not treat the limb-threatening compartment pressure. Therefore, emergency fasciotomy is the primary life-saving and limb-saving intervention

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A doctor receives a telephonic call from the mother of an 8-year-old boy, who informs that the boy has just been bitten by a monkey. The child was playing with his friends when a group of monkeys appeared nearby. Some of the children shouted and threw sticks and stones at the monkeys, who became angry and aggressive. One of the monkeys bit the lady’s son in the forearm and blood is visible over the wound. The nearest health facility is 3 kilometres away. Consider the following statements regarding how the doctor should respond: 1. Advise the mother to rush with the child to the health facility without waiting for anything. 2. Advise the mother to first thoroughly wash the wound with plenty of soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, and then seek treatment. 3. Advise the mother that the animal bite is category I and risk is very low, as the bite was provoked. 4. Advise the mother to seek treatment for the boy’s wound but the boy requires no treatment or prophylaxis for rabies as it is a monkey bite. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

This is a Category III rabies exposure because the child has sustained a transdermal monkey bite with visible bleeding. Monkey bites are recognized as potential rabies exposures and should not be dismissed because the bite was provoked.

1. Statement 1. Advise the mother to rush with the child to the health facility without waiting for anything: Incorrect.

• The child should certainly reach a health facility promptly, but the first immediate step is thorough wound washing, which should not be delayed while travelling.

2. Statement 2. Advise the mother to first thoroughly wash the wound with plenty of soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, and then seek treatment: Correct.

• The wound should be washed and flushed thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, followed by prompt medical assessment.

3. Statement 3. Advise the mother that the animal bite is category I and risk is very low, as the bite was provoked: Incorrect.

• A bleeding bite is Category III, not Category I.
• Provocation does not eliminate rabies risk. Category III exposure requires rabies vaccination plus rabies immunoglobulin/monoclonal antibodies when indicated.

4. Statement 4. Advise the mother to seek treatment for the boy’s wound but the boy requires no treatment or prophylaxis for rabies as it is a monkey bite: Incorrect.

• Monkey bites can transmit rabies and may also transmit other infections. Therefore, rabies PEP cannot be omitted simply because the animal was a monkey.
questions.learning: 2 only This is a Category III rabies exposure because the child has sustained a transdermal monkey bite with visible bleeding. Monkey bites are recognized as potential rabies exposures and should not be dismissed because the bite was provoked.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a diagnosed fracture is referred to a higher center. On examination, the forearm pulses are not palpable. Based on the X-ray of the upper arm shown, which artery is most likely to have been injured?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, which is a common pediatric elbow injury. In this type of fracture, the sharp edge of the proximal bone fragment is frequently displaced anteriorly, where it can easily compress or lacerate the brachial artery. This explains the loss of distal pulses in the forearm. If untreated, this vascular compromise can lead to Volkmann's ischemic contracture. The radial artery (Option A) and ulnar artery (Option B) are branches of the brachial artery that begin distal to the elbow; while they would lose their pulse, the primary site of injury is the parent vessel. The anterior interosseous artery (Option D) is a deeper branch and is not typically the cause of major pulse loss in this context. Management requires urgent orthopedic reduction and potentially vascular repair. Identifying the high risk to the brachial artery in supracondylar fractures is a classic and life-saving requirement in emergency medicine and orthopedics

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Except for which of the following, all are cofactors for Dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: Dehydrogenases are a class of oxidoreductase enzymes that catalyze the removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate. These enzymes require specific electron-carrying cofactors to function, most notably NAD (Option C), NADP (Option A), and FAD (Option B) . These cofactors accept the hydrogen atoms and are reduced to NADH, NADPH, or FADH2, respectively. SAM (S-Adenosyl Methionine), however, is NOT a cofactor for dehydrogenase enzymes. Instead, SAM is the universal methyl group donor utilized by methyltransferase enzymes in biological systems. While NAD, NADP, and FAD are central to redox reactions and the electron transport chain, SAM is strictly involved in methylation reactions. Therefore, SAM is the correct "except" choice as it functions in a completely different class of biochemical reactions than the dehydrogenases. Understanding these cofactor specificities is fundamental to mastering metabolic pathway regulation
questions.learning: Dehydrogenases are a class of oxidoreductase enzymes that catalyze the removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate. These enzymes require specific electron-carrying cofactors to function, most notably NAD (Option C), NADP (Option A), and FAD (Option B) .

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Identify the stage of sleep based on EEG finding highlighted in red.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. REM sleep

The marked area in the given EEG shows sawtooth waves that are characteristic of REM sleep.

Sleep is comprised of two distinct physiological states, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and REM sleep. Stages I to IV make up the NREM sleep with marked lower physiological functions than during wakefulness. Dreams which occur during this state are usually lucid and purposeful.

REM sleep is characterized by a high level of brain activity. The physiological activity is similar to that during wakefulness. In REM sleep,

• Pulse, respiration, and blood pressure are increased.
• Brain oxygen use increases during REM sleep.
• Thermoregulation is altered - Poikilothermia prevails during REM sleep.
• There is loss of muscle tone - body movements are absent during REM sleep.
• There is partial or full penile erection - This is used to evaluate the cause for impotence.
• Dreams are abstract and surreal.

In normal adults, a REM episode has a latency of about 90 minutes during which the sleep is in the NREM stage. This latency is shortened in narcolepsy and depressive disorders.
questions.learning: REM sleep — The marked area in the given EEG shows sawtooth waves that are characteristic of REM sleep. Sleep is comprised of two distinct physiological states, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and REM sleep.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with blurred vision, dizziness, and a severe headache after consuming an unknown amount of homemade alcohol earlier the same day. He is disoriented on examination, and laboratory investigations show a high–anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which metabolite is primarily responsible for the toxicity in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of blurred ("snowfield") vision, dizziness, and metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap after consuming homemade alcohol are classic for methanol poisoning. Methanol (Option A) itself is not directly toxic. It is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde (Option C), which is then rapidly converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase into formic acid. Formic acid is the primary metabolite responsible for the toxicity; it inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia, optic neuropathy, and severe metabolic acidosis. Acetic acid (Option D) is the non-toxic product of ethanol metabolism. Formaldehyde is an intermediate but is too short-lived to be the primary driver of systemic toxicity. Treatment involves ethanol or fomepizole to block the formation of these toxic metabolites
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of blurred ("snowfield") vision, dizziness, and metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap after consuming homemade alcohol are classic for methanol poisoning.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with a gradual decrease in vision and elevated IOP in the right eye. The left eye is completely normal. Gonioscopy is as shown. The patient recalls being hit in the eye with a cricket ball ten years ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angle recession glaucoma

Angle recession glaucoma is a form of secondary open-angle glaucoma that develops months to years after blunt ocular trauma due to a tear between the longitudinal and circular fibers of the ciliary muscle, causing damage to the trabecular meshwork.

The gonioscopy image shows a markedly widened ciliary body band, the hallmark of angle recession.

• Cause: Blunt ocular trauma → tear of the ciliary muscle → angle recession → trabecular dysfunction.
• Diagnosis: Gonioscopy is essential in every patient with a history of blunt ocular trauma.
• Treatment: Similar to primary open-angle glaucoma (topical IOP-lowering drugs); filtration surgery may be required if medical therapy fails.

Differentiate from Other Secondary Glaucomas

• A. Pigmentary glaucoma: Bilateral, young myopic males; Krukenberg spindle, dense trabecular pigmentation.
• B. Pseudoexfoliative glaucoma: Elderly; dandruff-like pseudoexfoliative material on lens and pupillary margin.
• D. Neovascular glaucoma: Iris neovascularization (rubeosis iridis) due to diabetes or CRVO.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following conditions are associated with Neurosecretory bodies except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adrenal cortical tumor

Neurosecretory (dense-core) granules are membrane-bound secretory vesicles present in neuroendocrine cells, storing peptide hormones and amines.

They are typically seen in neuroendocrine tumors, such as:

• Medullary thyroid carcinoma (from parafollicular C cells)
• Pituitary adenoma
• Paraganglioma / pheochromocytoma

Adrenal cortical tumors arise from steroid-producing cortical cells, which synthesize hormones from cholesterol in smooth ER and mitochondria, not from stored secretory granules.

Abrasion collar: Gyroscopic movement of the bullet, the skin's elasticity, and the grease and dirt particles on the bullet's surface are the major causative factors of abrasion and grease collar. They are seen on the skin around the wound of entry at all ranges. Depending on the angle of entry made by the bullet, i.e.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which label is incorrectly marked in the basal ganglia diagram?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) External capsule, as it is incorrectly marked in the diagram. The external capsule is a thin white matter tract located lateral to the putamen and medial to the claustrum. In the figure, label D does not point to this thin white band; instead, it appears to indicate a broader cortical or subcortical region, making the labeling incorrect. Other options are correctly marked: (A) Caudate nucleus is correctly identified. It lies adjacent to the lateral ventricle and appears as a curved gray matter structure along its margin, which matches the diagram. (B) Globus pallidus is also correctly labeled. It is situated medial to the putamen and forms the medial part of the lentiform nucleus, usually shown as a lighter shaded region. (C) Putamen is correctly marked as well. It lies lateral to the globus pallidus and is a major component of the basal ganglia, forming the outer part of the lentiform nucleus. Thus, only the external capsule is mislabeled, while all other structures are accurately represented
questions.learning: The correct answer is (D) External capsule, as it is incorrectly marked in the diagram. The external capsule is a thin white matter tract located lateral to the putamen and medial to the claustrum.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What effect does inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺ -ATPase have on cardiac muscle function?
questions.explanation: Inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump directly causes depolarization of cardiac muscle cells. This pump normally transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell per cycle, maintaining the resting membrane potential by keeping the intracellular environment relatively negative. When this pump is inhibited (as by cardiac glycosides like digoxin), Na⁺ accumulates inside the cell because it can no longer be actively expelled. This rise in intracellular Na⁺ reduces the concentration gradient that drives the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX), which normally expels Ca²⁺ using the Na⁺ gradient. As a result, intracellular Ca²⁺ also rises, and the membrane becomes less negative — i.e., depolarized — due to Na⁺ accumulation and altered ionic balance. Why other options are wrong: (A) Hyperpolarization and then depolarization is incorrect because Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition never causes an initial hyperpolarization phase. The immediate consequence is always Na⁺ accumulation leading directly to depolarization, with no preceding hyperpolarization stage involved. (C) Hyperpolarization is incorrect because hyperpolarization would require increased K⁺ efflux or Cl⁻ influx making the cell more negative. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition does the opposite — it accumulates positive Na⁺ ions intracellularly, making the membrane potential less negative, not more. (D) Repolarization is incorrect because repolarization refers to the restoration of resting membrane potential after an action potential, driven by K⁺ efflux. Pump inhibition does not selectively activate repolarization channels; instead it disrupts the baseline ionic gradient causing sustained depolarization

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the cells secrete surfactant in lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type 2 pneumocyte

Type 2 pneumocytes secrete surfactant in the lungs.

Alveolar Lining Epithelial Cells

Two types

* Type I cells – The primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium); Helps in gas exchange

* Type II cells  – Granular pneumocytes produce surfactant

Type II cells make 60% of epithelial cells in alveoli but type I cells form 95% of the total surface area because of its flat surface.

Type II cells are stem cells which help in replenishing damaged Type 1 pneumocytes in conditions like drug-induced pulmonary toxicity by amiodarone, bleomycin etc.

Other cells – Pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAMs/type 3 alveolar cells), lymphocytes, plasma cells, neuroendocrine cells (APUD cells-Amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation), and mast cells.

Clinical correlate :

* Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm neonates is due to insufficient surfactant production.

* Lung maturity of the fetus can be assessed by determining the ratio of lecithin to sphingomyelin (L:S ratio) in the amniotic fluid. A ratio of >2 indicates maturity.

* Shake test/Bubble test/Clement test: Formation of stable foam in the presence of surfactant.

* Phosphatidylglycerol levels in Amniotic fluid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?
options: Fingers are held in mild extension
Most common involvement is index finger
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It affects APL and EPB

De Quervain's disease is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the extensor tendons of the first dorsal compartment, namely extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) and abductor pollicis longus (APL).

It is prominent among females, especially pregnant women. Most commonly thumb is involved.

Finkelstein's test: On grasping the patient’s thumb and quickly abducting the hand ulnar ward, the pain over the radial styloid tip is excruciating. It’s the most pathognomonic objective sign but is also seen in other conditions like radial nerve entrapment and arthritis.

Treatment:

• Majority of the patients are treated medically
• Only few require the release of the 1st dorsal compartment which houses the APL and EPB tendons.
questions.learning: It affects APL and EPB De Quervain's disease is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the extensor tendons of the first dorsal compartment, namely extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) and abductor pollicis longus (APL).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Koebner's phenomenon is seen in all of the following, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpes

Koebner's phenomenon is not seen in herpes.

Koebner’s phenomenon/ isomorphic response is the development of lesions in previously normal skin that has been subjected to trauma. If the same response is seen from the spread of an infective agent ( like molluscum contagiosum, viral warts), it's called pseudo-Koebner’s phenomenon.

Any of the following can elicit an isomorphic response: physical trauma, including friction, pressure, incision and laceration, skin grafting, bites, vaccination skin tests, burns, freezing, and ultraviolet (UV) and ionizing radiation.

It is seen commonly associated with psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. Other associated disorders include Darrier’s disease, pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen nitidus, DLE, necrobiosis lipoidica, and Grzybowski syndrome.
questions.learning: Herpes Koebner's phenomenon is not seen in herpes. Koebner’s phenomenon/ isomorphic response is the development of lesions in previously normal skin that has been subjected to trauma.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A dead body is discovered with multiple injuries consistent with a violent assault. Examination reveals one bruise on the right side of the neck and three linear bruises on the left side, along with curved, semilunar abrasions beneath the angle of the jaw and a fractured hyoid bone. Additional injuries are noted on the left thigh, back, scapula, pelvis, and shoulder, with associated fractures. Based on these findings, what is the most likely cause of death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Throttling

Throttling (manual strangulation) is characterized by finger and thumb pressure marks on the neck, along with internal injuries such as hyoid bone fracture.

• Asymmetrical bruises on neck:

• Single bruise on one side (thumb)
• Multiple bruises on opposite side (fingers)

• Semilunar (crescent-shaped) abrasions:

• Caused by fingernails

• Fractured hyoid bone:

• Strong indicator of manual strangulation

Associated findings:

• Signs of struggle/assault:

• Injuries on thigh, back, scapula, pelvis, shoulder

• May have congestion, petechiae, cyanosis

Why not others:

• Ligature strangulation: Continuous ligature mark, not finger marks
• Gagging: No neck compression signs
• Mugging: Non-specific trauma, lacks classical neck findings
