questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with a history of tuberculosis presents with dyspnea on exertion. On examination, it is noted that the JVP rises during inspiration. A chest radiograph of the patient is given below. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constrictive pericarditis

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of tuberculosis now presenting with positive Kussmaul's sign, and pericardial calcification seen on chest radiograph suggest a diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis.

Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic type of pericarditis that results when there is healing of acute fibrinous pericarditis or absorption of chronic pericardial effusion. While the most common cause in developing countries is tuberculosis, in developed countries, it occurs following viral pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, or as a manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis and SLE. The main abnormality which occurs in constrictive pericarditis is the inability of the ventricles to fill because of the rigid and thickened pericardium. Unlike tamponade, this restriction is not uniform through the diastole. Ventricular filling is normal early in the diastole but stops suddenly when the elastic limit of the pericardium is reached. Y-descent on the JVP curve is prominent in constrictive pericarditis because it represents the rapid early filling of the ventricles. A sudden stop in ventricular filling and subsequent rising pressure is seen as a square root sign in the JVP curve.

The patient presents with exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. There may be a paradoxical rise in venous pressure during inspiration (Kussmaul's sign). Apart from constrictive pericarditis, Kussmaul's sign can be positive in tricuspid stenosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right heart failure, and pulmonary embolism. The ECG often shows low-voltage QRS complexes and diffuse flattening of T-waves. A chest radiograph may show pericardial calcification, especially in tuberculous pericarditis.
questions.learning: Constrictive pericarditis — The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of tuberculosis now presenting with positive Kussmaul's sign, and pericardial calcification seen on chest radiograph suggest a diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement about obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)?
options: Atypical antipsychotics is the first line treatment
Prevalence is 7 -10 percent in general population
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Depression is a common comorbidity

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is commonly associated with depression. The lifetime prevalence of the major depressive disorder in patients with OCD is 67 percent. Other common psychiatric comorbidities in patients with OCD are social phobia, alcohol use disorders, panic, and personality disorders.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) comprises symptoms that include intrusive thoughts, preoccupations, and compulsions. These recurrent obsessions or compulsions cause severe distress to the patient. The patient might have an obsession, a compulsion, or both.

An obsession is a thought, feeling, or sensation that is repetitive and intrusive. A compulsion is a conscious, recurrent behavior, eg: counting, checking, and are done to reduce the anxiety associated with the obsession. However, this act may not reduce the anxiety and might increase the anxiety even more.

Symptom patterns:

• Contamination - This is the most common symptom pattern of OCD.  The patient feels that the objects are contaminated. They repeatedly wash their hands or avoid touching objects which are thought to be contaminated. In extreme cases, patients may rub the skin off their hands due to excessive hand washing or may refuse to leave the house in fear of germs.
• Pathological doubt - This is the second most common symptom pattern. The patient presents with an obsession with doubt and a compulsion to check. This obsession arises due to possible danger or violence (e.g., forgetting to turn off the stove or not locking a door) which is followed by multiple trips to check, for example, if the stove is turned off, if the door is locked, etc.
• Intrusive thoughts -This is the third most common symptom pattern. These patients have intrusive obsessional thoughts without compulsion. These thoughts could be sexual or an aggressive act that the patient doesn't agree. The patients might report themselves to the police or confess to a spiritual leader.
• Symmetry - This is the fourth most common pattern which can lead to a compulsion of slowness. Patients can take hours to eat a meal or shave their faces.

Diagnosis:

1. Presence of obsessions, compulsions or both
2. Symptoms are time-consuming
3. Symptoms not related to substance abuse
4. Not better explained by other mental disorders

Treatment of OCD includes:

• Pharmacotherapy: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) or clomipramine
• Behavioral therapy: Approaches include:

• exposure and response prevention
• desensitization
• thought stopping
• flooding
• implosion therapy
• aversive conditioning

A combination of behavioral and pharmacotherapy is most effective.

Other options

Option A - Atypical antipsychotics are not the first-line in the treatment of OCD. They can be given only when SSRIs and clomipramine (tricyclic antidepressant) are not effective.

Option B - The prevalence of OCD among the general population is 2-3 percent and not 7-10 percent.

Option D - Contamination is the most common obsession.
questions.learning: Depression is a common comorbidity Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is commonly associated with depression. The lifetime prevalence of the major depressive disorder in patients with OCD is 67 percent.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about Factories Act?
options: Children under 14 years of age must not be employed in factories
A child of 16 years can be employed only between 6 AM and 8 PM
The maximum working hours for an adult is 72 hours per week
A child of 16 years can work till 5 hours per day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Children under 14 years of age must not be employed in factories

Factories act prohibits children of <14 years from being employed.

Children between 15–18 years can be employed only in certain industries and work only between 6 AM–7 PM. They should not be made to work for more than four and a half hours.

The maximum working hours for an adult industrial worker should be not more than 48 hours per week, not exceeding 9 hours a day; if overtime is paid, then it should be not more than 60 hrs per week.
questions.learning: Children under 14 years of age must not be employed in factories Factories act prohibits children of <14 years from being employed. Children between 15–18 years can be employed only in certain industries and work only between 6 AM–7 PM.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents with sudden-onset perineal pain. On examination, foul-smelling discharge, and necrotic tissue as seen in the image is noted. Which of the following is true about the given condition?
options: Anti-gas gangrene serum indicated for all cases
Urinary diversion is the next step
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection

The given condition is likely to be Fournier gangrene. It is a mixed flora aerobic and anaerobic infection.

Fournier's gangrene is a polymicrobial infection and a type of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, external genitalia, and perianal region. Risk factors include immunocompromised states such as HIV, alcoholism, and diabetes. The infection may be precipitated by minor procedures in the perineal area, such as a bruise, scratch, urethral dilatation, injection of hemorrhoids, or opening of a periurethral abscess. The infection spreads along the dartos, Scarpa, and Colles fascia.

The sequence of events that lead to the development of gangrene are as follows: A mixed infection of the aerobic and anaerobic bacteria  → fulminating inflammation of subcutaneous tissue → obliterative arteritis of the arterioles that supply the scrotal skin → gangrene.

Clinical features of Fournier gangrene are scrotal pain, fever, prostration, and pallor. Cellulitis spreads rapidly and may be associated with eschars, necrosis, flaking skin, and crepitus. The testis is usually not affected.

Diagnosis is majorly clinical and very rarely made by laboratory or imaging findings.

The steps in the management of this condition:

1. IV fluids
2. IV antibiotics
3. Urgent surgical excision followed by skin grafting in later stages. Wide surgical excision is often necessary.

When the infection has been controlled, a vacuum-assisted dressing may be helpful. Skin grafting is essential for a patient surviving an acute episode. Despite the best therapy, mortality rates are around 50%.

Other options:

Option A: Anti-gas gangrene serum is a treatment for gas gangrene that is of historical importance and is no longer used. Treatment of gas gangrene is now done with antibiotics.

Option B: While urinary diversion and other supportive measures are useful in the management of the condition, it is not the next best step.

Option C: The blood supply of the testes is separate from that of the overlying skin, and hence, testes can be preserved during debridement.
questions.learning: Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection — The given condition is likely to be Fournier gangrene. It is a mixed flora aerobic and anaerobic infection.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child was brought with bony deformities as shown in the radiograph below. It could be due to the deficiency of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin D

The given pediatric radiograph depicts the bowing of legs, which occurs due to rickets that results from the deficiency of vitamin D. Deficiency of vitamin D and calcium results in poor mineralization of bone, leading to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

Rickets presents with skeletal changes like bowing of legs and bone pain once the child starts to walk. Radiological features show cupping at metaphyses, fraying, and widening of the growth plate. Prominent costochondral joints (rachitic rosary), craniotabes, frontal bossing, scoliosis, fractures, and dental anomalies may also be seen. The only cutaneous manifestation of vitamin D deficiency is alopecia.

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin A deficiency results in night blindness, xerophthalmia, and keratinization of the skin.

Option C: Vitamin K deficiency leads to hemorrhagic disease in newborns and elevated prothrombin time and bleeding. Vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the synthesis of coagulation proteins. Toxicity due to vitamin K results in hemolysis, hyperbilirubinemia, and kernicterus in the newborn.

Option D: Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy, which occurs due to defective collagen formation resulting in generalized bleeding tendencies and poor wound healing. Radiographic features of scurvy include the white line of Frankel, Trummerfeld zone, Pelkan spurs, and periosteal elevation. Tender nodules at the costochondral junctions, known as the scorbutic rosary, are characteristic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On a chest radiograph, which of the following occupational diseases is most likely to be mistaken as a case of tuberculosis of lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

• Silicosis is the occupational lung disease most commonly mistaken for pulmonary tuberculosis on chest X-ray.
• Causative agent: Free crystalline silica dust.
• High-risk occupations: Mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone cutting, foundry work, ceramics, and glass industries.
• Chest X-ray findings:

• Multiple small rounded upper lobe nodules
• Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)
• “Eggshell” calcification of hilar lymph nodes (classic finding).

• Major complication: Silicotuberculosis due to impaired macrophage function.
• Silicosis also increases the risk of lung cancer, COPD, and cor pulmonale.

Other Important Pneumoconioses

• Anthracosis (Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis): Coal dust exposure.
• Asbestosis: Lower lobe interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaques; associated with bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma.
• Siderosis: Iron dust exposure; benign pneumoconiosis with little or no fibrosis.
• Byssinosis: Cotton dust exposure; presents with chest tightness and occupational asthma (“Monday chest tightness”).
questions.learning: Silicosis • Silicosis is the occupational lung disease most commonly mistaken for pulmonary tuberculosis on chest X-ray. • Causative agent: Free crystalline silica dust. • High-risk occupations: Mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone cutting, foundry work,…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following side effects are seen most commonly with Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Embryopathy

Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative which is highly teratogenic when orally administered. It is commonly used to treat cystic nodular acne. It inhibits the migration of neural crest cells during embryogenesis and affects the development of multiple organs. These defects are collectively termed retinoic acid embryopathy.

Embryopathy or developmental disorder of an embryo comprises a large variety of abnormalities and is more common than any individual defect. Specific anomalies may include ventriculomegaly, maldevelopment of the facial bones or cranium, microtia or anotia, micrognathia, cleft palate, conotruncal heart defects, and thymic aplasia or hypoplasia.

Isotretinoin also increases the risk of spontaneous abortions and stillbirths in pregnancies exposed in the first trimester of this medicine. Presenting with pregnancy during treatment with isotretinoin is a failure of prevention strategies.

The guidelines for isotretinoin usage are as follows:

* Isotretinoin is a teratogenic drug that should not be taken during pregnancy and nursing.

* Patients should take 2 pregnancy tests before starting isotretinoin and take a monthly pregnancy test while on the medication, and another test 1 month after stopping the medication.

* It is recommended to use two birth control methods concurrently, beginning one month before treatment to one month following the end of isotretinoin treatment.

* Isotretinoin should be reserved for the treatment of severe, nodulocystic acne and should not be used for milder forms of acne.

Other options:

Option B: Lithium is used in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is a teratogen associated with Ebstein's anomaly which is a rare cardiac condition characterized by severe tricuspid regurgitation and right atrial enlargement.

Option C: Valproic acid is the anti-epileptic which confers the greatest risk to the developing fetus while used in pregnancy. It is associated with an increased risk of neural tube defects in the fetus.

Option D: Tetracyclines are associated with yellowish-brown discoloration of deciduous teeth when used after 25 weeks of gestation.
questions.learning: Embryopathy Isotretinoin is a vitamin — A derivative which is highly teratogenic when orally administered. It is commonly used to treat cystic nodular acne.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements about working of septic tanks: 1. They are recommended for large communities, rather than small communities. 2. There should be no air space between the level of liquid in the tank and the undersurface of the cover. 3. Liquid effluent from the outlet pipe is free from all pathogens. How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. None of the statements

A septic tank is an on-site sewage disposal system used for individual houses and small communities where a centralized sewerage system is not available. It works by anaerobic digestion, where solids settle and decompose, while the liquid effluent is discharged for further treatment in a soak pit or dispersion trenches.

• 1. They are recommended for large communities\, rather than small communities. ✗

• Septic tanks are designed for individual households and small communities, not large populations.

• 2. There should be no air space between the level of liquid in the tank and the undersurface of the cover. ✗

• A septic tank should have an air space (about 30 cm) between the liquid level and the cover to allow gas accumulation and proper functioning.

• 3. Liquid effluent from the outlet pipe is free from all pathogens. ✗

• The effluent still contains pathogenic microorganisms and requires further disposal/treatment through a soak pit, leach field, or other methods.
questions.learning: None of the statements — A septic tank is an on-site sewage disposal system used for individual houses and small communities where a centralized sewerage system is not available.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man has a history of recurrent sinus infections and chronic productive cough since childhood. High-resolution CT of the chest shows bronchiectasis, and a chest radiograph demonstrates dextrocardia with complete situs inversus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia. Impaired ciliary motility leads to defective mucociliary clearance and abnormal embryonic left-right axis determination.

The classic triad consists of:

• Chronic sinusitis
• Bronchiectasis
• Situs inversus (or dextrocardia)

Other features include:

• Recurrent otitis media
• Chronic productive cough
• Male infertility (immotile sperm)
• Female subfertility/ectopic pregnancy due to impaired fallopian tube cilia

Why not the other options?

• A. Cystic fibrosis: Also causes recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis, but is associated with pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, elevated sweat chloride, and does not cause situs inversus.
• C. Young syndrome: Characterized by bronchiectasis with obstructive azoospermia, but ciliary function is normal and situs inversus is absent.
• D. Primary immunodeficiency: May cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections but does not produce the characteristic combination of bronchiectasis with situs inversus.

High-yield pearl

| Disorder | Key defect | Characteristic features

| -------- | ---------- | -----------------------

| Kartagener syndrome (PCD) | Defective dynein arms → impaired ciliary motility | Sinusitis + bronchiectasis + situs inversus

| Cystic fibrosis | CFTR mutation | Bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, ↑ sweat chloride

| Young syndrome | Unknown cause | Bronchiectasis + obstructive azoospermia; no situs inversus

| Primary immunodeficiency | Immune defect | Recurrent infections without laterality defects
questions.learning: Kartagener syndrome Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A female was recently diagnosed with mild depression. What is the preferred treatment for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cognitive behavioral therapy

In recent onset mild depression, the preferred management is cognitive-behavioral therapy alone.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is based on the psychological significance of the cognitive triad:

* An individual's beliefs about themselves

* Their personal world (including the people in their lives)

* Their future.

Treatment of depression:

* In recent‐onset mild depression, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is preferred and antidepressants are not recommended.

* Antidepressants (SSRIs) are recommended for the treatment of moderate to severe depression and for dysthymia along with CBT.

* For treatment‐resistant depression, recommended strategies include augmentation with lithium or an antipsychotic or the addition of a second antidepressant.

* The use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is supported in severe and treatment-resistant depression.

Somatic and newer treatment modalities for depression include:

* Vagus nerve stimulation for resistant depression

* Repeated transcranial magnetic stimulation

* Phototherapy

* Deep brain stimulation
questions.learning: Cognitive behavioral therapy — In recent onset mild depression, the preferred management is cognitive-behavioral therapy alone. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is based on the psychological significance of the cognitive triad: * An individual's beliefs…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Name the outlet forceps from the following:
questions.explanation: In the classification of obstetric instruments, Wrigley forceps are specifically categorized as outlet forceps. They are shorter and lighter than standard forceps, designed for use only when the fetal head is on the perineum (at the station or lower) and the scalp is visible at the introitus. Their primary use is to assist in the final stages of delivery, often for maternal exhaustion or non-reassuring fetal heart patterns. Piper forceps (Option B) are specialized long-curved forceps used exclusively for the delivery of the after-coming head in breech presentation. Kielland's forceps (Option C) are designed for rotation of the fetal head from malpositions like occipitoposterior or transverse. Das forceps (Option D) are a general-purpose Indian modification of the Simpson forceps, typically used for low or mid-cavity deliveries. Choosing the correct forceps based on the station and position of the head is vital for procedural safety, as Wrigley’s minimal size reduces the risk of maternal pelvic floor trauma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
An unimmunized 2-year old child presented with coryza, conjunctivitis, and bluish-white spots in his buccal mucosa near the lower molar teeth. A day later, he developed a maculopapular rash on the face and neck. What is the nature of the causative virus?

ss - Single stranded
ds - Double-stranded
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enveloped ss RNA

Fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash and Koplik spots are suggestive of measles. Measles virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus.

Koplik spots are small, bluish-white ulcerations on the inner aspect of the cheek at the level of premolars. These are pathognomic for measles. The measles virus, a paramyxovirus, has an incubation period of 7-18 days. After this, the prodrome phase begins with mild fever, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and pathognomic Koplik spots. This is followed by the eruptive stage, characterised by the appearance of maculopapular rash on the 4th day of fever. The rash begins on the face and spreads to the torso and extremities. Lymphadenopathy may be present.

These are multinucleated giant cells formed by the fusion of infected cells. The images below show the characteristic rashes and the Koplik spots seen in measles.

The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media. Sinusitis and mastoiditis are also seen. The most common cause of death in measles is pneumonia, which may be giant cell pneumonia. It is caused by the virus directly or can be due to superadded bacterial infection. Black measles or hemorrhagic measles is a fatal complication characterized by hemorrhagic skin eruptions. It is rarely seen nowadays.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare but fatal complication characterized by cognitive decline, spasticity of limbs, and seizures. It is insidious in onset and clinical manifestations usually begin 7-10 years after primary measles infection. It is caused due to persistent infection with a genetically altered variant of the measles virus within the central nervous system. Other complications include croup, tracheitis, bronchiolitis, diarrhea and vomiting, febrile seizures, and encephalitis.

The diagnosis of measles infection is mainly clinical but may be confirmed by serological demonstration of IgM antibodies. IgM antibodies appear 1-2 days after the rash and are detectable for 1 month. The management is mainly supportive. There is no role for antivirals. Low serum retinol levels in children with measles are associated with higher morbidity and mortality and hence vitamin A therapy is indicated for all patients with measles.

Live attenuated vaccine for measles is safe and effective with no evidence of person-to-person transfer of vaccine strains. It is a freeze-dried product requiring reconstitution. 0.5ml is administered subcutaneously in the right upper arm in 2 doses- at the 9th month and between the 16th - 24th month.
questions.learning: Enveloped ss RNA Fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash and Koplik spots are suggestive of measles. Measles virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless ocular ulcer. Examination reveals a long, branching corneal ulcer with desquamated epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painless corneal ulcer is a hallmark of reduced corneal sensation, often due to damage to the trigeminal nerve. The finding of a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium without the classic "terminal bulbs" seen in viral infections identifies it as a neurotrophic ulcer. This condition results from impaired trophic support and lost sensory supply, leading to poor healing and epithelial breakdown. Fungal ulcers (Option A) are typically painful and follow vegetative trauma, showing feathery margins. Dendritic ulcers (Option B) are usually caused by herpes simplex virus and are typically painful unless sensation is already lost; they feature distinct terminal bulbs. Bacterial ulcers (Option C) are acutely painful and purulent with stromal infiltration. Thus, the painless nature and branching pattern specifically point to a neurotrophic etiology

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida with a normal vaginal delivery develops intractable postpartum haemorrhage, not responding to uterine massage and uterotonics. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Balloon tamponade

Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as:

• ≥500 mL blood loss after vaginal delivery
• ≥1000 mL after cesarean section
• Or any blood loss causing hemodynamic instability

Most common cause:

Uterine atony (≈70–80%)

Other causes are remembered as the 4 Ts:

| Cause | Explanation

| ----- | -----------

| Tone | Uterine atony (most common)

| Trauma | Lacerations, uterine rupture

| Tissue | Retained placenta

| Thrombin | Coagulation disorders

Management follows a stepwise escalation approach.

| Step | Treatment

| ---- | ---------

| 1 | Uterine massage

| 2 | Uterotonics (Oxytocin, Methylergometrine, Carboprost, Misoprostol)

| 3 | Balloon tamponade

| 4 | Surgical procedures

| 5 | Hysterectomy

When atonic PPH fails to respond to massage and first-line uterotonics, the next step is a mechanical tamponade—most commonly a Bakri balloon—as recommended in stepwise PPH algorithms. It provides rapid intrauterine pressure, buys time, and often avoids surgery. Uterine artery embolization or surgical devascularisation are reserved for balloon failure, and hysterectomy is the final life-saving option.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A researcher wants to predict systolic blood pressure from body mass index (BMI) using statistical analysis. Which statistical measure is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coefficient of regression

Regression is used when:

• One variable is used to predict another variable.

Example:

• BMI → Predict BP
• Age → Predict lung function

Regression equation:

Y = a + bX

where, b is the regression coefficient.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: New A 55 yr old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of having a dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below. This patient most likely suffers from ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemochromatosis

The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. Liver microscopy shows hepatocellular iron, which is stained blue with Perl's prussian blue stain.

Hemochromatosis is an inherited or acquired metabolic disorder caused by excessive iron absorption. Iron overload leads to the accumulation of iron in parenchymal organs such as the liver and pancreas followed by heart, joints, and endocrine organs.

The characteristic triad of hemochromatosis includes:

* Micronodular cirrhosis

* Diabetes mellitus in 75% to 80% of patients

* Abnormal skin pigmentation in 75% to 80% of patients

Note: The total body iron pool ranges from 2 to 6 gm in normal adults. In hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm, more than one-third of which accumulates in the liver.
questions.learning: Hemochromatosis — The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. Liver microscopy shows hepatocellular iron, which is stained blue with Perl's prussian blue stain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the diagnostic criteria for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) as defined by the Modified Rotterdam Criteria? 1. Obesity 2. Delayed menstruation 3. Hirsutism 4. Insulin resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

Modified Rotterdam Criteria (2003)

Diagnosis of PCOS requires any 2 out of the following 3 criteria after excluding other causes.

| Criterion | Description

| --------- | -----------

| Oligo-ovulation / anovulation | Irregular or delayed menstruation

| Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism | Hirsutism, acne, ↑ testosterone

| Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound | ≥20 follicles or ovarian volume ≥10 mL

Thus in the options:

• Delayed menstruation → represents oligo-ovulation
• Hirsutism → represents hyperandrogenism

Hence 2 and 3 are correct.

Polycystic Ovaries on Ultrasound

Typical ultrasound features:

• ≥20 follicles measuring 2–9 mm
• Peripheral arrangement called “string of pearls”
• Ovarian volume ≥10 mL

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 5-year- old child who presents with abdominal distension and a soft, fluctuant mass that is mobile perpendicular to the line of mesenteric attachment?

This movement happens because the cyst is located between the layers of the small bowel mesentery. A peritoneal cyst (Option A) would not show this specific directional mobility. A lipoma (Option B) is a solid fatty mass and would not be fluctuant. A pseudocyst (Option D) is usually fixed in the retroperitoneum and follows an episode of pancreatitis, which is rare in a healthy 5-year-old. Chylolymphatic cysts are thin-walled lymphatic malformations that contain milky chyle. While often asymptomatic, they can cause pain or intestinal obstruction due to their size. The definitive treatment is surgical enucleation. Therefore, the characteristic mobility defines this congenital lymphatic anomaly

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which pairing correctly matches the trauma patients brought to the casualty?
options: Penetrating injury to eustachian tube- CSF otorrhea
Penetrating injury to eye- Battle sign
questions.explanation: In clinical neurology and trauma assessment, specific physical signs are linked to localized brain injuries. A lesion in the midbrain (specifically the pretectal area or superior colliculi) characteristically results in vertical gaze palsy, a component of Parinaud's syndrome. Option A is incorrect because an extradural hemorrhage typically causes an ipsilateral dilated pupil (Hutchinson's pupil) due to uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve, not a pinpoint pupil (which suggests pontine injury or opioid overdose). Option B is incorrect because CSF otorrhea results from a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone, not an isolated injury to the eustachian tube. Option C is incorrect as the Battle sign (ecchymosis over the mastoid) is a classic indicator of a base of skull fracture in the middle cranial fossa, not a direct eye injury. Therefore, the connection between gaze palsy and midbrain pathology is the only anatomically and clinically correct pairing provided in the list

options: Demyelination of A and B fibers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Demyelination of A and B fibers

The underlying cause of Guillain-Barré syndrome is demyelination of A and B fibres.

Erlanger and Gasser classified nerve fibres into types A, B, and C, with type A fibres further subdivided into α, β, γ, and δ fibres.

* Type A fibers are the typical large- and medium-sized myelinated fibers of spinal nerves.

* Type B fibers are smaller fibres with minimal myelination. They transmit impulses of the ANS, including the bladder.

* Type C fibers are small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disease that causes fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy. It is a T-cell-mediated immune response.

GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acute gastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

It presents with the following features:

* Ascending motor paralysis (lower limbs > upper limbs)

* Sensory deficits may or may not be seen

* Deep tendon reflexes—absent

* Transient bladder dysfunction—severe cases

* Autonomic manifestations—loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias.

Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular and endoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electron microscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination induced by the actions of activated macrophages.

There are several types of Guillain–Barré syndrome:

* Demyelinating

* Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP)—most common

* Axonal

* Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)

* Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)

* Regional GBS syndromes: Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS)

Other options:

Option A and D: Spinal cord inflammation/demyelination point to conditions like transverse myelitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The first heart sound coincides with which phase of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isovolumetric contraction

The first heart sound coincides with the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle.

The time between the closure of the mitral valve and the opening of the aortic valve is the isovolumic contraction period. It begins with the closure of mitral and tricuspid valve which is responsible for the first heart sound. During this period, the ventricles contract as a closed chamber till the aortic and pulmonary valves open.

Events of the Cardiac Cycle

Systole

* Isovolumetric Contraction
The ventricular muscle continues to contract, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.
It correlates with the ‘c’ wave of JVP.

* Ventricular Ejection
When the ventricular pressures rise above aortic and pulmonary pressures the valves open, and ventricular ejection begins. Peak pressures in the left and right ventricles are about 120 and 25 mmHg, respectively.

Diastole

* Protodiastole
Before the semilunar valve closes, even though ventricular muscle is relaxed, blood flow into great vessels is due to momentum of blood.

* Iso-volumetric Relaxation
The ventricular muscle continues to relax, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.

* Ventricular Filling
Isovolumetric relaxation ends when the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure and the AV valves open, permitting the ventricles to fill.

* Atrial Systole
During the last third of diastole, the atria contract and give additional thrust to the inflow of blood into the ventricles. It correlates with 'a' wave in JVP.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presented with a history of discomfort while swallowing food. She has no history of fever, sore throat, or smoking but has a history of Marfan's syndrome in her father. On examination of the oral cavity, there is unilateral swelling of the tonsils along with pulsation. What is the most likely cause of the swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm

The history of Marfan's syndrome( autosomal dominant disease) along with the pulsation of the tonsils is suggestive of an extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm.

Even though the tonsils are supplied by the external carotid artery branches an internal carotid artery aneurysm can push the tonsil medially which gives the pulsation. The external carotid artery is more superficial in its course and would not lead to the medial displacement of the tonsils.

The internal carotid artery which gives no branches in the cervical region can cause kinks, elbowing, etc which leads to aneurysms when it lies close to the pharynx. In children, the tonsillo-carotid distance increases with growth to a maximum value of 25 mm.

Note: A common differential in a unilateral swelling of the tonsil is Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) which requires incision and drainage as the treatment. Hence aneurysms need to be ruled out before the procedure as trauma to the internal carotid artery can be devastating since it supplies the brain too.
questions.learning: Extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm — The history of Marfan's syndrome( autosomal dominant disease) along with the pulsation of the tonsils is suggestive of an extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a type 2 diabetes mellitus patient, serum insulin levels are found to be raised. He is advised to exercise to improve insulin resistance. Which of the following GLUT will help to improve insulin resistance after exercise ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GLUT 4

There is an increase in the number of GLUT 4 receptors in response to exercise. This increases the insulin dependent glucose uptake into the cells, contributing to a decrease in insulin resistance.

GLUT-4 is an insulin-dependent GLUT. Other GLUTs are not insulin-sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane.

Insulin resistance is a condition in which the cells in muscles, fat, and liver are less responsive to insulin and have difficulty absorbing glucose from the blood. The pancreas then produces more insulin to facilitate the entry of glucose into the cells.

An arbitrary but clinically useful benchmark considers patients insulin resistant if they require greater than 1 unit/kilogram/day of exogenous insulin to maintain glycemic control. Patients requiring greater than 200 units of exogenous insulin per day are considered severely insulin resistant.

Other options

Option A:  GLUT 1 receptors are present in the red blood cell, brain, kidney, colon, retina, and placenta. It is responsible for glucose uptake.

Option B: GLUT-2 is found in the liver, pancreatic β cell, small intestine, and kidney. Its function is the rapid uptake or release of glucose.

Option C: GLUT-5 is present in the small intestine and is involved in the absorption of fructose.
questions.learning: GLUT 4 — There is an increase in the number of GLUT 4 receptors in response to exercise. This increases the insulin dependent glucose uptake into the cells, contributing to a decrease in insulin resistance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with symptoms and examination findings characteristic of a particular respiratory disorder. Based on the clinical details provided, what is the condition being described?
questions.explanation: The provided High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) image shows advanced lung remodeling characterized by multiple, clustered cystic spaces with thickened walls, often referred to as "honeycombing" or "cystic bronchiectasis". Bronchiectasis is defined by the permanent, pathological dilation of the bronchi. While pulmonary tuberculosis (Option A) can lead to bronchiectasis as a sequela, the HRCT shows a primary pattern of diffuse airway dilation. COPD (Option B) would typically show hyperinflation and emphysematous destruction (centrilobular or panacinar), but not these discrete, large-walled cysts. Bronchial asthma (Option C) is a functional disorder of the small airways that generally shows a normal HRCT or mild bronchial wall thickening, but not gross cystic cavitation. Therefore, based on the definitive radiological visual of dilated, cyst-like bronchi, bronchiectasis is the condition described. This finding explains symptoms like chronic purulent cough and postural sputum production

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The non-contraceptive uses of oral contraceptives include all of the following except:
options: Reduction in the risk of ovarian cancer
Protection against sexually transmitted diseases including HIV
Reduction in the risk of endometrial cancer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protection against sexually transmitted diseases including HIV

The non-contraceptive uses of oral contraceptives include all except protection against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), including HIV.

Oral hormonal contraceptives can be combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) or progesterone-only minipills.

COCPs are a combination of ethinylestradiol at a dose of 20–30 mcg and an orally active progestogen. It is taken starting on the first day of the cycle for 21 days. They are taken at a fixed time of the day, preferably after a meal. Mala-N and Mala-D both contain levonorgestrel (0.15 mg) + ethinylestradiol (30 mcg). Mala-N is supplied free of cost in Family Planning Clinics in India. Each strip contains 21 hormonal tablets and 7 non-hormonal (iron) tablets.

The mechanism of action is the prevention of ovulation by suppression of the pituitary hormones FSH and LH. Progesterone also acts on the cervical mucus, making it thick and impenetrable by sperm. The pregnancy rate with the COCP is 0.3 per 100 woman-years.

Benefits of the COCP:

• It is effective in controlling fertility.
• It causes regular cycles and reduces menstrual blood loss and are, therefore, useful in menorrhagia and polymenorrhea.
• It lowers the incidence of benign breast neoplastic diseases, such as fibrocystic disease.
• It reduces the incidence of functional ovarian cysts and ovarian (Option A) and endometrial malignancy (Option D). The incidence of ovarian cancer is reduced by 40% and that of uterine malignancy, by 50%, if taken for 1 year; this effect lasts as long as 10 years after stoppage.
• It reduces the incidence of ectopic pregnancy (Option B) by suppressing ovulation and reducing the risk in pelvic inflammatory disease.
• It is useful in endometriosis, acne, and polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD).

Side effects:

• Higher incidence of breast cancer reported among users
• Suppression of lactation
• Occurrence of pituitary adenoma and adenoma of the liver
• Reduced carbohydrate tolerance (therefore, contraindicated in diabetic women)
• Migraine, depression, weight gain, and lethargy (due to progesterone)
• Increased risk of pulmonary embolism and cerebral thrombosis

Ninety-nine percent of women will regain normal menstrual cycles within 6 months of stopping the pills, while the return of fertility is slightly delayed.

Barrier methods like condoms prevent the transmission of STDs.
questions.learning: Protection against sexually transmitted diseases including HIV The non-contraceptive uses of oral contraceptives include all except protection against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), including HIV.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient is not able to see the lateral fields. He was having a mild headache for a few weeks and now presented to the clinic. Visual field examination shows the following finding. What is the probable site of the lesion based on the image displayed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Optic chiasma

The visual field defect in the image is indicative of bitemporal hemianopia, so the probable site of the lesion is the optic chiasma.

Hemianopia or hemianopsia refers to loss of sight in half the visual field. Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma. The most common cause of this is pituitary gland tumours. Other causes include suprasellar aneurysms, chronic arachnoiditis, suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma.

Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia to emphasize the fact that the parts of the visual field that are lost in each eye do not overlap.

Individuals with this condition are able to see in both left and right central visual fields, with both eyes open. However, all information from the most peripheral parts of visual fields (which are seen only by the nasal retinas) is lost.

Other options:

Lesions at the occipital lobe, optic tract and optic radiation would all cause homonymous hemianopia. Here, either the right or left half of the binocular field of vision is lost, due to the loss of the temporal half of one field and the nasal half of the other.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The given ECG depicts which of the following conditions:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ventricular bigeminy

The given ECG shows a premature ventricular complex (PVC) that occurs every second beat (ventricular bigeminy).

PVCs exhibit premature timing by arising before the anticipated occurrence of the subsequent regular heartbeat. They display an aberrant QRS-T appearance, where the QRS complex appears unusually wide (0.12 sec or longer), and the T wave and QRS complex point in opposite orientations (discordant).

Frequent PVCs can manifest in different patterns. When two PVCs occur consecutively, they are termed a pair or couplet.

If three or more PVCs occur in succession (triplet), it is classified as ventricular tachycardia (VT). The repetitive pattern of one normal beat followed by one PVC is known as ventricular bigeminy.

When the repeating sequence involves two normal beats followed by a PVC, it is called ventricular trigeminy. Similarly, if three normal beats are followed by a PVC, it is referred to as ventricular quadrigeminy.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with conductive hearing loss and is diagnosed with otosclerosis. What is the surgical treatment of choice for this condition?
options: Stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis
questions.explanation: In otosclerosis, abnormal bone deposition causes fixation of the stapes footplate, leading to conductive hearing loss. The classical and exam-accepted surgical treatment of choice is stapedectomy with prosthesis placement, where the fixed stapes is removed and replaced by a prosthetic device that transmits sound vibrations to the inner ear. This procedure has a high success rate in improving hearing and has been traditionally considered the standard treatment in many exam contexts. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Stapedotomy: A newer, less invasive modification where only a small hole is made in the footplate. Though widely used in practice, many exams still consider stapedectomy as the classical answer. (C) Stapes mobilization: An older technique with high recurrence rates, now largely abandoned. (D) Lempert’s fenestration: A historical procedure, no longer used in modern practice. Thus, as per exam standards, the answer is stapedectomy with prosthesis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with central cyanosis and a radiological image of a boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for cyanosis in the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

The image above shows a boot-shaped heart. Cyanosis, oligemic lung fields, and a boot-shaped heart (cœur en sabot in French) point towards tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

Radiological features: "Coeur en sabot" is due to cardiac apex elevation as a result of right ventricular hypertrophy. The cardiac silhouette has been likened to that of a boot (“coeur-en sabot”). The hilar areas and lung fields are relatively clear because of diminished pulmonary blood flow or the small size of the pulmonary arteries. The aorta is usually large.

Clinical findings in TOF:

* Right ventricular hypertrophy, causing a left anterior hemithorax bulge.

* Single S2 or soft P2 because of the stenotic pulmonary valve

* Systolic thrill in the left sternal border in the 3rd and 4th parasternal spaces.

* The large 'a wave in the jugular pulse is a reflection of the forceful contraction of the right atrium at the end of diastole, as there is reduced distensibility of the hypertrophic right ventricle.

* There is a loud and harsh systolic murmur due to the right ventricular outflow tract(RVOT) obstruction. It becomes louder, longer, and harsher as obstruction increases in severity from mild to moderate.

However, in severe obstruction, especially during a tet spell, the murmur becomes less prominent as the blood is shunted towards the aortic valve and not through RVOT.

Other options:

Option B: ASD is characterised by an abnormal opening in the atrial septum, allowing communication between the right and left atria. Ostium secundum ASD is the most common type of ASD.

Option C: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart defect. Commonly seen in maternal diabetes and fetal alcohol syndrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Revised How much oxygen is given to a term infant with respiratory distress during resuscitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 21%

Resuscitation in term infants is done by using 21% oxygen or room air.

In term infants with apnea, gasping or heart rate <100/min, positive pressure ventilation (PPV) is given by bag-mask device in room air with 21% oxygen. Room air in term infants is effective and may reduce the risk of hyperoxia, reduced cerebral blood flow and generation of free radicals.

If there is no improvement in 30 seconds, ventilative corrective steps should be taken and then oxygen concentration titrated as needed to obtain the expected saturation. If the heart rate falls below 60 then chest compressions are started, intubated and FIO2 is increased to 100%.

Resuscitation of most preterm infants can be initiated with a slightly higher fraction of inspired oxygen (21–30%) and titrated as needed.

The flowchart below shows the steps to be followed in neonatal resuscitation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with acute appendicitis was brought to the hospital within 24 hours of symptom onset. Which of the following statements is/are true regarding this condition? 1. McBurney's point tenderness is a reliable clinical sign 2. Ultrasound (USG) is the preferred investigation in pregnant women and children 3. Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass 4. Interval appendectomy is mandatory after conservative management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

1) Acute Appendicitis

Typical progression:

Visceral pain phase

• Pain begins around the umbilicus
• Because visceral afferents from the appendix enter T10 spinal segment

Parietal peritoneal irritation

• Inflammation reaches parietal peritoneum
• Pain localizes to right lower quadrant

This is where McBurney’s point tenderness appears.

• Junction of lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of the line between: Umbilicus-Right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)

2) Ultrasound is preferred in pregnant women and children ✔️

• Ultrasound has no radiation
• Safe for pregnancy and pediatrics

It can detect:

• Inflamed appendix
• Appendix diameter > 6 mm
• Peri-appendiceal fluid

3) Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass ✔️

An appendicular mass forms when the body tries to contain infection by surrounding the inflamed appendix with: Omentum and Bowel loops

Instead of immediate surgery, conservative treatment is given.

This is called Ochsner–Sherren regimen, which includes:

• Nil by mouth
• IV fluids
• Antibiotics
• Observation

Surgery is avoided initially because operating on a mass can injure surrounding bowel.

4) Interval appendectomy is mandatory-This is false.

Earlier practice:

• After conservative treatment, surgery was done 6–8 weeks later (interval appendectomy).

Current practice:

• Not mandatory anymore
• Done only if symptoms recur.

Many patients remain completely asymptomatic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant is scheduled for cleft lip repair. During the surgical procedure, which of the following muscles is primarily corrected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbicularis oris

Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominence, disrupting the orbicularis oris muscle.

Orbicularis oris forms the sphincter of the mouth and is essential for lip seal and feeding.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At which stage of clinical trials is a newly developed drug usually approved for marketing and made available to the public?
questions.explanation: Phase III is the stage at which a newly developed drug is evaluated for regulatory approval and subsequently marketed and made available to the general public. Phase III trials are large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted on thousands of patients (typically 1,000–3,000) across multiple centers. These trials compare the new drug against existing standard treatments or placebo, establishing definitive evidence of efficacy, safety, optimal dosage, and side effect profile. Upon successful completion of Phase III, the pharmaceutical company submits a New Drug Application (NDA) to regulatory authorities like the FDA or CDSCO, after which the drug receives marketing approval. Why other options are wrong: (A) Phase I is incorrect because Phase I trials are conducted on a small group of healthy volunteers (20–80 people) primarily to assess safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. No efficacy data is established here and marketing is nowhere near consideration at this stage. (B) Phase II is incorrect because Phase II trials involve moderate number of patients (100–300) with the target disease, primarily evaluating therapeutic efficacy, optimal dosing, and short-term side effects. While promising results emerge here, this data is insufficient for regulatory marketing approval. (D) Phase IV is incorrect because Phase IV trials occur after marketing approval, representing post-marketing surveillance. They monitor long-term safety, rare adverse effects, and new indications in the general population — the drug is already available to the public at this point
questions.learning: Phase III is the stage at which a newly developed drug is evaluated for regulatory approval and subsequently marketed and made available to the general public.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A woman presented with sudden onset of dysphagia, dysarthria and gait ataxia. MRI revealed an acute infarct in the right dorsolateral medulla. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wallenberg syndrome. The symptoms of dysphagia and dysarthria are due to the involvement of nucleus ambiguus. Ataxia is a feature of inferior cerebellar peduncle involvement.

Option B: Lateral medullary syndrome is also known as Wallenberg syndrome.

Option C: Medullary tegmental paralysis is also known as Babinski-Nageotte syndrome.

Option D: Midbrain stroke syndrome is also known as Weber syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A factory worker sustained burns involving 25% of his body while on duty. He later developed infections and related complications. Under the ESI Act, which of the following benefits is he entitled to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extended Sickness benefit

The patient developed a long-term complication (infections after burns) due to a serious condition, and under the ESI Act, such chronic or prolonged illnesses fall under the category of extended sickness benefit.

Extended sickness benefit covers those with more than 20% burns with infection or complication. Leave is given up to a maximum period of two years. The diseases for which extended sickness benefits are applied are TB, leprosy, empyema, HIV, malignancies, plegias, etc. During this period, 80 per cent of the wages are paid.

ESI act was amended to provide cash and medical benefits to employees during sickness, maternity, and employment injury. People with monthly earnings up to 21,000 are covered under this scheme. Cash benefits are made through branches and cash offices. The medical benefits are made available through ESI dispensaries, clinics, hospitals, etc. The benefits provided to the insured persons are:

* Medical benefits - Complete medical care is provided to the insured person and his/ her family members.

* Sickness benefits - include a periodic cash payment for 91 days to the insured sick person. 70% of the average daily wages is given as the daily rate if the person is under medical treatment.

* Enhanced sickness benefit - includes 14 days of leave given for tubectomy and 7 days of leave for vasectomy. The amount payable is equal to the full wages.

* Maternity benefits - cash payments equal to full wages are paid to the insured person for up to 26 weeks in cases of pregnancy.

* Disablement benefit - cash payment and free medical treatment are given for temporary or permanent disablements and occupational diseases.

* Dependant's benefit - if an employment injury causes the death of the insured person, the dependants are eligible for periodic payments.

* Funeral expenses of Rs 15000 are payable to the dependants.

* Rehabilitation allowance - the insured person and the family members continue to get medical treatment after permanent disablement and retirement.
questions.learning: Extended Sickness benefit — The patient developed a long-term complication (infections after burns) due to a serious condition, and under the ESI Act, such chronic or prolonged illnesses fall under the category of extended sickness benefit.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents with high-grade fever and a purpuric rash. Cerebrospinal fluid examination shows gram-negative diplococci. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic triad of high-grade fever, purpuric rash (petechiae/ecchymoses), and signs of meningitis. The definitive diagnostic clue is the CSF finding of gram-negative diplococci. This is the pathognomonic microscopic appearance of Neisseria meningitidis (the meningococcus). Pseudomonas (Option B) and E. coli (Option D) are Gram-negative rods (bacilli). Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) is a major cause of meningitis but would appear as Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. The purpuric rash is highly characteristic of meningococcemia, resulting from vascular damage and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Neisseria meningitidis is a leading cause of bacterial meningitis in young adults and can cause rapid clinical deterioration. Immediate treatment with intravenous Ceftriaxone and respiratory isolation are required. Given the Gram-stain morphology and the characteristic rash, Neisseria meningitidis is the only possible causative agent
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic triad of high-grade fever, purpuric rash (petechiae/ecchymoses), and signs of meningitis. The definitive diagnostic clue is the CSF finding of gram-negative diplococci.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which tissue in the human body is most sensitive to the effects of radiation?
questions.explanation: The radiosensitivity of a tissue is generally proportional to its rate of cell division and inversely proportional to its degree of specialization (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau). The "bone marrow" (Option C) contains hematopoietic stem cells that are rapidly and continuously dividing, making it one of the "most radiation-sensitive" tissues in the body. Acute exposure to high doses of radiation can lead to bone marrow syndrome, characterized by severe pancytopenia and immune suppression. Skin (Option A) is also sensitive but less so than the bone marrow. Muscle tissue (Option B) and nervous tissue (Option D) are composed of highly specialized, non-dividing (permanent) cells, making them relatively "radioresistant". Understanding tissue sensitivity is crucial in clinical radiology and oncology for calculating safe diagnostic doses and for planning radiotherapy while minimizing collateral damage to vital organs. Protective measures, such as lead shielding, are specifically designed to protect the most sensitive areas from unnecessary exposure
questions.learning: The radiosensitivity of a tissue is generally proportional to its rate of cell division and inversely proportional to its degree of specialization (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old baby comes with complaints of deafness, cataract, and patent ductus arteriosus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Congenital rubella syndrome

The most likely diagnosis is congenital rubella syndrome based on the clinical findings.

Triad of Gregg is seen in babies with congenital rubella syndrome. The features include:

• Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
• Cataract
• Sensorineural Hearing loss (SNHL)

Rubella or German measles is a serious infection in pregnancy that causes abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester. Transmission of the virus occurs through nasopharyngeal secretions (droplet transmission). The mother usually has a fever and generalized body rash. The rash is maculopapular in nature that begins from the face and spreads to the trunk and extremities later. The incidence and severity reduce as the pregnancy advances and is rare after 20 weeks of gestation.

There is no specific treatment for rubella virus infection in mothers. Post-exposure passive immunization can be beneficial if given within 5 days of exposure to droplets. The incidence of this disease has reduced due to the availability of MMR vaccines. MMR vaccines can be administered only to non-pregnant females as it is a live, attenuated virus. Pregnancy should be avoided for at least 1 month after vaccination.

Other options:

Option A: Herpes simplex infection can be acquired in utero, intrapartum, or during the neonatal period. The intrauterine infection causes skin vesicles, eye findings (chorioretinitis, keratoconjunctivitis), and microcephaly/hydranencephaly. Intrapartum infection presents with either:

• Skin, eye, and mouth disease
• Encephalitis
• Disseminated disease with sepsis-like presentation

Option B: Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs due to primary infection in immunologically normal pregnant women. First-trimester infection results in severe disease and third-trimester disease result in milder disease. It presents with a triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracerebral calcifications.

Option C: Pregnant females infected with cytomegalovirus (CMV) present with infectious mononucleosis-like symptoms, that is fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and polyarthritis. Transmission to the fetus increases as pregnancy advances and is maximum in the third trimester. Congenital infection includes growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial (periventricular) calcifications, chorioretinitis, mental and motor deficits, hepatosplenomegaly, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenic purpura. Most infected neonates are asymptomatic at birth and later present with these symptoms. Sensorineural hearing loss is a common sequela of congenital CMV infection.

Other infections which cause congenital malformations are:

Organism
Defects

Toxoplasma

Hydro/microcephaly, convulsions, chorioretinitis, diffuse cerebral calcifications

Parvovirus
Non-immune hydrops

Syphilis

Hutchinson's triad:

• Interstitial keratitis
• Hutchinson's teeth
• Eighth nerve deafness
questions.learning: Congenital rubella syndrome — The most likely diagnosis is congenital rubella syndrome based on the clinical findings. Triad of Gregg is seen in babies with congenital rubella syndrome.

• Pain typically radiates from flank to groin (loin-to-groin pattern)

questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient has undergone a surgical procedure for a swelling in his left groin. The image of the procedure is as shown. What procedure has been performed?

Correct answer: B. Lichtenstein’s repair

The image represents Lichtenstein tension-free mesh hernioplasty, one of the standard open repairs for an inguinal hernia.

In this procedure:

• The mesh is fixed inferiorly to the inguinal ligament and superiorly to the conjoint tendon/internal oblique aponeurosis.
• A slit is made in the lateral part of the mesh to accommodate the spermatic cord.
• The two tails of the mesh overlap around the cord, creating a new internal ring.
• It is a tension-free repair, unlike traditional tissue-based repairs.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: ETDRS study was related to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic macular edema

Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) was a randomized clinical trial that studied the effect of photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema.

The results of the study demonstrated the beneficial effects of focal photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema. The study resulted in the recommendation that all eyes with clinically significant diabetic macular edema should be considered for focal photocoagulation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of breast cancer underwent tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She now presents with respiratory distress, and imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radiation pneumonitis

A patient with a history of breast cancer who previously received Tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy now presents with respiratory distress. Imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities, suggesting a likely diagnosis of radiation pneumonitis.

Radiation pneumonitis is an inflammatory reaction in the lungs that occurs as a result of radiation therapy, commonly seen in patients treated for breast cancer, lung cancer, or lymphomas. It typically develops within weeks to months after radiation exposure and presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath. The condition arises due to damage to the alveolar and capillary structures, leading to increased vascular permeability, inflammatory infiltration, and pulmonary oedema. Imaging findings, particularly on CT scans, may show areas of ground-glass opacities, consolidation, or haziness, often in the radiation field.

If left untreated, radiation pneumonitis can progress to pulmonary fibrosis, causing long-term respiratory complications. Management involves corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and supportive care, including oxygen therapy if needed.

Prevention strategies include limiting the radiation dose, using advanced radiotherapy techniques to minimize lung exposure, and closely monitoring high-risk patients. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to improving outcomes and preventing long-term lung damage in affected individuals.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Arrange the following causes of neonatal mortality from maximum to the least (according to the verbal autopsy report 2010-2013 data).

1. Prematurity and low birth weight
2. Birth injuries and birth asphyxia
3. Congenital anomalies
4. Sepsis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1>2>4>3

According to verbal autopsy report 2010-2013 data, the correct sequence of causes of neonatal mortality from maximum to least is prematurity and low birth weight> birth injuries and birth asphyxia> sepsis> congenital anomalies. (1>2>4>3)

Neonatal deaths are deaths that occur during the neonatal period, that is between birth and 28 completed days after birth. It is calculated by using the following formula:

Neonatal mortality rate = Number of deaths of children under 28 days of age in a year x 1000/Total live births in the same year

Important causes of neonatal mortality include ( from maximum to least)

• Prematurity & low birth weight
• Birth asphyxia & birth trauma
• Neonatal pneumonia
• Other non-communicable diseases
• Sepsis
• Congenital anomalies
• Diarrhoeal diseases
• Injuries
• Tetanus

Note: Recent 2020 SRS (Sample Registration System) report shows the following:

• Neonatal mortality rate to be 20.
• Infant mortality rate to be 28.
• Under 5 mortality rate to be 32.
questions.learning: 1>2>4>3 According to verbal autopsy report 2010-2013 data, the correct sequence of causes of neonatal mortality from maximum to least is prematurity and low birth weight> birth injuries and birth asphyxia> sepsis> congenital anomalies.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about longevity dividend?
options: The intervention can delay the onset of the disease
Small amounts of damage is accumulated over time
The older you are the more prone you are to disease
Economic and health benefit for the society
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The intervention can delay the onset of the disease

The intervention can delay the onset of the disease (Statement 1) is true about longevity dividend.

The longevity dividend is a horizontal approach to public health which is based on a broader strategy which means to foster health for all generations. This can be done by developing a new model for health promotion and disease prevention. The longevity-dividend model aims to prevent or delay the root causes of disease and disability by decimating the one major risk factor which is biological aging.
questions.learning: The intervention can delay the onset of the disease — The intervention can delay the onset of the disease (Statement 1) is true about longevity dividend.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the name of the sign demonstrated in the contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head shown below?
questions.explanation: The Holman Miller sign (or antral sign) is a classic radiological feature observed in juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA). It refers to the anterior bowing or displacement of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus by the tumor mass, which originates in the sphenopalatine foramen. This sign is highly characteristic of JNA, which typically affects adolescent males and presents with recurrent, severe epistaxis and nasal obstruction. Aquino Sign (Option A) involves the blanching of a tumor upon carotid compression. Teardrop sign (Option C) and Hanging drop sign (Option D) are associated with orbital blowout fractures where orbital contents herniate into the maxillary sinus. In the context of a 14-year-old male with severe spontaneous nasal bleeding, the Holman Miller sign on CT provides definitive evidence of the expansive nature of a nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is noted to have a right transverse palmar crease, an associated cardiac defect, survival beyond infancy, and mild intellectual disability. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The features described, including a transverse palmar crease, cardiac defect, and intellectual impairment, are classic for Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21). In this case, the survival into childhood with only "mild" impairment suggests Mosaicism, which occurs in about 1% of cases. Mosaicism results from a post-zygotic mitotic error, leading to a mixture of normal and trisomy 21 cells; this often results in a milder clinical phenotype than full meiotic nondisjunction. Tetralogy (Option A) likely refers to Tetralogy of Fallot, a heart defect that can occur in syndromes but is not a chromosomal abnormality itself. Haploid (Option B) refers to a single set of chromosomes (23), which is incompatible with human life. Monosomy (Option C) is the loss of a chromosome, such as in Turner syndrome (45,X). Mosaicism allows for a broad range of developmental outcomes
questions.learning: The features described, including a transverse palmar crease, cardiac defect, and intellectual impairment, are classic for Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) threshold on Shakir’s tape that indicates severe acute malnutrition?
questions.explanation: cm Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a rapid and effective screening tool for assessing nutritional status in children aged 6 to 59 months. According to WHO standards and Shakir's tape classification, a MUAC of less than is the diagnostic criterion for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). This measurement corresponds to the "Red" zone on a standard tri-colored Shakir's tape. A MUAC between and (Option B) indicates Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM), represented by the "Yellow" zone. Measurements above (Option C and D) are considered normal and fall in the "Green" zone. MUAC is preferred in field settings because it is simple to use and correlates well with the risk of mortality. Children identified with SAM require urgent referral for therapeutic feeding and medical management. This screening is a core component of the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) protocol used by frontline health workers

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following will increase the GFR?
options: Decrease in bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decrease in bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure

A decrease in Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure causes an increase in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

A decrease in Bowman's Capsule Hydrostatic Pressure increases GFR because it reduces the opposing force to filtration, thus enhancing the net filtration pressure and increasing the amount of filtrate formed.

Factors that can increase the GFR are as follows:

* Increase in glomerular capillary filtration coefficient Kf: This coefficient depends on the hydraulic conductivity and surface area of the glomerular capillaries.

* Decrease in Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure: Conditions with urinary tract obstruction can lead to an increase in this pressure and a fall in GFR.

* Decrease in glomerular colloid osmotic pressure: Accumulation of plasma proteins that are not filtered from the blood contributes to this pressure, and an increase reduces further filtration and GFR. It is directly proportional to the following factors: Arterial plasma colloid osmotic pressure.

* Filtration fraction : An increase in filtration fraction concentrates the plasma proteins and raises the glomerular colloid osmotic pressure which in turn decreases the GFR.

Other options :

Option A: Efferent Arteriole Dilation reduces the resistance to blood leaving the glomerulus. This leads to a decrease in glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. A reduction in hydrostatic pressure lowers the driving force for filtration, resulting in a decreased GFR.

Option B: Afferent Arteriole Constriction decreases blood flow into the glomerulus. This lowers the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. Lower pressure reduces the filtration rate across the glomerular capillary wall, leading to a decrease in GFR.

Option C: Increase in Glomerular Plasma Flow: If glomerular plasma flow increases but the efferent arteriole doesn't constrict, the extra blood flow is quickly carried away. This prevents a significant rise in the pressure inside the glomerular capillaries. As a result, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) doesn't significantly increase, because the necessary increase in filtration pressure doesn't occur.
