questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During a hysteroscopic removal of a submucosal fibroid, a fluid deficit of 2000 mL is estimated in a patient. What is the immediate complication of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pulmonary edema

The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of fluid overload, and pulmonary edema is the immediate complication anticipated in this scenario.

In the context of hysteroscopic procedures, the term fluid deficit refers to the difference between the volume of distension fluid introduced into the uterine cavity and the volume of fluid that is removed or accounted for during the procedure. A large fluid deficit indicates that a significant amount of the distension fluid has been absorbed into the patient's bloodstream.

When a large volume of fluid is absorbed during a hysteroscopic procedure, it can lead to fluid overload. This excess fluid in the bloodstream can increase the pressure in the blood vessels, particularly in the pulmonary circulation. The elevated pressure can cause fluid to leak from the small blood vessels in the lungs into the air spaces, resulting in pulmonary edema.

Pulmonary edema can lead to shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and impaired gas exchange, as the fluid-filled air spaces in the lungs make it difficult for oxygen to pass from the air into the bloodstream. In severe cases, it can lead to respiratory failure and can be life-threatening. Prompt recognition and management of fluid overload during hysteroscopic procedures are crucial to minimizing the risk of complications like pulmonary edema.

Hysteroscopy is an operative procedure that provides the endoscopic view of endometrial cavity and tubal ostia via the cervix. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic. A hysteroscopic image of a uterus with carcinoma is shown below.

Therapeutic indications of hysteroscopy
Diagnostic indications of hysteroscopy

• Uterine septum
• Asherman syndrome
• Retained IUCD
• Polypectomy
• Submucous fibroid
• Abnormal uterine bleeding
• Tubal sterilization using sclerosing agents

• To study the endocervical mucosal lining
• Congenital malformations of the uterus
• Endometrial tuberculosis
• Asherman syndrome
• Misplaced IUCD
• Endometrial lesions
• Endometrial polyp
• Cornual tubal blockage

Complications of hysteroscopy include :

• Early complications:

1. Anesthesia complications- air embolism can occur
2. Uterine perforation
3. Thermal injury with cautery and laser
4. Sepsis
5. Allergic reaction to dextran and glycine
6. Fluid overload occurs and can lead to pulmonary edema if the fluid deficit is more than 1000 mL. It can be managed by diuretics.
7. Cerebral edema
8. Cardiac failure

• Late complications:

1. Hematometra following cervical stenosis
2. Pelvic inflammatory disease
3. Uterine rupture during pregnancy
4. Dysmenorrhea
5. Amenorrhea

Other options:

Option A: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is a kidney disorder involving damage to the tubule cells of the kidneys, which can lead to acute kidney injury (AKI). While fluid overload can be a risk factor for AKI, it is not the immediate complication of a fluid deficit of 2000 mL in this clinical scenario.

Option B: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a serious disorder where the proteins that control blood clotting become overactive. It is not directly related to a fluid deficit during a hysteroscopic procedure and is therefore not the immediate complication in this case.

Option D: Thromboembolism refers to a blood clot that forms in a blood vessel and then breaks loose, traveling through the bloodstream and potentially causing a blockage in another part of the body. Although any surgical procedure carries a risk of thromboembolism, it is not the immediate complication related to a fluid deficit of 2000 mL in this scenario.
questions.learning: Pulmonary edema — The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of fluid overload, and pulmonary edema is the immediate complication anticipated in this scenario.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 12-year-old presented with fever and difficulty swallowing. He had swelling in the marked region and was advised to undergo surgery. Post-surgery the gauze continued to soak with blood. Which of the following vessels must have been injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paratonsillar vein

The given image is a cadaveric specimen with the arrow pointing towards, the tonsillar fossa, and the given clinical vignette is suggestive of tonsillitis. Post tonsillectomy hemorrhage is commonly venous in origin, from the paratonsillar/ external palatine vein.

Torrential hemorrhage can be due to injury to an aberrantly large or aberrantly placed tonsillar arterial branch of the facial artery.

Blood supply of the tonsils:

Arterial supply:

• The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main supply.
• Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
• Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery.
• Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.
• Descending palatine branches of the maxillary artery.

Venous supply:

• Veins from the tonsils drain into paratonsillar vein which joins the common facial vein and pharyngeal venous plexus.

Types of Hemorrhage seen during/post tonsillectomy:

• Primary hemorrhage:

• Occurs during surgery due to injury to blood vessels.
• Can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

• Reactionary hemorrhage:

• It occurs within 24 hours of surgery.
• It may be due to dislodgement of the clot, slippage of ligature, or return of blood pressure to normal.
• It is managed by removal of clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor.
• If not controlled the patient is anesthetized and hemorrhage is managed by re-exploration.

• Secondary hemorrhage:

• It occurs between 24 hours to 10 days (most common between 5th to 8th postoperative days).
• It is due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane.
• The patient is started on IV antibiotics and if not controlled, general anesthesia is given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and dyspnea. On oral examination, a pseudomembrane is seen over the tonsils. What is the mechanism of action of the toxin produced by the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

This child with pseudomembrane over tonsil has diphtheria, in which the toxin inactivates the elongation factor EF-2.

Diphtheria toxin is an exotoxin that consists of two fragments - A and B. It acts by inhibiting protein synthesis. Fragment B helps in binding the toxin to the cells while fragment A inactivates the elongation factor (EF-2) responsible for protein synthesis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa also produces toxins with a similar mechanism of action.

This infection presents as fever and sore throat, which progresses to dyspnea due to obstruction by the pseudomembrane. Bull's neck appearance is seen due to cervical lymphadenitis. Complications like damage to the heart (myocarditis), kidney (tubular necrosis), liver, and adrenal glands can develop due to the toxin.

Neisser's or Albert's stain will show the bacilli with metachromatic granules situated at the poles of the bacilli. Tellurite blood agar is the selective culture medium.
It is treated mainly by neutralizing with antitoxin and antibiotics to arrest more toxin production.

Pearl PF0802: Mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins

The mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins are as given below:

Increase in cAMP

* Bordetella pertusis

* Bacillus anthracis

* Vibrio cholerae - Cholera toxin

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat labile toxin

Increase in cGMP

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat stable toxin

Inhibition of protein synthesis

* Diptheria toxin: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Pseudomonas: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Clostridium difficile

* Enterohemorrhagic E.coli (EHEC)-Shiga-like toxin: inhibit 60S

* Shigella dysenteriae- Shiga toxin: inhibit 60S
questions.learning: Inhibition of elongation factor-2 (EF-2) — This child with pseudomembrane over tonsil has diphtheria, in which the toxin inactivates the elongation factor EF-2.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens in cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trypan blue

Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility. It is used in anterior capsulotomy like capsulorrhexis.

In capsulorrhexis, an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens. Continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC) is considered to be superior to all the pre-existing methods because when done correctly, it does not leave any edges or tears.In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydrodissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.
questions.learning: Trypan blue Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility. It is used in anterior capsulotomy like capsulorrhexis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady who is a known case of seizures was on carbamazepine. She was prescribed erythromycin for her recent URTI. A few days later, she developed ataxia. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carbamazepine toxicity

Carbamazepine → metabolized by CYP3A4 → normal levels

Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the main enzyme responsible for carbamazepine metabolism. This raises serum carbamazepine levels, causing toxicity with neurologic signs like ataxia and diplopia. The interaction is due to reduced hepatic clearance, not increased metabolism. Drug–drug inhibition leading to accumulation explains the symptoms.

B) Erythromycin toxicity

• Causes GI upset, QT prolongation
• NOT ataxia

C) Rebound epileptic episode

• Would cause seizures, not ataxia

D) Increased hepatic metabolism

• Opposite happened!
• Metabolism is inhibited, not increased
questions.learning: Carbamazepine toxicity Carbamazepine → metabolized by CYP3A4 → normal levels Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the main enzyme responsible for carbamazepine metabolism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: As a medical practitioner in India, how will you prescribe alprazolam to a patient?
options: 1 mg OD before bedtime for 7 days
0.5 mg daily before bedtime for 7 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 0.5 mg daily before bedtime for 7 days

The correct method of prescribing alprazolam is 0.5mg daily before bedtime for 7 days.

The drugs are prescribed in generic names legibly and preferably in capital letters. The prescription should have details to identify the patient and medication that needs to be dispensed and the therapeutic purpose. The use of abbreviations, especially Latin is discouraged. The dosage should be written in metric measure.

Guidelines for drug prescription:

The parts of an ideal prescription are as follows.

• Date
• Name and address of the doctor
• Superscription(Rx symbol)
• Information about the patient
• Name and dose of the drug prescribed(Inscription)
• Dispencing directions to the pharmacist(Subscription)
• Instructions for the patient
• Signature of the doctor

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A diabetic man presents with seizures. Radiological imaging reveals a lesion, and histopathological examination shows liquefactive necrosis. What is the most important underlying mechanism responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis is the standard type of necrosis observed in central nervous system (brain) tissue following infection or ischemia. The primary mechanism responsible is enzymatic degradation. Because the brain is rich in lipids and lacks a supportive fibrous stroma, the hydrolytic lysosomal enzymes released by activated microglia and infiltrating neutrophils quickly digest the dead tissue into a liquid mass. While ischemia (Option C) triggers the process, the actual transformation into liquefactive necrosis is due to the enzymatic action rather than the lack of blood flow itself. Mechanical injury (Option B) causes hemorrhage or trauma but not the classic histological pattern of liquefaction. Increased intracranial pressure (Option D) leads to herniation but not this specific type of necrosis. Thus, enzymatic digestion is the critical driver of the liquefactive process
questions.learning: Liquefactive necrosis is the standard type of necrosis observed in central nervous system (brain) tissue following infection or ischemia. The primary mechanism responsible is enzymatic degradation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For performing a transurethral resection in cases of bladder tumors, which of the following lasers is most commonly used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nd-YAG laser

Lasers are used in urology for cutting, coagulation, and tissue vaporization. In transurethral management of bladder tumors (laser TURBT/fulguration), the preferred laser is one that provides deep coagulation and good hemostasis, especially for superficial tumor ablation.

Nd:YAG (Neodymium-doped Yttrium Aluminium Garnet) laser is most commonly used because it:

• has deep tissue penetration

• provides excellent coagulation

• is effective for tumor coagulation/fulguration via endoscopic approach

Why others are less suitable:

• Ho:YAG: mainly used for stone fragmentation and prostate enucleation (HoLEP); more precise cutting with shallow penetration.

• Argon: limited depth, less commonly used for TUR of bladder tumors.

• CO₂ laser: not practical endoscopically in bladder due to poor transmission through fluids.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for severe acne?
questions.explanation: Oral isotretinoin is the most effective and appropriate treatment for severe, nodulocystic, or treatment-resistant acne. It is a systemic retinoid that addresses all four pathogenic factors of acne: it reduces sebum production, normalizes keratinization, inhibits bacterial colonization (P. acnes), and has anti-inflammatory properties. Regarding the other options, topical tretinoin (Option A) is suitable for mild comedonal acne but is insufficient for severe cases. Systemic steroids (Option C) are not used to treat acne and can actually induce "steroid acne" as a side effect. While antibiotics (Option D), such as doxycycline, are useful for moderate inflammatory acne, they do not provide the long-term remission required for severe, scarring disease. Given its potency and ability to prevent permanent scarring, isotretinoin is the gold standard for severe presentations, despite its required monitoring for side effects

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following structures are not removed in radical neck dissection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sublingual gland

Sublingual gland is not removed in radical neck dissection (RND). Submandibular gland is removed in RND.

RND involves the removal of:

• All lymph nodes from Levels I through to V (submental, submandibular, upper, middle, and lower jugular, and posterior triangle regions) along with its fibrofatty tissue.
• The spinal accessory nerve
• Internal jugular vein
• Sternocleidomastoid muscle
• Tail of parotid
• Submandibular gland
• Omohyoid muscle
questions.learning: Sublingual gland Sublingual gland is not removed in radical neck dissection (RND). Submandibular gland is removed in RND.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Type 2 lepra reaction is caused by __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type III hypersensitivity reaction

Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) or type 2 lepra reaction is caused by type III hypersensitivity reaction which is immune-complex mediated.

Type 2 lepra reactions (ENL) are mainly seen in multibacillary disease; LL(50%)>BL(15%). They can occur before, during, or after treatment, and are commonly recurrent. These reactions are caused by immune complexes (type 3 hypersensitivity).
ENL presents with painful, erythematous nodules on the face and extensor surfaces of limbs. Systemic manifestations like fever, malaise, anorexia, neuritis, uveitis, dactylitis, arthritis, myositis, etc. can also be seen.

Treatment of type 2 lepra reactions includes high-dose steroids, thalidomide (drug of choice in young men with severe ENL), and clofazimine.

Type 1 lepra reaction, on the other hand, is caused by type IV hypersensitivity reaction i.e. cell-mediated immune inflammation within existing skin lesions.
questions.learning: Type III hypersensitivity reaction Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) or type 2 lepra reaction is caused by type III hypersensitivity reaction which is immune-complex mediated.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Under normal physiological conditions, why is hemoglobin unable to pass through the glomerular filtration barrier?
options: It is a large molecule bound with another protein
It gets attracted to the negative charge of the glomerular filtration barrier
questions.explanation: Under normal physiological conditions, hemoglobin is contained within red blood cells and does not reach the glomerular filtrate. However, if free hemoglobin is present in the plasma due to mild hemolysis, it is rapidly bound by a plasma protein called haptoglobin. This hemoglobin-haptoglobin complex is too large to pass through the pores of the glomerular filtration barrier, thus preventing hemoglobinuria and protecting the renal tubules from oxidative damage. Option B is incorrect because the glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged due to heparin sulfate proteoglycans, which "repels" rather than attracts negatively charged proteins like albumin or hemoglobin. Therefore, "Both A and B" (Option C) is incorrect as statement B is physiologically backwards. Hemoglobinuria only occurs when the hemolytic rate exceeds the binding capacity of haptoglobin (haptoglobin depletion), allowing free hemoglobin dimers to be filtered. This distinction is critical in hematology and nephrology for differentiating between various hemolytic anemias and mechanical trauma to red cells

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation presents to you with complaints of feeling light-headedness and dizziness when she lies on her back and feels relieved if she lies on her side or when walks. What is the most likely reason behind this?
options: Excessive venous pooling at the feet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IVC compression

This condition is known as Supine Hypotensive Syndrome. In late pregnancy, the enlarged uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the woman lies on her back.

Gravid uterus compresses IVC

↓

Reduced venous return to heart

↓

Decreased cardiac output

↓

Maternal hypotension

↓

Dizziness and light-headedness

Common features include:

| Symptom | Reason

| ------- | ------

| Dizziness | Reduced cerebral perfusion

| Nausea | Hypotension

| Pallor | Decreased cardiac output

| Tachycardia | Compensatory response

It may also reduce uteroplacental blood flow.

Best management:

• Left lateral position

This shifts the uterus away from the vena cava.

Supine position → IVC compression

Left lateral position → venous return restored
questions.learning: IVC compression — This condition is known as Supine Hypotensive Syndrome. In late pregnancy, the enlarged uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the woman lies on her back.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Halothane causes a fall in blood pressure: 1. There is a 20–30 mmHg decrease in blood pressure commonly. 2. The early fall in blood pressure becomes parallel to the depth of anaesthesia. 3. Cardiac output decreases with deepening of anaesthesia. 4. Baroreceptors are triggered due to a fall in blood pressure. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

Halothane produces dose-dependent cardiovascular depression, leading to a 20–30 mmHg fall in arterial blood pressure, primarily due to reduced myocardial contractility and cardiac output. Unlike many other inhalational anesthetics, halothane blunts the baroreceptor reflex, so reflex tachycardia does not occur despite hypotension.

Why is A correct?

• 1. There is a 20–30 mmHg decrease in blood pressure commonly: 20–30 mmHg decrease in blood pressure commonly occurs ✓
• 2. The early fall in blood pressure becomes parallel to the depth of anaesthesia: The fall in blood pressure increases with the depth of anesthesia ✓
• 3. Cardiac output decreases with deepening of anaesthesia: Cardiac output decreases as anesthesia deepens ✓
• 4. Baroreceptors are triggered due to a fall in blood pressure: Baroreceptors are triggered due to a fall in blood pressure ✗. False – Halothane depresses the baroreceptor reflex, preventing the expected compensatory tachycardia.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 Halothane produces dose-dependent cardiovascular depression, leading to a 20–30 mmHg fall in arterial blood pressure, primarily due to reduced myocardial contractility and cardiac output.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with blackish discoloration of the nasal cavity and posterior buccal mucosa and has a history of prolonged high-dose steroid use. What is the most appropriate drug for treating this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of black necrotic tissue in the nasal and oral cavities of an immunosuppressed patient (high-dose steroid user) is highly diagnostic of invasive mucormycosis. This is a surgical and medical emergency. The standard first-line antifungal agent for mucormycosis is systemic Amphotericin B (preferably in its lipid formulation). Amphotericin B is a potent broad-spectrum fungicidal drug that remains the only agent with reliable efficacy against the Mucorales fungi. Fluconazole (Option A) and Itraconazole (Option C) are not effective against these aggressive fungi and should never be used as primary therapy for this condition. Griseofulvin (Option D) is only used for superficial skin infections (dermatophytes). Management must include both immediate administration of Amphotericin B and urgent surgical debridement of the necrotic tissue to prevent intracranial extension
questions.learning: The presence of black necrotic tissue in the nasal and oral cavities of an immunosuppressed patient (high-dose steroid user) is highly diagnostic of invasive mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient, 10 years post-mastectomy, presents with multiple confluent, hemorrhagic, necrotic, elevated purple-black papules on the right upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This presentation describes Stewart-Treves Syndrome, which is the development of Lymphangiosarcoma in a limb affected by chronic, long-standing lymphedema. It classically occurs in women approximately 10 years after a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. The lesion characteristically appears as confluent, purple-black, hemorrhagic nodules that may undergo necrosis. While cutaneous metastasis (Option A) can occur after breast cancer, it usually presents as firm, flesh-colored nodules rather than the distinct vascular-necrotic appearance of an angiosarcoma. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option C) arises from the epidermis and lacks this specific hemorrhagic/vascular profile. Kaposi sarcoma (Option D) is an opportunistic malignancy associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in different clinical contexts (e.g., HIV/AIDS). Lymphangiosarcoma is highly aggressive with an extremely poor prognosis due to rapid hematogenous spread. Treatment often involves radical amputation, though survival rates remain low. The primary prevention strategy is the aggressive management of post-mastectomy lymphedema through compression garments and physical therapy to reduce the chronic stimulus for malignant transformation
questions.learning: This presentation describes Stewart-Treves Syndrome, which is the development of Lymphangiosarcoma in a limb affected by chronic, long-standing lymphedema.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the complication associated with IV bolus oxytocin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypotension

An IV bolus of oxytocin can lead to hypotension. Thus, they are administered as dilute solutions at a controlled rate.

Oxytocin acts via G protein-coupled coupled receptors and the phosphoinositide-calcium second messenger system which contracts the uterine smooth muscle. It also acts via the release of prostaglandins and leukotrienes which augment the action of uterine contraction.

Oxytocin at smaller doses increases both the frequency and the force of contraction while at higher doses it produces sustained contractions. Other effects include contraction of myoepithelial cells leading to the ejection of milk and weak antidiuretic and pressor activity due to activation of vasopressin receptors.

Excess activation of vasopressin receptors can lead to water intoxication and hyponatremia. They also have a vasodilating property, particularly at high doses which can provoke hypotension.

Contraindications to oxytocin use include fetal distress, fetal malpresentation, placental abruption, and previous extensive uterine surgery.
questions.learning: Hypotension — An IV bolus of oxytocin can lead to hypotension. Thus, they are administered as dilute solutions at a controlled rate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman is being assessed for induction of labor. On vaginal examination: Cervical dilation: 2 cm, Effacement: 20%, Cervical consistency: Soft, Position: Midline, Station: –2. What is the modified Bishop Score?
questions.explanation: The modified Bishop score is calculated based on five cervical parameters to assess the readiness for induction: Cervical dilation (2 cm): 1 point. Effacement (20%): 1 point (Note: 0–30% is typically assigned 0 or 1 depending on the specific scale used in the source). Consistency (Soft): 2 points. Position (Midline): 1 point. Station (–2): 0 points. Summing these gives a total score of 5. A Bishop score of ≤5 indicates an unfavorable cervix, meaning cervical ripening agents (like prostaglandins) are generally required before initiating oxytocin induction. Scores ≥8 are considered favorable for successful induction. Options A, C, and D are incorrect as they do not match the mathematical sum of the clinical findings provided. Therefore, this patient has an unfavorable cervix for immediate induction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient is planned for cholecystectomy. Which of the following is not an advantage of laparoscopic surgery?
options: Earlier return to normal physiological function
Longer duration of stay in hospital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Longer duration of stay in hospital

Longer duration of stay in the hospital is not an advantage of laparoscopic surgeries.

Laparoscopic surgeries are performed by introducing a rigid laparoscope through a port into the peritoneal cavity. Carbon dioxide is insufflated into the abdominal cavity to create a pneumoperitoneum. The other laparoscopic instruments used for dissection are introduced via other surgically created ports.

Evidence shows that laparoscopic surgery has short-term benefits over open surgery. Laparoscopic surgery has a better outcome with regard to blood loss, postoperative pain, length of stay, better cosmetic appearance, fewer adhesions, better anatomical perception, and earlier recovery.

The disadvantage of laparoscopic over open surgery is not knowing the extent of the thermal burns due to the relative lack of visibility of the entire instrument.
questions.learning: Longer duration of stay in hospital Longer duration of stay in the hospital is not an advantage of laparoscopic surgeries. Laparoscopic surgeries are performed by introducing a rigid laparoscope through a port into the peritoneal cavity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with lytic lesions on the skull is suspected of a diagnosis of Langerhan cell histiocytosis. Which of the following is a characteristic finding on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Birbeck granules

The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance. It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy.

The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH.

Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules are seen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a and langerin (CD207) markers.

The image below shows histopathological image of Langerhan cells with folded nuclei.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system.

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

• Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease)
• Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)- The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad.
• Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH.
questions.learning: Birbeck granules — The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are features of a major surgical site infection (SSI), except:
options: Excessive pain at the surgical site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Excessive pain at the surgical site

A major surgical site infection (SSI) is suggested by features indicating significant local infection and/or systemic involvement.

• (a) Significant amount of pus — Correct: A large amount of purulent discharge strongly suggests a significant SSI.
• (b) Delayed return home — Correct: Major SSI can prolong hospitalization and delay discharge.
• (c) Excessive pain at the surgical site — Incorrect / Not a defining criterion: Pain can occur with SSI, but excessive pain alone is not a characteristic criterion used to define a major SSI.
• (d) Patient being systemically ill — Correct: Fever, tachycardia, malaise, or other systemic features suggest a significant/major SSI.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Malar telangiectasia is classically associated with diseases such as scleroderma. Such an association of malar telangiectasia can also be seen with which of the following cardiac lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic mitral stenosis

Malar telangiectasia (malar flush) is a characteristic facial finding seen in chronic severe mitral stenosis due to long-standing pulmonary hypertension, reduced cardiac output, and peripheral vasodilatation. Although telangiectasia is classically associated with connective tissue disorders such as systemic sclerosis, a similar malar flush is a well-recognized clinical sign of advanced mitral stenosis.

• Chronic mitral stenosis causes:

• Low cardiac output
• Pulmonary hypertension
• Peripheral vasodilatation

• This produces the characteristic pinkish-purple malar flush (“mitral facies”) over the cheeks.

Why not the other options?

• B. Aortic regurgitation: Characterized by bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, Corrigan pulse, Quincke’s sign, etc., not malar flush.
• C. Constrictive pericarditis: Presents with raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, and pericardial knock, not malar telangiectasia.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Causes features of heart failure without the characteristic mitral facies.
questions.learning: Chronic mitral stenosis Malar telangiectasia (malar flush) is a characteristic facial finding seen in chronic severe mitral stenosis due to long-standing pulmonary hypertension, reduced cardiac output, and peripheral vasodilatation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The HIV sentinel surveillance includes all of the following populations except ______________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. STD clinic attendees

Sentinel surveillance of HIV is usually not done for STD clinic attendees.

Sentinel surveillance is used to augment the notification systems used in the surveillance of diseases.

Till 2012-13, STD sites were also included in the HIV sentinel surveillance but from 2014-15, these sites were entirely discontinued, since the STD data had significant biases.

The study population for HIV sentinel surveillance includes:

• Female sex worker: Women who are engaged in consensual sex for money or payment in kind, as a means of livelihood in the last six months
• Men who had anal or oral sex with a male partner in the last month.
• Injection drug users: Men and women who use addictive substances or drugs for recreational or non-medical reasons, through injections, at least once in the last three months.
• Hijra/Transgender: Person whose identity does not conform unambiguously to conventional notions of male or female gender roles, but combines or moves between these.
• Single male migrants: Single male, living at a place other than the place of usual residence without his spouse or family, for the purposes of work and visiting his home town at least once a year.
• Long-distance truckers: Truckers who travel more than 800 km one way between source and destination.
• A pregnant woman of age 15-49 years and attending the antenatal clinic for the first time.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with pruritic, hypopigmented macules and confluent patches on the chest. Skin scraping and KOH preparation show numerous yeast-like cells with short branching filaments, described as having a “spaghetti and meatballs” appearance. Which microorganism is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of hypopigmented macules on the chest (Pityriasis versicolor) and the pathognomonic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on a KOH mount are diagnostic for Malassezia furfur. The "spaghetti" refers to the short, thick hyphae, and the "meatballs" refer to the clusters of round yeast cells. Trichophyton (Option B) causes dermatophytosis (ringworm) and would show long, branching septate hyphae. Candida (Option D) typically shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast on microscopy. Chlamydospores (Option C) are thick-walled resting spores seen in certain fungi but are not a causative agent. Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast that is part of the normal skin flora but overgrows in hot, humid conditions. Therefore, the unique visual pattern described and pictured definitively identifies Malassezia as the causative organism
questions.learning: The clinical description of hypopigmented macules on the chest (Pityriasis versicolor) and the pathognomonic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on a KOH mount are diagnostic for Malassezia furfur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents to the outpatient department with clinical features as shown in the given image. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a child with generalized edema (anasarca), particularly noticeable in the face and limbs. This clinical presentation is characteristic of "Kwashiorkor," a form of severe protein-energy malnutrition. The edema results from severe hypoalbuminemia, which reduces plasma oncotic pressure. Other classic signs include a "moon face," "flaky paint" dermatosis, and sparse, reddish hair. "Marasmus" (Option B) is characterized by severe muscle wasting and a "skin and bones" appearance without edema. While Nephrotic syndrome (Option C) also presents with generalized edema and hypoalbuminemia, Kwashiorkor is far more common in pediatric populations in specific social contexts and is usually accompanied by growth failure and dietary history. Nephritic syndrome (Option D) presents with hematuria, hypertension, and more localized (periorbital) edema. Management of Kwashiorkor requires careful nutritional rehabilitation to avoid refeeding syndrome

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with complaints of hematuria and recurrent urinary tract infection. You notice the following finding in his CECT. What is the likely condition indicated by the arrow in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given image shows a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation.

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys. Horseshoe kidneys are a type of renal fusion anomaly. They are formed when the lower poles of the two kidneys fuse during organogenesis to form an isthmus. They are typically low-lying as the inferior mesenteric artery interferes with its ascent due to its size and the presence of an isthmus.

It presents as a fixed, nonmobile, firm mass in the midline at the level of the 4th lumbar vertebra and is resonant on percussion. It is associated with an increased risk of infection, stone formation, hydronephrosis, and tuberculosis.

It has a 2:1 male preponderance. Individuals with horseshoe kidneys are prone to reflux, obstruction, and stone formation.

Other options:

Option A: The image of polycystic kidney disease on CT abdomen is shown below: Multiple bilateral cysts are seen.

Option C: Hydronephrosis is aseptic dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system due to partial or intermittent obstruction to urinary outflow.

Option D: Pancake kidney (also known as discoid kidney, disc kidney, lump kidney, fused pelvic kidney, or cake kidney) is a rare renal fusion anomaly where both the upper and lower poles of the kidney are fused giving it an appearance of a pancake. questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old child has hoarseness, weak cry with examination findings shown below. Which infection is it associated with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HPV 16 and 18

• Juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is usually caused by HPV 6 and 11.
• HPV 11 is associated with more aggressive disease.
• Rare malignant transformation is linked to high-risk HPV types 16 and 18.
• Patients present with hoarseness and airway obstruction.
• Diagnosis is by laryngoscopy.
• Treatment is repeated surgical debulking.
• Adjuvant therapies include cidofovir and bevacizumab.
• HPV vaccination reduces disease burden.
• Tracheostomy is avoided unless absolutely necessary.
• HPV 6/11 → papillomas; HPV 16/18 → malignancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is being evaluated for endocrine disorders. It is noted that some hormones are stored in secretory granules before release, while others are synthesized on demand and not stored. Which of the following hormones is not stored before secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cortisol

• Hormones differ in their storage and release mechanisms based on their chemical nature.
• Peptide and protein hormones (e.g., insulin, growth hormone):

• Synthesized in advance
• Stored in secretory granules
• Released by exocytosis on demand

• Thyroid hormones (T3/T4):

• Unique among amines
• Stored extracellularly in the colloid (thyroglobulin) of the thyroid gland
• Released after proteolysis

• Steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol):

• NOT stored
• Synthesized on demand from cholesterol
• Rapidly diffuse out of cells after synthesis

Why not other options:

• A. Insulin: Stored in pancreatic β-cell granules
• B. Thyroxine (T4): Stored in colloid (thyroglobulin-bound form)
• C. Growth hormone: Stored in anterior pituitary granules

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man suffered damage to his right knee's lateral side. He complains of having trouble walking two days later because his toes continue to drag on the floor. Additionally, he observes numbness over the dorsum of the foot and upper lateral aspect of the leg. What is the most likely injured nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Common peroneal nerve

The clinical scenario, combined with a high-stepping gait (foot drop), indicates common peroneal nerve injury. This is associated with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the first interdigital space.

The nerves supplying the marked areas are shown below.

The common peroneal nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

The first interdigital space is supplied by the deep fibular nerve, while the dorsum of the foot (except the lateral and medial borders) is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus Brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital webspace

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient reports dysphagia that is more severe for liquids than for solids. Which characteristic radiological sign is most likely to be observed in this condition?
options: Apple-core lesion AAns (A) Rat-tail sign Dysphagia that is worse for liquids than solids is a classic clinical indicator of a motility disorder, most commonly achalasia cardia. In achalasia, the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) fails to relax, leading to esophageal dilation and a characteristic smooth, tapered narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. On a barium swallow radiograph, this tapering is known as the "Rat-tail sign" or "Bird's beak sign". Regarding the distractors, a filling defect (Option B) is a non-specific term for space-occupying lesions like polyps or tumors. A "corkscrew esophagus" (Option C) is seen in diffuse esophageal spasm, which usually presents with chest pain and intermittent dysphagia. An "apple-core lesion" (Option D) is characteristic of annular constricting carcinomas, typically found in the colon rather than the esophagus. Therefore, the rat-tail sign is the definitive radiological hallmark of achalasia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30 year old male patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the image of the swelling and the X-ray film. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoclastoma

The clinical presentation and the X-ray showing an eccentric expansile lesion with a soap bubble appearance are suggestive of osteoclastoma or giant cell tumor (GCT).

Osteoclastoma usually affects young adults in the age group of 20-40 years. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Radiographic findings in GCT:

* A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Eccentric location, most often subchondral

* Expansion of the overlying cortex

* Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called soap bubble appearance

* No calcification within the tumor

* No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.

Treatment :

* Extended curettage and bone grafting.

* En-bloc wide resection and reconstruction are done for advanced stages, local recurrence, and tumors not responding to other methods.

* Resection without reconstruction is done for lesions in expandable bones like distal ulna, clavicle, etc.

* Irradiation and/or embolization are used for inoperable lesions in the spine and pelvis.

* Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.

* Denosumab is approved for use in unresectable tumors in skeletally mature patients.

Other options:

Ewing's sarcoma:

It is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Osteosarcoma:

It is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on X-ray.

Osteochondroma:

Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the condition in the image?
questions.explanation: The image is a Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU), the gold standard for evaluating the anterior urethra. It shows a clear, focal area of narrowing (stricture) in the bulbar segment. Urethral strictures in the bulbar region are commonly caused by "straddle" injuries or instrumentation. A membranous urethral injury (Option B) or tear (Option C) is usually associated with pelvic fractures and would show extravasation of contrast rather than a clean narrowing. Benign Prostate Hyperplasia (Option D) affects the prostatic urethra (much more proximal) and would show an elongated, narrowed segment or a "J-shaped" ureter on IVP, rather than a focal anterior stricture. Patients with bulbar strictures typically present with a poor urinary stream, straining, and incomplete emptying. Treatment options include urethral dilation, internal urethrotomy, or definitive urethroplasty. Identifying the exact location and length of the stricture on RGU is essential for planning the correct surgical approach

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of hysterectomy presents with vaginal bleeding. Speculum and vaginal examination reveal no obvious abnormality. What is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vaginal cuff (vault) granulation tissue

Vaginal cuff (vault) granulation tissue is the most common cause of vaginal bleeding after hysterectomy, particularly within months after surgery, although it can present later. It results from excessive granulation tissue at the vaginal vault closure.

• Presentation: Spotting or postcoital bleeding after hysterectomy.
• Examination: Small, friable, red granulation tissue at the vaginal cuff (may require careful speculum examination).
• Treatment: Chemical cauterization with silver nitrate or excision if persistent.

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect?

• A. Cervical ectropion: Impossible after total hysterectomy because the cervix has been removed.
• B. Cervical polyp: Cannot occur after total hysterectomy.
• C. Endometrial carcinoma: Cannot arise if the uterus has been removed (except in supracervical hysterectomy, where only the cervix remains).
questions.learning: Vaginal cuff (vault) granulation tissue Vaginal cuff (vault) granulation tissue is the most common cause of vaginal bleeding after hysterectomy, particularly within months after surgery, although it can present later.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Takayasu arteritis most commonly involves:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Arch of aorta

Takayasu arteritis most commonly involves the arch of aorta and its branches. It is also known as the aortic arch syndrome.

Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries. It causes irregular thickening of the vessel wall with intimal hyperplasia leading to narrowing of the lumen and organ ischemia.

It may have various clinical presentations depending on the vessel involved:

* Arch of aorta and its branches:

* Subclavian artery- leads to weak pulses in the upper extremities. Hence it is also known as pulseless disease.

* Carotid arteries- leads to weak pulses, blindness, neurological deficits

* Distal aorta- leads to claudication of the legs

* Pulmonary artery- leads to pulmonary hypertension

* Coronary arteries- leads to myocardial infarction

* Renal arteries- leads to systemic hypertension
questions.learning: Arch of aorta Takayasu arteritis most commonly involves the arch of aorta and its branches. It is also known as the aortic arch syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the Total Fertility Rate in India at present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.0

According to the Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report 2020, the Total Fertility Rate at present is 2.0.

India's Total Fertility Rate (TFR) declined from 2.1 in 2019 to 2.0 in 2020. In 2020, Bihar recorded the highest TFR at 3.0, while Delhi, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal reported the lowest at 1.4.

Over the decades, the TFR has shown a significant downward trend, dropping from 5.2 to 4.5 between 1971 and 1981, and from 3.6 to 2.0 between 1991 and 2020.

The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is expressed as the "average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if she were to experience the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her reproductive years (typically ages 15-49).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is used for wound infection grading?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Southampton grading

Southampton wound grading system is used to score the severity of wound site infection.

Southampton wound grading system:

• Grade 0 - Normal healing
• Grade I - Normal healing with different grades of erythema
• Grade II - Erythema with other signs of inflammation at different parts of the wound.
• Grade III - Clear or serosanguinous discharge at different sites
• Grade IV - Pus discharge

Other options:

Option A: American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA)  grading is used in pre-anesthetic checkups to assess a patient's physical health and fitness for anesthesia and surgery.

Option B: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) is a set of clinical criteria used to identify and monitor critically ill patients with high-grade burns, severe trauma, and other major surgeries.

Option D: Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II)  is a scoring system used to assess the severity and predict the outcome of pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the best diagnostic test for evaluating endometrial pathology?
questions.explanation: Hysteroscopy-guided endometrial biopsy is considered the gold standard for evaluating endometrial pathology because it allows for direct visualization of the uterine cavity. This enables the clinician to identify and perform targeted sampling of suspicious areas, such as polyps, submucosal fibroids, or localized carcinomas, which significantly increases diagnostic accuracy. Pipelle biopsy (Option A) is a minimally invasive office procedure that is effective for detecting diffuse disease but can easily miss focal lesions. Dilatation and curettage (Option C) is a "blind" procedure that has a higher risk of sampling error for localized pathologies. Transvaginal sonography (Option D) is an excellent non-invasive screening tool to measure endometrial thickness but cannot provide a definitive histological diagnosis. Therefore, the ability to "see and sample" makes hysteroscopy-guided biopsy the superior diagnostic choice for suspected uterine abnormalities
questions.learning: Hysteroscopy-guided endometrial biopsy is considered the gold standard for evaluating endometrial pathology because it allows for direct visualization of the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Patient underwent cholecystectomy and black pigmented gallstones were noticed. Which of the following is the least likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HbD Punjab

Pigmented gallstones are commonly found in chronic hemolytic syndromes such as sickle cell disease, HbH disease, and beta thalassemia minor, but not in HbD Punjab.

Hemoglobin D-Punjab (HbD Punjab), also known as Hemoglobin D-Los Angeles, is one of the most common hemoglobin variants worldwide. It is derived from a point mutation in the beta-globin gene. It is a normal variant and rarely presents as any clinical symptoms. Moreover, this variant can exist in association with other hemoglobinopathies such as thalassemias and sickle cell disease, which can lead to hemolysis. However, just a mere presence of HbD Punjab without associated hemoglobinopathies won't cause hemolysis or pigmented gallstones.

Any type of hemolytic anemia is a risk factor for the development of pigment gallstones.

There are two main types of gallstones:

* Cholesterol stones—which consist of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate

* Pigment stones—made of bilirubin calcium salts

Other Options:

Option A: In sickle cell anemia, HbS is present in which valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta chain. This results in a change in the shape of the RBCs from biconcave to sickle-shaped. This can cause an increase in hemolysis and an increase in pigmented gallstones.

Option B: In HbH disease, excess β-globin chains form β4 tetramers. They are seen in older children with α-thalassemia. This may lead to pigmented gallstones due to hemolysis.

Option C: β-Thalassemia minor arises due to the deficient synthesis of β-chains. Normal adult RBCs have HbA, along with HbA2 and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) in small amounts. There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in β-thalassemia. This can also cause an increase in hemolysis and an increase in pigmented gallstones.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An elderly female with a central line undergoes surgery. On postoperative day 3, she develops fever and tachycardia. A culture from the tip of the central line revealed brown buff colonies. Microscopy showed gram-positive organisms that reproduce by budding. What is the likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Candida

The given clinical scenario along with microscopy showing gram-positive budding yeasts cells and brown buff colonies is suggestive of invasive candidiasis.

Candida species are yeast-like fungi that can cause bloodstream infections, particularly in patients with central lines or other invasive devices. It is a common cause of central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI) and frequently presents with fever and signs of systemic infection..

The most common species implicated in candidal infections are C. albicans, C. parapsilosis, and C. glabrata. Clinically, infection with candida can present as cutaneous & mucosal candidiasis, systemic candidiasis, or rarely, as chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

Cutaneous and mucosal infections manifest as thrush affecting the tongue, lips, gums, and palate. It is seen as a patchy to confluent whitish pseudomembranous lesion and is commonly associated with AIDS. Candida may also invade the vaginal mucosa leading to vulvovaginitis, and the nails, and around the nail plate leading to onychomycosis.

Morphologically, they are yeast-like fungi. They exist as yeast and pseudohyphae (Shown in the image below). It appears as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Candida albicans form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

When colonies of Candida albicans are inoculated in serum, the yeast cells start to form elongations called germ tubes within 2 hours, when kept at 37 °C. The image below shows germ tube formation, also known as the Reynolds Braude phenomenon, seen in Candida albicans.

Other options:

Option A: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a gram-positive cocci that commonly colonizes the skin and can cause infections related to indwelling devices, such as central lines. However, it does not reproduce by budding, and the description of brown buff colonies does not fit.

Option B: Streptococcus species are gram-positive cocci that are typically found in chains. They do not reproduce by budding, and the brown buff colonies seen in the culture do not align with the typical appearance of Streptococcus in culture.

Option D: Aspergillus is a mold that forms septate hyphae, not yeast-like cells, and does not reproduce by budding. Additionally, Aspergillus forms colonies with a different characteristic appearance, usually described as greenish or fuzzy, rather than brown buff.
questions.learning: Candida — The given clinical scenario along with microscopy showing gram-positive budding yeasts cells and brown buff colonies is suggestive of invasive candidiasis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient presents with distant visual acuity of 6/18, which improved on pin-hole testing. On ocular examination findings as shown in image were seen. Patient has which of the following refractory error.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Index Myopia

Index myopia is caused by an increase in the refractive index of the lens, most commonly due to nuclear sclerosis (early cataract).

• Elderly patient with decreased distance vision (6/18)
• Improves with pinhole → refractive error
• Improved near vision (“second sight”) → hallmark of nuclear cataract
• Slit lamp: nuclear sclerosis

Pathophysiology:

• Increased lens density → ↑ refractive index
• Light bends more → image shifts in front of retina → myopia

Why not others:

• Axial myopia: Due to increased eyeball length
• Curvatural myopia: Due to increased curvature (cornea/lens)
• Positional myopia: Due to forward displacement of lens

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An 11-year-old girl was found to be quiet and shy in her classroom with intermittent crying, for the past few days. It was discovered that her uncle was touching her genitalia inappropriately. The duty of the principal is to report this to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Police

The principal has to report this case to the police.

The POCSO Act, 2012 is a comprehensive law for the protection of children from the offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography. This is done while safeguarding the interests of the child at every stage of the judicial process by incorporating child-friendly mechanisms for reporting, recording of evidence, investigation, and speedy trial of the offence through designated special courts.

Section 21(1) of the POCSO Act, 2012 requires mandatory reporting of cases of child sexual abuse to the law enforcement authorities and applies to everyone including parents, doctors, and school personnel. Failure to report a suspicion of child abuse is an offence under the Act.
questions.learning: Police — The principal has to report this case to the police. The POCSO Act, 2012 is a comprehensive law for the protection of children from the offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who recently underwent surgery has complaints of nausea and vomiting. He was prescribed a drug called aprepitant. What is its mechanism of action?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NK-1 antagonist

The class of drugs most preferred in patients suffering from postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), following surgery are the NK1 antagonists like aprepitant.

Substance P is a neuropeptide that interacts with neurokinin-1 (NK-1) receptors. NK1 antagonists inhibit substance P at central and peripheral receptors. Aprepitant, fosaprepitant are examples of NK1 antagonists. It also acts on the chemotrigger zone whose location is shown below.

PONV Physiology: Afferents from the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ), vagal neurons in the gastrointestinal system, neurons from the vestibular system and midbrain afferents relay within the vomiting centre in the reticular formation of the brainstem which then project into the nucleus tractus solitarius.

Risk factors for PONV are divided into:

• Patient factors

• Female>male
• Age<50 years
• Prior history of motion sickness
• Non-smokers > smokers (CTZ is desensitized)

• Preoperative factors

• (Fasting and anxiety, while possibly contributing to PONV, have yet to be demonstrated)

• Intraoperative factors

• Surgical - Cholecystectomy, gynaecological and laparoscopic procedures have higher incidences
• Drugs - Nitrous oxide, Opioids, Cyclopropane,
• General anaesthesia has a times more risk of developing PONV than regional anaesthesia.

• Postoperative factors

• Pain and early ambulation contribute to a higher risk of PONV.

Scoring systems used to grade PONV are the Apfel score and the Koivuranta score.

Drugs used in the prophylaxis and treatment of PONV:

• 5-HT 3 antagonists - ondansetron, palonosetron
• Butyrophenones- droperidol
• Dexamethasone
• Transdermal scopolamine
• Aprepitant

Note: Double-blind studies have found no difference in the efficacy between aprepitant(NK1 antagonists) and ondansetron (5HT3 antagonist) in the first 24 hours following surgery. But after 24 hours aprepitant has proven to be more productive than ondansetron in the management of PONV.
questions.learning: NK-1 antagonist — The class of drugs most preferred in patients suffering from postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), following surgery are the NK1 antagonists like aprepitant.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a symptom of severe dehydration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thirsty child

A thirsty child signifies some dehydration, not severe dehydration.

Clinical features of severe dehydration in a child include:

• Drowsy, lethargic, or unconscious, with deeply sunken eyes and absent tears
• Sunken fontanelle
• Drinks poorly or not able to drink
• Deep breathing
• Skin pinch goes back very slowly (recoil in >2 seconds)
• Tachycardia, with bradycardia in most severe cases
• Weak, thready, or impalpable pulse
• Prolonged capillary refill
• Cold, mottled, and cyanotic extremities
• Minimal urine output

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following types of amyloid protein is typically seen in a patient who develops amyloidosis secondary to long-standing chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. AA

Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis results from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, chronic osteomyelitis, inflammatory bowel disease). Persistent inflammation increases hepatic production of Serum Amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant, which is cleaved and deposited as AA amyloid in tissues.

• AA amyloid is derived from Serum Amyloid A (SAA) and is the characteristic amyloid protein in secondary amyloidosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. β2-Microglobulin: Associated with long-term hemodialysis-related amyloidosis.
• C. AL: Derived from immunoglobulin light chains; seen in primary amyloidosis and multiple myeloma.
• D. Transthyretin (ATTR): Seen in senile systemic amyloidosis and familial amyloid polyneuropathy/cardiomyopathy.

| Amyloid Protein | Associated Disease

| --------------- | ------------------

| AA | Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis due to chronic inflammation

| AL | Primary amyloidosis, Multiple myeloma

| Aβ | Alzheimer disease

| β2-Microglobulin | Hemodialysis-associated amyloidosis

| ATTR (Transthyretin) | Senile systemic and hereditary amyloidosis
questions.learning: AA Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis results from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, chronic osteomyelitis, inflammatory bowel disease).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are the changes seen in irreversible cell injury?
questions.explanation: Cell injury is categorized as reversible or irreversible based on whether the cell can recover if the stress is removed. The appearance of large, flocculent amorphous densities within the mitochondrial matrix is a hallmark sign of irreversible injury, indicating the "point of no return". This finding reflects permanent mitochondrial membrane damage and loss of ATP production. Regarding the distractors, cellular swelling (Option D) and bleb formation (Option A) are early, reversible changes caused by the failure of energy-dependent ion pumps. Clumping of nuclear chromatin (Option C) is also a reversible finding associated with decreased intracellular pH. True irreversibility is defined by profound membrane dysfunction (mitochondrial, plasma, and lysosomal) and severe nuclear changes like pyknosis or karyolysis. Thus, amorphous mitochondrial densities are the specific structural indicators that the cell is destined for death

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in "green"?
questions.explanation: The image shows an anatomical illustration of the larynx/throat from anterior view, with the green structure marked at the entrance of the larynx — classic position of the epiglottis, a leaf-shaped cartilaginous flap that guards the laryngeal inlet. Key Anatomical Features: 1. Leaf/spoon-shaped structure at laryngeal inlet 2. Located posterior to tongue base 3. Guards the laryngeal opening during swallowing 4. Attached to thyroid cartilage anteriorly via thyroepiglottic ligament Why other options are wrong: (B) Hyoid bone is incorrect because hyoid bone is a U-shaped bone located superior to the thyroid cartilage : it would appear higher up in the neck and has a distinctly different horseshoe shape. (C) Thyroid cartilage is incorrect because thyroid cartilage forms the anterior shield-shaped prominence of the larynx (Adam's apple) : it is a large bilateral plate structure, not the rounded leaf-shaped structure marked green here. (D) Cricoid cartilage is incorrect because cricoid cartilage is a complete ring-shaped cartilage located inferior to thyroid cartilage : it lies lower in the larynx, not at the laryngeal inlet where the green structure is marked

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following in respect of Ormeloxifene: 1. It is a research product of Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow. 2. It is a steroidal compound. 3. It is a potent antiestrogen with weak estrogenic properties. 4. It does not inhibit ovulation. Which of the above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Ormeloxifene (Centchroman/Chhaya) is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) and a non-steroidal oral contraceptive developed in India. It is included in the National Family Planning Programme under the brand name Chhaya.

• 1. It is a research product of Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI)\, Lucknow. ✅

• Ormeloxifene was developed by the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow.

• 3. It is a potent antiestrogen with weak estrogenic properties. ✅

• It acts as an antiestrogen on the uterus and has weak estrogenic effects on bone and other tissues.

• 4. It does not inhibit ovulation. ✅

• Its primary contraceptive action is preventing implantation by altering endometrial receptivity and accelerating ovum transport.
• Ovulation is usually not inhibited.

Incorrect statement:

• 2. It is a steroidal compound. ❌

• Ormeloxifene is a non-steroidal SERM.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Ormeloxifene (Centchroman/Chhaya) is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) and a non-steroidal oral contraceptive developed in India.
